Question: How do you think Wednesday Addams has changed since the original Addams Family movie and TV shows?
Answer: The main change is that Wednesday became the breakout star of the franchise, which has some knock on effects on the rest of the franchise. If you watch the original TV show, Gomez and Morticia are the main characters and Wednesday usually just shows up for a couple of quick lines. And since then every iteration has beefed up her role until now it is literally the Wednesday show. I blame Christina Ricci! The original Addams Family TV show was of the genre of kooky family sitcom, and like most family sitcoms, the focus was on the parents. Child actors have lots of limitations. The Addams Family movie featured a much more rounded distribution. Gomez and Morticia were still the stars, but Fester and Wednesday got a lot more to do, comparatively. But Christina Ricci was magical casting. She absolutely destroyed her part. It was a once in a lifetime performance by a child actor. Wednesday was the breakout character of those films. And so in the sequel, Addams Family Values, Wednesday’s role was expanded to essentially anchoring half the movie. And the kids that grew up with those films, grew up idolizing Wednesday. She became one of the principle drivers of the Hot Topic generation, and this is hopefully the last time I will ever say “Hot Topic generation.” Every Addams Family project has to give priority to Wednesday now. She can not simply be one of the family. She’s the star. Which means introducing a weird tension in the family that never used to be there. In the 2019 animated Addams Family movie, much of the drama of the movie rests on the conflict between Wednesday and her parents. Which is not something that really exists in the classic Addams Family material. Wednesday taking up more and more and more space in the franchise reached its apotheosis with Netflix’s Wednesday where… the entire rest of the family is written out, except for Thing. It is now possible to do the Addams Family without the Addams Family. She is the only character now. That’s the main change that has happened to Wednesday over the years. She has moved from being one member of an ensomble cast to being the undisputed and only star.

This is more of the less the background of Deep Space Nine. Question: How does "Alien: Romulus" deepen the mythology of the "Alien" franchise?

Prometheus and Alien: Covenant did a lot of things, but one thing they definitely did was deepen the mythology. I maintain that if you pay attention to those films, they make sense. But I think I am in the minority in that opinion. But there were lots of revelations about the nature of the Aliens and the Engineers and Weyland-Yutani in those films. A lot of them. So many. So it takes all that stuff and simplifies it and integrates it. The black goo that was so important in those two films is now much easier to explain. What Weyland-Yutani is after is back to being quite simple after being complicated by the existence of Peter Weyland. Also there are some ideas taken from, of all places, Alien Resurrection but done better and so Romulus retroactively makes that film fit better. It’s been forty-five years, and the Alien sequels have been all over the place, both in terms of quality and in terms of where they took the story. Romulus’s approach is about taking all those films, bringing them back to the basics of the original and integrating them together. I think the film adds less to the lore than it does an amazing job of cleaning up the, at this point, extremely messy lore.

Disney and 20th Century Fox's shared rights over the Marvel brother and sister allows the characters to appear in both an X-Men and Avengers film played by two different sets of actors. Question: Would Denzel as Magneto and Giancarlo as Professor X sell well and fit in the MCU?
Answer: I actually don't like either of them for the role. Magneto has to be a German Jew who went through the Holocaust. He has to have to experienced all of it, from the rise of Hitler to the first laws to the death camps, to the liberation. The central animating principle of Magneto is “never again.” A concept so closely tied to the Holocaust that it has its own Wikipedia page. Magneto, as a character, has to have experienced all this. He has to have seen the signs that lead to the Sentinels and the death camps, and he has to say to them “never again!” full of unending fury. That is who Magneto is and why the character works. The brilliant writer Asher Elbein wrote an excellent essay on the essential Jewish nature of Mangeto: Magneto is one case where the ethnicity of the character is inextricable from the character. He has to be a German Jew. The idea behind casting Denzel Washington as Magneto was from a foolish belief that Magneto couldn't be from World War II (just say he doesn't age, which is what the comics are now doing), so make the character a Civil Rights era Malcolm X type. And while there are a lot of parallels between Nazi Germany and the United States’s treatment of African-Americans (including a funneling of ideas between the two), those parallels don't reach the place the X-Men and Mangeto need them to. Chris Claremont, the most important X-Men writer of all time, is Jewish and worked in Israel with Holocaust survivors. He filled the X-Men with Holocaust imagery. He made the allusions and they are specific to the Holocaust. In fact the whole notion that Professor Xavier was based on MLK and Magneto on Malcolm X was a Scott Lobdell concept, who came after Claremont. Claremont based Magneto on Menachem Begin. If you wanted to make a US specific version of the X-Men, it would be interesting, but it would not be the X-Men that we know. It would not be impersonal machines killing people en mass, it would not be death camps, and it would not be giant “M” tattoos. At least not if you are talking about the Civil Rights era and not the way the US has treated the Native Americans (hmm… thinking about it now, Lily Gladstone would make an interesting Magneto). So, no l, I don't think Denzel Washington should play Magneto. And I think the impulse behind it is strictly from not being willing to just say Magneto hasn't aged since his mutation activated. Giancarlo Esposito should not play Xavier for a much simpler reason. Professor Charles Xavier is possibly the most famous fictional character who requires a wheelchair. If an actor did not want to portray him using a wheelchair, they are the wrong actor. The moment Esposito said, “I don't want to be in a wheelchair” that should have ended any possibility of him playing Xavier.

Question: What impact do you think the shift in focus from established dramas to new and diverse shows will have on the Emmy Awards landscape?
Answer: Of the 75th Primetime Emmy Nominees for Outstanding Drama, only The Crown, Succession, and Better Call Saul had their final seasons. B B, The Last of Us, White Lotus, Andor, and Yellowjackets were all renewed and have seasons upcoming. And yet none of them managed to air in the eligibility window for this year's Emmys. The year before Euphoria, Severance, Squid Game, and Stranger Things all were renewed with upcoming seasons. They all missed not just one, but two Emmy eligibility windows. The 76th Emmys having only one returning drama nominee, The Crown, does not reflect a change in the content of televison or a change in the taste of the Academy. It reflects a structural change in how TV is made. Even as episode counts keep shrinking, production hiatuses keep getting longer. The breaks between seasons keep getting longer and longer. So shows that are Emmy locks keep missing eligibility windows. Instead of, as has been traditional, a fairly stable slate of nominees featuring shows that get nominated year after year, it is an unstable group of nominees which just consists of whoever made a season that year. This is more exciting. And something like Fallout, which would almost certainly get crowded out in previous years, now can scure a nomination. But it also is extremely frustrating because the wait times between seasons are just killing any momentum those shows achieve. I loved Squid Game, but I really am struggling to care about season two because it has just been so long. Same thing with Severence. Some of this is just addiction to celebrity. Casting Pedro Pascal in your zombie show can generate a lot of hype, but filming will have to work around a very busy schedule. Some of this is just structural issues since Covid. A lot of it is just poor management by streaming services. And significantly lower pay given to creative teams, necessitating them not being able to focus on single projects. But the shift from previously established dramas is not because of the Academy becoming disillusioned with those dramas. House of the Dragon is absolutely going to get a nomination next year. It is all about shows missing eligibility windows.

Question: Why are some mutants more lethal than others?

Plague/Pestilence (another of Apocalypse’s horsemen) sheds incredibly deadly viruses. The X-gene is, essentially, purely random with every manifestation just being some untapped potential within humanity. Sometimes those will be cool and amazing abilities that make people’s lives better, like always having good luck, other times it will be… killing people by touching them. As I said earlier, functionally mutants who simply have bad genes act as a metaphor for disability. It isn’t a perfect metaphor, but nothing in the X-Men is ever a perfect metaphor, just a highly adaptable one. Rogue is regularly shown needing special accommodation. Question: What did you think of Beau DeMayo's work as the original showrunner of X-Men '97?
Answer: Steve Shives has described nostalgia-bait reboots and legacy characters as, essentially, jangling keys in front of an audience of adults they consider toddlers. “’member that thing that you loved? Look at the keys! Look at the shiny keys!” What sets X-Men ’97 apart is that it is only interested in what doors those keys unlock, not the keys themselves. X-Men ’97 is better than any of the X-Men movies, better than the original cartoon, and better than all but the absolute best X-Men comics. The sole flaw in the show is that the ten episode season. The, very stupid, decision to make the season that short forces it to act as a runaway train, burning through plot. A long season would have given the plots more time to develop and allow for more characterization for the characters who are underserved. But literally the best problem to have is this incessant desire to have more. The writing is so incredibly smart, and there are so many moments that can be pulled out to demonstrate just how unparalleled the show is. One of the most oft cited examples is that when Storm loses her powers the thing that really shows how cut off she is, is being scared by an unexpected clap of thunder. But I would like to talk about Gambit, and how brilliantly he is written in the season. Gambit is not in the season all that much. But every time he appears he is doing something to get the audience to like him. He is funny or sassy or cute. And there is a lot of interesting aspects to the Rogue-Magneto-Gambit love triangle, but one of the main ones is that it gets the audience to implicitly side with Gambit throughout. And gives him a chance to, instead of being bitter or angry, be a stand up guy. When Gambit dies, it is extremely painful. And not because of what he did in the original cartoon, because of who he is in this cartoon, the one that you are actually watching. And Gambit is almost never shown fighting in the episodes before his death. His powers are irrelevant to the emotions the audience is feeling. There are two dozen mutants with powers similar to Gambit’s. What the show wants you to feel pain for is Gambit the person, not the powerset, dies. It is such smart, economic writing. Magneto says the following at the UN in episode two: Charles Xavier entrusted me with his dream, and it does not ask you to love or embrace my kind as your own, but merely to accept that this is a shared world with a common future, and that my kind, like yours, have the right to live in it. I am trying to be better. Please. Do not make me let you down. And then three episodes later they destroy Genosha. The writing of these episodes is so crisp and clear and portentous. The structure is beyond parallel. This is how you write a show, you set up the dominos with care and precision and then you knock them down. You make the characters matter so we, in the audience, feel their pain and their joy. You don’t coast on nostalgia, begging the audience “’member this? ‘member that?” X-Men ’97 is not interested in being the original X-Men animated series. It wants to push into new territory, be something different. Evolve the characters and setting. There are things in this season way beyond anything that happens in the original series. The entire season is built on the concept that Magneto might be right, and that even a completely good faith attempt to follow Xavier’s dream is doomed to death. While still respecting the original material, it is a radical departure in both tone and story. And it truly does understand the X-Men. This is a franchise about the poisonous nature of bigotry. It’s about civil rights. It understands that the Sentinels are the X-Men’s true archnemesis, not Magneto or Apocalypse. And X-Men ’97 is unafraid to be stridently political. The show opens with the Friends of Humanity, one of the more radical concepts from the original series as they are just a hate group. And, wow, do we get a vast cornucopia of prejudice and oppression in action over the course of the season. We get Sunspot’s mother who is privately “okay” with mutants, but wants to make sure her son isn’t being a little too mutant in public… and then she sends him off with the Sentinels. We get Trish Tilby doing journalism that is “not afraid to ask the hard questions” on mutants which basically consists of harassing a grieving father over his missing child until he snaps back at her. We get everything from microaggressions up to the genocide of Genosha. And, in case you missed the point, we get flashbacks from Magneto to the actual Holocaust. Not a made up version, the actual Auschwitz concentration camp. And there’s an entire episode about the optics of actually helping the people who just survived a genocide! And we get the “Magneto was right” speech, which is one of the most stridently and radical things I have ever seen. X-Men ’97 is unafraid to get dark, to be mature. How, how can you as a human, ever accept crap like the ending of Man of Steel after seeing the destruction of Genosha in X-Men ‘97? It’s so raw, and real, and painful and tragic… How can superhero movies even exist anymore? How can we just accept poorly animated figures punching each other in an empty CGI city? The destruction of Genosha so perfectly captures the feeling of terror and tragedy. So many people die on screen. So many dead bodies. So many of which are real characters who really did matter, even just in that episode. Go back, rewatch it. See how much effort went into filling Genosha with life before the destruction. This is meaningful. When Age of Ultron came out I actually praised it for feeling like it had consequences and stakes to a superhero battle, and a sense of place and sense of loss. Wow, was my bar too low. Every detail of episode five, “Remember It” is designed to make you feel the enormity of the genocide. Make you feel and understand what is being lost. Seeing Pixie and Glob Herman play in a fountain or Exodus, Multiple Man, and Dazzler dance. It is astounding what they achieved in so little time. But it isn’t just death and destruction that demonstrates X-Men ‘97’s maturity. Marvel has never produced anything as sensual as the Magneto/Rogue dance. It’s beautiful. It’s erotic. It’s passionate. The MCU is full of pretty people who are incapable of feeling lust or passion. It’s really not a mystery why people ship Cap with Bucky, given the dead battery that is all his canonical romances. Remember when the MCU tried to get us to think there was something between the Hulk and Black Widow? Just embarrassing. Also it is extremely funny that people thought the sex would be toned down on the show because of one shot of Rogue from behind before it premiered. And the fact is that X-Men ’97 is the first X-Men adaptation since possibly the original cartoon that actually wants to be an adaptation of the X-Men. Not just be Wolverine and some hangers on. Look at the glory moments the show gives Storm and Rogue. Storm and Cyclops get more development in single episodes of this show than in the entire Fox film series. It gives all its characters depth and complexity and pathos. It’s so good! Beau DeMayo was not the only writer on the show. He was working with an extremely talented team of writers and animators. But the work they achieved was extraordinary. Every time I rewatch an episode, I discover brilliant things I didn’t notice before. I hope that that team is talented enough to execute on this level without him. But X-Men ’97 is an unparalleled success. I was fully expecting it to be a mediocre retread with nothing to say for it but nostalgia and fan service, and instead I got one of the most interesting, poignant, mature, complex shows I have ever seen. I literally have to stop myself from saying more because there is so much to praise about this show.

Question: What would you like to see in the second season of X-Men '97?

I don’t want it to overlap with the regular episodes (again, ten episode seasons). There is too much to cover in simply an episode, or even a trilogy. And I do not want to spend an entire season in an alternate universe. But Disney+ loves miniseries, and if there is ever a storyline perfect for the miniseries format, it is “Age of Apocalypse.” Plus we could get regular “Age of Apocalypse” specials between seasons, sort of the way that South Park does regular specials between its seasons for Paramount+.

Question: What is this new obsession with the word unaliving? What is wrong with the far simpler homonym killing?
Answer: The Youtuber Lindsay Ellis recently released a video on Yoko Ono and the Beatles. In that video there is a lengthy digression on Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love. It almost reaches the level of a running joke how much she has to bleep, mute and cover up just to get past YouTube's censors. If you read the description on the video, she has this to say: The amount of editing and censorship I had to do to keep this video from getting age restricted (including even the Birth of Venus gag) was funny at first, then it was frustrating, and then it was just farcical, at points veering into disrespectful once it gets into heavier territory towards the middle of the video (which is why there's an unaliving prevention service at the bottom of the video). It took me almost a week of trial and error to make it inoffensive enough to be seen by people who are not logged into the app. When people use websites like YouTube or TikTok, they aren't the customers, they're the products. Those websites exist to deliver eyeballs to advertisers. And advertisers do not want to place ads next to content that deals with dark subject matter. Advertisers want their ads on a Mr. Beast video where he fixes 1,000 blindness. They don't want to be on a video going over the grizzly details of a murder suicide. Platforms usually don't completely censor such videos. But they do algorithmically supress them. They do age gate them. This is something that has been known for years about true crime content. The views might be high, but it is significantly more difficult to monetize. This is also well known about gay themed content. And, of course, on the opposite side, you have mommy vloggers, people who are doing incalculable harm, but are extremely advertiser friendly. The thing about algorithms is that they can be pretty easily exploited. You can talk about grape all you like if you call it “grape.” There isn't a person monitoring every video, it is just a computer that checks for key words. So all you have to do is avoid those words. “Unalive” has become so ubiquitous that it probably is now just slang instead of a workaround. But it didn't start out as some cutesy slang term like “fleek.” We operate inside the systems we have to and we exploit them in the ways in which they left themselves vulnerable.

Question: What is the origin of the name "Scarlet Witch" for Wanda and Pietro's character in Marvel comic books?
Answer: Jack Kirby considered several names for the character before publication, including "Jinx," "Witch Woman," "The Sorceress," "Evil Eye", and "Miss Witch." On the back of a page of X-Man #4 artwork, someone discovered his attempts to workshop the name. Included among these names is “The Scarlet Witch.” I assume he went with Scarlet Witch, because she was a witch who wore red. And it invoked The Scarlet Letter. Scarlet Witch’s backstory in the issue is quite different from Hester Prynne’s story, but both involve mobs of angry towns people. Scarlet Witch is the best name he considered. It’s neither generic nor silly, and has a certain gravitas to it. But you can see the other options.

Question: Are you surprised that Lupita Nyong'o was afraid of cats before working with cats Schnitzel and Nico in "A Quiet Place: Day One"?
Answer: Not really, in many African cultures there is a degree of prejudice against cats. Lupita Nyong’o actually gave an interview about this, specifically. “The only reason why I'm not afraid of cats is because of [my character] Sam,” Nyong’o shares. “I had to get over my fear in order to play her. I tried to get the animal changed in the movie, [the director] Michael [Sarnoski] wouldn't have it. So I had to get exposure therapy to cats before I started filming. I had to spend time with cats over a period of a few weeks to get acclimatizsed and to understand them enough not to be suspicious of them because I really needed to look like I was a cat owner.” As Nyong’o spent more time with her feline friends on set, she got a bit attached, to say the least. “By the time I was finishing this film, I was crying. I was crying as I said goodbye to [the cats] Nico and Schnitzel,” Nyong’o says. “I had grown so attached to them. They're so cute. And they were so talented. And so when the time came, when I was going through a hard moment, I was like, ‘you know what, I'm gonna get myself a cat’.” Nyong’o famously adopted her own cat in the midst of heartbreak. Last year, after she announced on Instagram that she had split from boyfriend Selema Masekela, Nyong’o shared that getting a cat helped her with her heartbreak. But since Nyong’o is Kenyan, we had to ask if her African background (Eduafo is Ghanian and had her own presumptions about cats before she adopted her own) added to why she was apprehensive about the animals. “Definitely,” Nyong’o said with a laugh. “My siblings cannot believe that I have a cat. You know, because my fear has been long standing. I had a few traumatic experiences with cats when I was little. Yeah. I wrote them off. The culture surrounding me did not help because they were like, why?” It is not an uncommon thing for people from some African cultures to dislike or be afraid of cats. This is something I have been aware of for years, I worked with some people from South Africa who were extremely against cats. And it is common enough that you can find people discussing online it with some regularity. And honestly, prejudice against cats is decreasing, but still fairly common most places. If you say you don’t like dogs people act like you killed a child, but if you don’t like cats most people just accept it. So I wasn’t particularly surprised when I heard Lupita Nyong’o was scared of cats prior to the film. I am really interested that she stated it was for both personal and cultural reasons, which makes a lot of sense. But she very much got over it. And now she adopted a cat. Nyong’o went through what a lot of people go through, which is that they have a bias against cats… and then actually spend some time around them. And instantly fall in love. This is known as the “cat dad” phenomena, where a father gets a cat for his kids, viewing it as a nuisance, and then becomes the person most obsessed with the cat. Cats are great.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What do you think the significance of finding a way to get a pizza is in 'A Quiet Place: Day One'?
Answer: Sam, the protagonist of A Quiet Place: Day One is a terminal cancer patient. She is going to die regardless of whether the aliens kill her or not. In fact, the longer she lives, the worse her situation is going to be, as her pain medication is obviously going to be increasingly more difficult to get. Due to her situation, she isn’t trying to find a way to survive, because survival isn’t something she is capable of. Instead she wants to get some genuine New York pizza from a pizzeria that her father used to take her to. Day One is about finding joy and meaning in what life we have. Sam is going to die, so the only question she faces is what does she want to do in the time before that happens. Which is… she just wants a slice of pizza. Relatable. The pizza, like most things relating to Sam, represents her life prior to her cancer diagnosis. She used to be able to go down to the pizzeria whenever she wanted. She agreed to go into New York City specifically for the pizza. It was all she wanted. And when the aliens land, she becomes determined to have the last slice ever. Her life was disrupted long before the aliens, and the pizza represents normalcy, independence, happiness to her. A major theme of Day One, and to an extent all the Quiet Place movies, is that you can still find happiness even in miserable circumstances. Pain is an inevitability, whether it is the pain of a lost child in the first film, or the pain of cancer in this one. But pain does not preclude joy. It does not erase happy memories. Even in the apocalypse, Sam can share her happiest memories with a friend. A huge part of the film is centered on Sam giving the best parts of herself to Eric, who is a complete stranger to her. Some of this is actually physically giving him things, she gives him Frodo and her father’s sweater, which represent her soul and her love respectively. But also some of it is giving him parts of her life. She shows him her apartment. She shows him the pizzeria and the jazz club. She continues to exist in him. And even if they aren’t what she wanted them to be, it is still giving of herself. It is a really interesting movie, with some profound and deep themes.

Question: At what point of Breaking Bad do you think Walt reached the point of no return?
Answer: Walt reached the point of no return in season one, episode five, “Grey Matter.” In that episode Walt and Skyler attend the birthday party of his former business partner Elliott Schwartz. Schwartz and Walt had started a business together, Grey Matter Technologies, out of college, with Walt’s then girlfriend Gretchen. Walt sold his ownership stake in the company for $5,000 to his partners, but then the company went on to become a billion dollar venture. Walt believes he was fucked over in all of this, which isn’t actually true and merely another sign of Walt’s incredible lack of self-awareness. In the episode “Grey Matter” Elliott and Gretchen offer Walt a job and offer to pay for his cancer treatment. All the financial problems that, allegedly, prompted Walt to cook meth would have vanished instantly. Walt turns them down. After the episode “Grey Matter” there is no illusion that circumstances are driving Walt’s behavior. The pitch for Breaking Bad is that a high school science teacher gets cancer and decides to cook meth to pay for his treatment. But that’s not actually true. It’s not true in the slightest. Walt always had other options. And this episode gives him the best option possible, on a platter, and he rejects it. Walter White became a drug kingpin entirely because that’s what he wanted to do. It wasn’t a path he was forced onto. It was one he chose. He was offered a path off, a very literal point of return, and he rejected it. If the viewer considered Walt a sympathetic protagonist up to this point, that should have been shattered. And all the murder and mayhem and chaos that follows in the series was all a result of Walt’s actively desiring to be in the drug business over any other possible path. Any illusions about who Walt is, either with the viewer or with Walt himself, is shattered by this episode.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What do you think of the character Frodo the cat in "A Quiet Place: Day One"?
Answer: I loved the cat. I think the cat is a fascinating addition to the film that works in a lot of interesting ways. And, also, every film should have a cat in it. Look at that cute cat! Thematically cats are so perfect for the Quiet Place franchise that I am surprised we haven’t gotten one before. Cats are ambush predators, are naturally silent animals. They meow to communicate with us, and they sometimes get the zoomies. But mostly they are quiet, and certainly when they want to be there are very few animals able to navigate the world as quietly as cats. Additionally cats are incredibly loving animals, which is why so many humans keep them as pets. They provide comfort and affection. Cats are the natural thematic antithesis of the aliens, while still also being the most common animal which follows the rules of the Quiet Place world. We see over and over and over that Frodo is the opposite of the aliens. Where they kill and provide nothing but misery, he brings people together and provides love and affection. But his role is incredibly important. Sam is, by her own admission, a mean person. She’s a strange, bitter and off putting protagonist. However, she has a cat. Frodo’s existence sands down her harsher edges. And Frodo acts as an intermediary, allowing her to bond with people in a way her naturally prickly nature wouldn’t allow for. We see this almost immediately at the play, she is able to bond with the child in front of her through the cat. Which sets up the most important relationship in the film, her bonding with Eric. Eric is alone in New York when the aliens land. He runs into Frodo and then basically just decides to follow Sam because she has a cat. Following the orders to evacuate to the south of the island almost got him killed, so he really has no where to go and anything he does will likely result in his death… so why not just follow the lady with the cat? This is, honestly, the most relatable that any protagonist in a horror movie has ever been. Frodo allows two people who are very much alone at the start of the film to bond with each other in the middle of the apocalypse. You are never alone when you are with a cat. And rescuing Frodo is a very potent metaphor for rescuing the best parts of Sam. Also the film, wisely, only ever once has someone risk death for Frodo. And that’s that juicy lore scene. It was more about mechanically positioning Eric to be able to see something happening. Every other time Frodo is in danger because all three of them are in danger. Frodo is a hero. Frodo brings people together. Frodo is the real breakout star of the film.

Question: What is the projected revenue for Disney's "Star Wars: Andor"?
Answer: Basically $0.00. There is a home video release that will probably make a small amount of money, but mostly it will make nothing. Because streaming is a bad system for making money. Because Andor is on Disney+, there is no licensing fee. Instead the monthly subscription fees of the entire user base are sliced up to cover everything on the entire platform. There is no direct way for Andor to generate revenue. Andor has to, instead, generate revenue indirectly. Either through retaining existing subscribers or enticing new subscribers. It is the latter that all of streaming is based off of. It is one of the main reasons why streaming shows get canceled prematurely. After about two seasons or so a show has basically tapped out of its ability to bring new subscribers in, therefore it is a waste of money to continue it. If this seems like it is very dysfunctional, it is. The entertainment industry replaced a system where everything is directly paid for in some way, with one where it is all indirect and for considerably less revenue. When you buy a movie ticket, you are directly paying for that movie. When you buy a DVD you are directly paying for that movie. When you watch TV advertisers are directly paying for that TV show in order to reach you. When you subscribe to a streaming service you are indirectly paying for everything on the site, whether you watch it or not. It is all very ridiculous.

Question: What does the world lose when someone like Stan Lee dies?
Answer: In Stan Lee's case we lost the best possible spokesman for comic books as a medium. Stan Lee engaged in plenty of shady business practices in his life, and he absolutely had a tendency to take credit for other people’s work. But he was a wildly charismatic individual in a medium where most people tend to be pretty awkward. Which made him the perfect advocate for the medium, the best possible face. The first time I really got to see Stan Lee was in a brief promotional video that he appeared in the Pizza Hut exclusive VHS of the pilot for X-Men the animated series. But in these five minutes you see everything that made Stan Lee great. He’s witty and funny, insightful and thoughtful, he’s a masterful story teller, he’s bombastic. And he just oozes charisma. He’s someone you want to listen to. There is only one person the general public knows who works in the comic book industry: Stan Lee. And that has been so lucky for the industry. My parents, who could not be less interested in comics, absolutely love him. The positive feelings people have for Stan the Man transfer over to the industry as a whole, and in their own way protect it from the many controversies that happened across Stan’s life. He’s also really funny. Here’s Stan Lee shitting on Rob Liefeld and Todd McFarlane for three minutes… His criticisms are spot on. There’s no replacing Stan Lee. The closest person that I can think of now is Neil Gaiman, and as much as I love Gaiman, he’s not this indefatigable presence who can always spin anything with the charm of a carnival barker. I’ve said that all video game companies are lucky that the mascot of the entire industry is Mario. And all comic books are lucky that the spokesman for the entire industry was, for decades, Stan Lee.

Question: What are the reasons for the negative reception of the live action Resident Evil movie? Is it considered a failure by fans of the franchise? Did it deviate significantly from the original source material?
Answer: The live action Resident Evil movies are among the most interesting movies I have ever seen in my life. They are utterly unlike anything else. They’re not good, but damn if they are not utterly fascinating. The first, and most important, thing to understand about Resident Evil as a franchise is that all of the movies were written by Paul W. S. Anderson and that he directed all but the second and third ones. There is a consistent creative team behind the films, which makes the creative choices even more bonkers. Milla Jovovich was cast as the protagonist of the original Resident Evil film, which is where she met Anderson. They started a relationship and eventually got married. The whole franchise primarily exists as a love letter to Jovovich, It is just an excuse to make her look good, give her as much to do as possible. It is the Wife Guy franchise. And, honestly, good for them. The original Resident Evil film is as close as any of the films get to being good. It takes some of the concepts from the original game, but ditches the plot and the characters for entirely original material. Our hero is Alice, who wakes up with amnesia in a mansion. She is almost immediately accosted by a group of mercenaries, alongside a journalist who happens to be there. The mansion is connected to a high tech lab which is run by an AI called the Red Queen which went homicidal and killed everyone. When they get down there they find there is a zombie outbreak, and all the mercenaries die. This sets up so much about the franchise moving forward. First off, any elements of the game, aside from the principle villains, the Umbrella Corporation, are going to be haphazardly deployed but even then only as aesthetics. The films will be slathered in allusions to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. The only character that actually matters is Alice. It will always end on a cliffhanger. The second film, Resident Evil Apocalypse, is the only time they really bother trying to adapt a game, Resident Evil 3 but with some elements of Resident Evil 2. It introduces Jill Valentine, the protagonist of Resident Evil 3, but she might as well be a completely original character. She’s basically completely unhinged. Also Carlos from the same game makes an appearance. Everyone is upstaged by Alice, who is uniquely special and powerful and fights Nemesis in hand to hand combat. This film has some interesting ideas. I really liked that the moment they realize a zombie outbreak is happening the Umbrella Corporation walls off the whole city. I also like how the protagonists go to all this effort to document everything happening in Racoon City, but Umbrella “debunks” the video and makes them into the villains. Also Alice gets psychic murder powers at the end of the film. The third film, Resident Evil: Extinction, is where things start going really off the tracks. All of society collapses in between the second and third films, and now they are doing Mad Max. Feels like maybe there was a movie missing in the franchise. This film introduces Claire Redfield, who is the protagonist of Resident Evil 2, well one of them. She is leading a convoy full of people who are going to die., because this is Mad Max, and is trying to get to Alaska. Claire, played by Ali Larter, is the closest thing this stupid franchise has to a secondary protagonist. She will show up in three of the films. These films love to drop characters and then pick them up later. They discover a secret Umbrella facility which is filled with clones of Alice that get rescued. The best thing about this film is that Umbrella can track Alice whenever she uses her psychic murder powers. The fourth film, Resident Evil: Afterlife, is the first film to really do what I truly love about these films. These films are obsessed with their own continuity, but in the weirdest way possible. Each film dedicates a massive portion of its running time to undoing all the creative choices of the previous film, This is despite the fact that they are all the creative vision of the same guy. It’s like Anderson never stops to consider what the next movie will be and then panics. So from this point on characters who are killed violently on screen will just show up alive again, characters will randomly flip from being heroes to villains and back again, whether Alice has her psychic murder powers or not changes. So you know how I mentioned Alice found all these clones of herself? The opening of this movie has them all dying. Anyway, Alice and Claire fly to LA where they crash land onto a prison. A prison where the most annoying possible people are holed up. Also Chris Redfield, the protagonist of Resident Evils 1 and 5 is being held prisoner in the basement? This film is utterly dire. Anywho, after all the characters who aren’t Alice or from a game die, they fight Albert Wesker, the villain of Resident Evil 1 on a boat. Also Jill Valentine shows up again, except I have no idea how you are supposed to tell it is her. I do not know this woman. Resident Evil: Afterlife is probably the worst film, which is saying something for this franchise. It’s really bad. Resident Evil: Retribution is good actually? Or at least, if not good, interesting. It’s worth watching. The plot is just straight up stolen from the novel Resident Evil: Underworld by S.D. Perry. But given what the last movie was like, stealing a plot was obviously a good idea. I just hope Perry got paid (I know she didn’t). Alice is in a giant Umbrella testing facility, where Umbrella uses clones to enact biological weapons scenarios. So Alice has to work her way through these massive domes, each of which simulates a different geographic location, which is fun. And she keeps running into people from previous movies… who I guess were all clones? Or maybe Umbrella harvested their DNA, brought it to this facility and cloned them? It’s unclear. Also Leon Kennedy is here for some reason, played by Estonian muscle hunk Johann Urb. Who is somehow able to pull off Leon’s hair. Ada Wong is also in this one, and I like her because my grandmother’s name was also Ada. Anyway, Albert Wesker, the villain from the previous movie, is now a good guy and working for the remains of the US government which have gathered at the White House as part of a last stand against against the Red Queen AI who is trying to kill all of humanity, which had, in the previous movie, been revealed to have always been benevolent. To prove he is good now, Wesker injects Alice with a drug which will give her back her powers, which had been removed in the previous film. And the movie ends with a hoard of zombies attacking the White House. Boy, that sure sounds like it will be interesting for the start of Resident Evil: The Final Chapter! Resident Evil: The Final Chapter begins with the battle at the White House already over. Wesker betrayed everyone off screen, and is now the bad guy…. again. And the Red Queen is actually benevolent… again. Also I am pretty sure Alice loses her powers, but don’t quote me on that. Lastly the villain is the guy from Resident Evil: Extinction that Alice had blown up on screen. And while Claire is back, for whatever reason, Leon almost certainly was killed off screen. So bummer. This movie they have a ticking clock that tells when the very last humans on Earth will die, despite that not making any sense whatsoever. And Alice has to infiltrate the original laboratory from the first Resident Evil film, again. She discovers she is the clone of the dying daughter of one of the founders of Umbrella. And she releases a virus that kills anything infected with the zombie virus. But remember this is the ultimate Wife Guy franchise, even though the whole movie is set up to be about Alice sacrificing herself for the world, Anderson couldn’t bare to kill her so Alice is just fine. These are not good films. The negative reception is entirely earned. And it really has nothing to do with deviations from the original source material. And I am not certain they would be good films if they tried to follow the source material more closely, the one which did certainly wasn’t good. Nonetheless, I love these dumpster fire films. I have watched them more times that I would care to admit. They’re also kind of fascinating relics, because each one is so very clearly a slice of its own particular time period.

Question: Why do some people view the term "woke" negatively? What is the negative connotation associated with being aware and wanting to improve the world for everyone?

Question: What happened to Doctor Who? Why are ratings down?
Answer: Since Doctor Who’s revival in 2005 there have been precisely two seasons that had better ratings than the season immediately preceding it: series four, David Tennant’s final season, and series eleven, Jodie Whittaker’s first season. Look at how happy they are! Aside from those two seasons, Doctor Who has been on an uninterrupted downward slide in the ratings since season two. This is broadly in line with the entire television industry, ratings have been in an uninterrupted decline since the ‘90s. The perpetually low rated 30 Rock, for example got a 3.9 rating in it’s third season. Which is four times the audience of the highest rated 2023 comedy, Young Sheldon, which got a 0.9 rating. Looking at the historical trendline of Doctor Who’s ratings, they seem fine. If anything they seem less steep of a decline than one would expect. There is a tendency to compare the ratings to the 60th anniversary specials, but those starred David Tennant and Catherine Tate, which is why they were significantly higher rated. As for why the ratings of all of television have been in decline for decades now: audience fragmentation, DVRs, streaming, piracy, greater competition…. This isn’t a Doctor Who issue, it’s the entire medium of television.

Question: Who is Doctor Aphra from the Star Wars comics?
Answer: Doctor Chelli Lona Aphra is a renegade archeologist who winds up being recruited by Darth Vader, who, at the time, was looking to build an independent and private armory. Aphra was created for the 2015 Darth Vader comic by Kieron Gillen and Salvador Larroca. The goal of that comic was to show how Vader recovered his reputation and standing from the destruction of the first Death Star. The Emperor is not exactly forgiving of failure on that scale. As part of that story, Gillen surrounded him with twisted and immoral versions of the core characters from the original film, with him standing in as the twisted and immoral version of Luke. So his allies are Queen Trios of Shu-Torun, the Wookie bounty hunter Black Krrsantan, and Doctor Aphra and her homicidal droids, 0–0–0 and BT-1. This seems like it would be tedious, but it works amazingly well. Doctor Aphra is the Han Solo of the team, a charming rogue and scoundrel. But while Han’s whole point is that underneath it all he has a heart of gold, Aphra… just doesn’t have one. As an archeologist, Aphra’s whole deal is finding the most dangerous tech in the galaxy and then selling it to whoever will buy it. She also has chronic backstabbing disorder, she has never met a person she didn’t eventually betray. She has no qualms about working with Vader and supplying him with whatever horrifying tech he can imagine. She is also extremely chatty, which counter balances Vader’s stoicism. Vader is a character who speaks rarely, and Aphra allows him to retain that aura of mystery and menace. She is the one to ask questions and deliver expository dialogue, so Vader doesn’t have to. Aphra was, more or less instantly, hugely popular. Sales of Darth Vader #3, her first appearance, went up by a dramatic amount. Almost immediately people were cosplaying as her at conventions. And she remained a very important part of the Darth Vader comic, until it ended about exactly the way you would assume an alliance between a Sith Lord and someone with a penchant for betrayal would end. In fact, my belief is that Aphra was supposed to die at the conclusion of her storyline. But you don’t kill popular characters. Marvel spun her off into her own comic, with Darth Vader only thinking he had killed her. It was Marvel’s first Star Wars comic about a completely original character not featured in any previous film or TV show. It was also originally written by Kieron Gillen and is very good. Aphra, now no longer working for Vader and hoping he doesn’t check up on her, is still an amoral archeologist finding the most dangerous tech in the universe and selling it on the black market. The volume starts out with a really funny story where Aphra loses her doctorate simply for the little oversight of technically faking the research that she did at university and also just a smidge of blackmail. What academic isn’t guilty of this? And as she is no longer an accredited archeologist, none of the artifacts she finds can be sold as they are no verified as legitimate archeological finds. So she has to get her accreditation back. Thrill as the character in this sci-fi series has to navigate her way through vast unknowable regions of university bureaucracy. I joke, but it is actually a lot of fun. It runs forty issues, and has a really fun crossover with the main Star Wars comic, entitled “The Screaming Citadel.” And it really walks the tightrope of not having Aphra be so immoral as to get the audience to turn on her, while not giving her heroic qualities. When all the Star Wars comics are rebooted, a new Doctor Aphra volume begins. This also runs forty issues. And it is here that they turn her character more distinctly heroic. No where near the level of Luke or Leia, but more similar to Han in his original appearance. Doctor Aphra is great because it is rarely tied into the grand stories of Star Wars. Instead it is personal and small crime stories about a really fascinating character. Aphra is easily my favorite Star Wars character and I am hoping she will be translated (well) into a form that more people are likely to see, meaning a movie or TV show.

Question: What impact do you think Marvel's decision to end the current volumes of Star Wars and Darth Vader comics will have on the future of Star Wars storytelling?
Answer: In early 2015 Marvel launched their Star Wars line with two ongoing comics, Star Wars and Darth Vader. The next year it would be joined by two more titles, Poe Dameron and Doctor Aphra. Star Wars, Darth Vader, and Doctor Aphra were all set in-between the events of A New Hope and Empire Strikes Back. In 2019, after four years, the entire Star Wars comic line was canceled. In 2020 the Star Wars comics were relaunched with Star Wars, Darth Vader, Doctor Aphra, and Bounty Hunters. This time all the comics were set between Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. I haven’t checked to see if there is any promotional material for upcoming Star Wars comics. But the thing is that Marvel has already canceled the entire line once before. So if I were to bet money, I would bet that Marvel is preparing to relaunch with comics set after Return of the Jedi, and those comics would be Star Wars, Doctor Aphra, and maybe a third title. Also a Darth Vader comic set some time in the past. The current timeframe of the comics is weird and difficult because Han Solo can’t appear. They actually wound up giving him his own comic, Han Solo and Chewbacca, in order to wedge him in somewhere. The decision to periodically reboot the whole line is, to me, not particularly impactful. It’s just saying “here’s where the movie happens.” The content of the comics, however, is going to be extremely impactful. The most obvious example of this is Doctor Aphra. She created just to be a supporting character in the Darth Vader comic (and, likely, to be killed by Vader). She became so popular she, a completely original character not in any movie, helmed two long running comic series and was added to multiple video games and has several toys. Comics are a low cost, low risk way to work out ideas. And so their main impact is in what transfers over to mediums that are exponentially more expensive.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What attracts the LGBTQ+ community to the X-Men franchise?
Answer: Chris Claremont and his… interesting, let's say, proclivities. Claremont was the writer of X-Men for sixteen years, from 1975 to 1991. Which is the single longest run on any title by anyone in Marvel or DC’s history. He then came back to the title in 2000 and wrote another hundred issues. Claremont took the X-Men from a struggling concept that was revived from cancelation to the number one selling comic. He is responsible for many of the most beloved characters and storylines. As I am found of saying, he made everything before him irrelevant and everything after him possible. He’s also a deeply fascinating individual, and he is certainly a writer who leaves a lot of himself on the page. Claremont was an actor, and his approach to writing was based in method acting. He would attempt to get into the head of every character. That’s how he radically reinvented Magneto, by trying to figure out what would make his silver age characterization make sense. Claremont is Jewish and lived on a kibbutz in Israel, where he worked with Holocaust survivors. His wife in the ’70s was a Wiccan high priestess in the NYC occult scene. And there are certain undeniable fetishistic aspects to his writing. Chris Claremont loves a strong woman, a really strong woman. His editors on X-Men were Louise Simonson and Ann Nocenti. Nocenti came up in the New York art world, and has talked about how most of her social circle at the time consisted of gay and trans people. The three of them would have meetings at the Pyramid Club, a famous New York City gay club. Emma Frost was based on a drag queen friend of theirs. Under Claremont’s direction, the X-Men had certain extremely strong recurring themes: powerful women, kink and fetish, gender non-conformity, homoeroticism that barely counts as subtextual. When LGBT people read the X-Men a whole mess of things immediately leap out with flashing lights and airhorns. Some of it is so blatant that most straight readers notice it. Storm is the main character of Chris Claremont’s run, both of them, actually. She gets the most focus, the most development. She gets the most glory moments.. But Claremont always put his female characters at the forefront of the comic. Jean’s whole transformation into the Phoenix and then descent into the Dark Phoenix being a perfect example. Over the course of his initial run on the X-Men he created two new male characters to join the team (Forge and Gambit) and four female ones (Shadowcat, Rogue, Rachel Summers, and Jubilee). Female characters are always the center of attention, the main focus. They dominate, while male characters are pushed to the margins and excluded. Nocenti has said that Claremont could not have cared less about Cyclops or Colossus and her job was to essentially force him to write things for those characters. So if your are more likely to identify with female characters than male ones, then, ironically, X-Men is easily the title to go to. Claremont’s comics go way beyond just having strong women as character traits. They are frequently highly fetishistic. There are near constant themes of bondage, domination, submission, slavery. There are multiple characters who are clearly dominatrixes. The Hellfire Club is just a BDSM club. The Morlocks all walk around in fetish gear. There’s a strangely huge emphasis on sexual corruption. Twice he has women get their arms replaced with tentacles! All this stuff that is just sitting there in the open in his comics is a radical departure from the compulsory heterosexuality that dominated the medium. In basically all other comics, female characters exist to be the objects of desire for the male perspective. In Claremont’s comics you would have things like the extremely butch Callisto torturing a nearly nude Angel in order to make him her sex slave. Even if none of this is your thing, you are still seeing a range of human sexuality on the page that is vast and chaotic, and unlike anything you could get elsewhere. If you were not interested in heterosexuality, this is truly revolutionary. To talk about gender non-conformity under Claremont, you really only need to point out the fact that he is the creator of Mystique. But, naturally, he hardly limited this to just her. Over in Excalibur he created Nigel Frobisher, a bank manager who transformed into the female mob boss Vixen. He loved a gender swapped counterpart to his characters. Rachel Summers is introduced as so androgenous that no one knows her gender. The male Shadow King takes possession of the female Karma. He masculinizes he female characters and feminizes his male ones. And then there are the ideas that didn’t make it into his comics that he wanted to do: that Mystique was Nightcrawler’s father not his mother, that Xavier would infiltrate the Hellfire Club as one of its female waitresses. Under Claremont gender is fluid and more about performance than biology. The incongruence between a person’s self-understanding and their actual body is explored almost incessantly. The gender boundary can be transgressed, and characters are frequently confronted alternative genders. Claremont plays with gender. In Uncanny X-Men annual #12 Storm gets to experience her most fervent wish: to run around Tokyo with her friend Yukio. The implications are as obvious as possible. Claremont has never written two female characters without a lesbian subtext. He even managed to canonize Mystique and Destiny by having the Shadow King refer to them with an extremely obscure word for “lover.” Rachel is introduced as the girlfriend of Franklin Richards, but the moment Claremont decides to use her regularly, she could not be less interested in men sexually. Wolfsbane and Mirage are constantly referred to as “soulmates.” Kitty gets implicitly partnered with both Magik and Rachel. While the emphasis is usually on the female characters, like always, most of the male characters get it as well, even if far more lightly. The most obvious being Juggernaut who is reintroduced with this effete male partner, Black Tom Cassidy, who he will abandon whatever scheme is attempting the moment Black Tom is threatened. There’s also Charles and Magneto. Doug and Warlock. Like I said, this is all barely subtext. And most of it could be put together even by the straight audience. But if you are gay, you can read it all, loudly and clearly. And all that is aside from the basic premise of the X-Men, where mutants are hated and persecuted for their immutable characteristics. And Claremont, being Claremont, one of their major adversaries is just conservative Christians. Like Billy Graham is one of their villains. Sure, they might call him “Reverend Stryker” but he is Billy Graham. Also Louise Simonson introduced some villains where literally just “The Right.” The adaptations of X-Men all tone down the excesses of Claremont. But none have ever managed to expunge them completely. And so a queer audience member is going to see this very strange property that is clearly meant for them. Something that is much more easy to relate to than, say, Superman. If you are really curious about this, then I suggest listening to Cerebro which is a podcast dedicated to a queer reading of the X-Men. It is extremely detailed, and they frequently interview the major writers and artists of the X-Men. There’s a great episode on Mojo with Ann Nocenti herself, which reveals a lot about Claremont’s time on the book.

Question: Star Wars is terrible, now. Why do progressive women have to ruin everything?
Answer: Star Wars is terrible now? Perhaps we should check in with what people were saying about Star Wars twenty years ago… Anyone claiming Star Wars is terrible now, as opposed to has been for most of its existence, has a lot of explaining to do. They have to explain why the exact same criticisms that were made about George Lucas were not just as valid as the ones they are currently making about Disney. Why all visceral hatred of George Lucas and the prequels was somehow not valid, but their reaction to Disney Star Wars is good and pure and true. And why anyone should believe them and think they are acting in good faith, given the sheer weight of historical evidence. I can respect people who have the opinion that Star Wars has been bad for twenty-five years. I can respect people who have the opinion that Star Wars was always bad. I can respect people who have the opinion that there is good and bad Star Wars in every era of its existence. I can respect the opinion of people who think that they personally do not find the most recent Star Wars output compelling, and they do recognize that such opinions are historically common (though I would argue that should be unpacked). But I really can't respect anyone claiming Star Wars is bad now.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Do you think the fire in Star Wars: The Acolyte will be explained in a satisfying way, or do you expect a cop-out answer like "silly and fun that defies all explanations of Earthly science"?
Answer: …It’s a murder mystery. Star Wars: The Acolyte is a murder mystery so the rules of murder mysteries are currently in effect. It has been wild to see that some section of the Star Wars fandom seem unfamiliar with how one of the main genres of literature works. Even the specific nature of this murder mystery, where the audience knows the killer’s identity and so the mystery is why they did it, is extremely common. I suppose since that same section of Star Wars fandom is refusing to watch the show for reasons that are… well… let’s just say not good. I suppose I will just have to explain what the episode showed. And explain the very basics of how mysteries work. Episode three, “Destiny” is the big backstory episode. However, it is told almost entirely from Osha’s perspective. In a detective novel this would be where the person hiring the detective explains their version of events. The reader inherently understands that there will be gaps and misunderstandings and assumptions in this version of the story. And the fun of the mystery will be investigating what happened and finding out the truth. Oshan wants to join the Jedi, but we are never actually told why. We aren’t told why she is so frightened of the Ascension ceremony. Her twin sister Mae wants to follow in their mother’s footsteps and lead the coven of witches (which are an obvious offshoot of the Nightsisters). Rather than let her sister join the Jedi, Mae locks her in their room, and then sets fire to the electrical wiring leading to the door. Notably, Mae is visibly crying while she does this. Why is she crying? We don’t know, the show completely with hold's Mae’s perspective, only giving us Osha’s. What prompted Mae is part of the mystery. Osha escapes the room through a horizontal airshaft. Two minutes after the fire was set, Osha sees an explosion above her, through a grate. Osha then walks to an enormous piece of equipment that seems to obviously be the complex’s power generator. It is clearly in bad shape, but still in tact. So it wasn’t what exploded above Osha. However, as she is standing there looking at it, it explodes. Osha then sees Mae, and they meet on the two sides of this ruined catwalk. They then have the following conversation: Osha: Where’s mamma? Where’s mamma? Mae: Mamma’s dead! Osha: What have you done? Mae: What have you done? The catwalk then collapses, and Mae falls into the chasm. Osha is rescued by the Jedi Sol, and as they make their way out of the complex they see all the witches have died. Osha wakes up on the Jedi ship and she askes Sol what happened. He says, “Mae started a fire. It destroyed everything, it killed—” And that’s where the episode leaves off. So knowing we are in a murder mystery, there are all sorts of questions you should be asking yourself. Why was Mae crying? If the explosion was caused by the fire, how did it get both above and across from where it started so quickly? Why is Mae convinced Osha did something? How does Sol even know Mae started a fire in the first place? How did a fire which all the Jedi survived kill all the witches? And, most importantly: is Sol lying? Or, if he is not lying, does he have an accurate understanding of what happened that night? Each of these questions directs the audience to a clearly created gap in Osha’s understanding of what happened that night. The episode offers an explanation for all the events: Mae didn’t want Osha to join the Jedi so she started a fire which got out of control and killed the witches. But since the audience is supposed to understand that we are watching a mystery, the audience should know not to take that story at face value. There was a bunch of things that happened that night that Osha was not privy to, and therefore the audience didn’t see. Since I am a fan of mysteries, I expect that the gaps of that night will be filled in. I expect that neither Mae nor Sol has a complete understanding of what happened. And we won’t know how satisfying that answer is until we get to it. I understand the urge to jump to the final page of a mystery novel, but the fun reading the whole thing. But it is very funny to see the the most basic elements of mystery writing treated as completely baffling to this particular section of Star Wars fans.

Question: Why is Pikachu often disliked compared to other starter Pokemon in the games? What sets it apart from the others that leads to this negative reception?
Answer: Pikachu was only ever a starter Pokémon in Pokémon Yellow and Pokémon Let’s Go Pikachu. The first gym leader you will face in the game is Brock, and Pikachu is all but useless. Name: Johan Torres
Question: How do you think the controversy surrounding Justice Alito reflects the current culture war?
Answer: I actually think it is really emblematic of the current culture war. Martha-Ann Alito is just completely wackadoodle. Samuel Alito openly and brazenly lied to congress. Every institution ran cover for them. And nothing will happen and we’re all just stuck with them. In January of 2021 the Alitos flew an upside down American flag outside their home. This is a symbol of Stop the Steal Trump supporters. Samuel Alito has given multiple explanations of what, exactly, happened, including in writing to congress. If you want the TL;DR version, Martha-Ann is completely unhinged Trump supporter who harasses people, Samuel Alito is likely as well, and he definitely lied to congress. So here is Samuel’s written statement to the Senate, which you can read on the Senate’s website. My wife’s reasons for flying the flag are not relevant for present purposes, but I note that she was greatly distressed at the time due, in large part, to a very nasty neighborhood dispute in which I had no involvement. A house on the street displayed a sign attacking her personally, and a man who was living in the house at the time trailed her all the way down the street and berated her in my presence using foul language, including what I regard as the vilest epithet that can be addressed to a woman. Samuel’s entire story relies upon the “trust me, bro” standard. He just asserts he didn’t know what the flag meant at the time, that he had nothing to do with it flying, that he asked her to take it down and she didn’t. So… a lot is riding on Samuel’s trustworthiness. But he is lying. Just openly lying. Those neighbors he talks about were texting the whole time. And, in fact, the police got involved in this situation. To better understand the clash, The Times interviewed Ms. Baden, her mother and her husband, as well as other neighbors, and reviewed the texts that Ms. Baden and her husband sent to friends after the episodes. Justice Alito, who did not respond to questions for this article, has in recent weeks given his own explanation of what happened. There are some differences: For instance, the justice told Fox News that his wife hoisted the flag in response to Ms. Baden’s vulgar insult. A text message and the police call — corroborated by Fairfax County authorities — indicate, however, that the name-calling took place on Feb. 15, weeks after the inverted flag was taken down. The altercation between the neighbors happened in February, a month after the upside down flag flying happened. Also the Alitos were the aggressors in every incident, something confirmed by multiple people in the neighborhood. The final – and most heated – encounter between Baden and the Alitos took place on Feb. 15, 2021. “My husband and I are just in the driveway. We're getting the trash cans. And then the Alitos” - both Justice Alito and Martha-Ann Alito - “walk up, they presumably were just taking a walk.”. Baden says she and her husband were startled to see them. “And then then Mrs. Alito says something like, ‘well, well, well, if it isn't the the f****** fascists, Emily and my husband's name and my mom's name, you're - you're a f****** fascist.’”. Baden says she was surprised to hear Martha-Ann Alito use each of their full names. Baden had never introduced herself by name, and she and her husband were not yet married and did not share a last name. The police get called, but they are called on the Alitos for stalking and harassing their neighbors. The police decided to not do anything about it. So the flag was raised a month before the incident that supposedly prompted it to be raised happened. And honestly how is an upside down American flag a response to this? Is Martha-Ann attempting to signal to the coast guard to intervene in her neighborhood feud… on dry land? It’s absurd and ludicrous. Samuel then just does not even offer an explanation of why the Appeal To Heaven flag was flying. We are just supposed to take it on faith that Martha-Ann somehow accidentally flew two flags associated with Stop the Steal, without knowing it. And that Samuel both didn’t know the meaning and had nothing to do with flying them. And we have to take his word for that, despite the fact that we know he lied to Congress in a written statement. But here’s where the story gets even spicier. The Washington Post had this story when it happened, and killed it. The incident documented by reporter Robert Barnes, who covered the Supreme Court for The Post for 17 years and retired last year, offers fresh details about the raising of the flag and the first account of comments about it by the justice’s wife. The Post decided not to report on the episode at the time because the flag-raising appeared to be the work of Martha-Ann Alito, rather than the justice, and connected to a dispute with her neighbors, a Post spokeswoman said. It was not clear then that the argument was rooted in politics, the spokeswoman said. I am not sure how the Washington Post could have investigated and came to the conclusion this was in any way unclear in how it was rooted in politics. But here we have the biggest newspaper in Washington DC killing a story that has vast implications for an entire branch of the American government. Some real preferential treatment going on. The Washington Post also published this ludicrous column by Kathleen Parker designed to salvage Martha-Ann’s reputation. Martha-Ann’s flag, first hoisted at her home a few days after Jan. 6, initially sparked only the ire of a neighbor. Perhaps the neighbor has reason to dislike Martha-Ann, who is funny, feisty, unfiltered and the life of any party, according to mutual friends and my limited impression of her. She and I met at a meet-and-greet when the Alitos moved to Washington years ago. Almost immediately, Martha-Ann enthusiastically invited me to be her walking partner. Long chatty walks with a Supreme Court justice’s wife? Mais oui! Your block or mine? There’s so much going on here. First off there is the completely inaccurate summation of the dispute. The fawning praise of Martha-Ann. And then there is the fact that the Alitos were schmoozing with the journalists who are supposed to be covering them. But here’s the thing… there’s nothing anyone can do about any of this. Samuel has got the job for life, and no one can make him recuse himself. He objectively lied to congress, but the only thing congress can do is impeach him, which they won’t. So I think this is actually the perfect incident to highlight the culture war. Martha-Ann is, very obviously, a complete nut. Just someone riddled with brain worms. And likely her husband is as well. He has complete impunity to do whatever he wants. He can break every rule and there will be no consequences. The media will coddle them, give them every benefit of the doubt, and give them fawning praise. There just are no consequences for their actions. The system is built entirely upon being too ashamed to be this brazen and that’s just what they are now. And we’re all stuck here.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What factors contributed to the popularity of "Ice Age"? Is it considered a good movie?
Answer: Talking dinosaur movies have always been popular. This is a well that Hollywood has gone to many times. The most famous is, obviously, The Land Before Time. But there is no shortage of animated dinosaur movies. Dinosaur, Dinotopia, We're Back! A Dinosaur's Story, The Good Dinosaur, ect. The Ice Age films are just talking dinosaur films, but with different aesthetics. There are multiple species of talking charismatic megafauna that are well known and popular working together… it’s just Pleistocene mammals rather than cretaceous dinosaurs. An exotic location… it’s just glaciers and tundra rather than volcanic jungles. Weirdly dark and incongruous elements to a silly movie about talking animals… the first Ice Age definitely had that. It’s actually so obvious that I am surprised it took so long for someone to think of doing it. Kids love woolly mammoths and sabretooth cats. I don’t even want to contemplate how many toys I had of those two. I still have a bunch. I realized as I was writing this that I have a stuffed woolly mammoth sitting on a shelf in my closet. Which I have had since I was like five. I was actually always looking for books and toys about Pleistocene mammals, because I loved them so much. I will also say a big part of the appeal is also Scrat, the squirrel thing. Scrat is the prototype upon which the Minions were built. He’s annoying… in the exact same way the Minions are annoying, but wildly popular… in the exact same way the Minions are wildly popular. As far as quality… the general consensus is that the first one is decent… and then there is a consistent drop to the point where they are obviously just phoning it in.

Question: Who is considered the most popular female superhero or villain in the world of comics?
Answer: It is Catwoman. Catwoman by a chasm so vast it makes the grand canyon look small. Catwoman has been played by at least eight actresses. She universally appears in every Batman adaptation. Name: Johan Torres
Question: Besides Palpatine, who would've been a better choice for Episode Nine?
Answer: I mean, obviously it should have been Kylo-Ren, but they were determined to give him a redemption arc. So, I am going to make a completely left field pick and say the Silentium. The Silentium are from the Legends, and they are an extra-galactic droid civilization. They are roughly analogous to UFOs, in that people occasionally see these giant droids but have no idea what they could possibly be doing. And droids are an interesting source of tension in the Star Wars universe. “The Force is what gives a Jedi his power. It's an energy field created by all living things. It surrounds us and penetrates us. It binds the galaxy together.” - Obi-Wan Kenobi The Force is generated by and a part of all living things. Which means that droids should exist entirely outside the Force. Droids are also sentient, and yet enslaved. And the people in Star Wars treat them truly terribly. There’s a lot of interesting stuff to play with here. If I was writing the final sequel film, and I had to include a Kylo-Ren redemption arc, my story would be that Rey discovers that the Silentium have been using droids across the galaxy to manipulate the last thirty to forty years in an effort to create perpetual conflict, and in particular the endless mass death of Force users. Which is the preliminary stage to destroying the Force all together. We would get flashbacks showing many of the key events of the sequel films were instigated by random droids. Like Kylo-Ren is gifted Darth Vader’s helmet by a droid at the Jedi academy, which is what Luke senses. Or droids manufactured Snoke to instigate a cosplay version of the Empire in the First Order. And then Kylo-Ren can learn he was manipulated by an intelligence that could not care less about either the light or dark sides of the Force. Which could pull him back. And then he could kiss Rey, just like he did in Rise of Skywalker. Redemption completed, high fives all around. I don’t think this would be particularly narratively satisfying, but it would still be more narratively satisfying than what we got. And that is my pitch to let me take the Star Wars universe in a very bizarre direction.
