Name: Johan Torres
Question: What can Congress do to hold Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito accountable?
Answer: Congress’s role is to impeach him in the house, and then convict him in the senate. Which should have already happened to both him and Clarence Thomas. But one of the many, many, many, many, many, many, many flaws in the constitution is that the checks and balances system is based entirely on the concept that the branches of government would be competing with each other, and that one branch would not abrogate their own power in order to advance their political goals. So the Supreme Court can be comically corrupt and congress effectively won’t be able to do anything about it. Because a portion of congress does not want to do anything about it. Realistically they can issue subpoenas to force Alito and Thomas to testify. They can do that every day from now until forever. But they obviously don’t want to do that either. So, in actuality, nothing. Nothing is going to happen.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Are transgenders, non-binaries, and genderfluids more common than most people think?
Answer: They’re actually less common than people think. Significantly less common. According to a YouGov poll, the median American thinks 12% of people are transgender. Which is bananas. It would mean that every person knows dozens of trans people, which they clearly don’t. This partially explains some of the more draconian laws that have passed. Partially. My state, for example, passed a law that barred trans women from playing sports. The law affected a single girl. In a state with over eleven million people. It’s so rare to find a trans woman playing sports that most people will never actually meet one. But mostly those laws are just about cruelty. You see this all the time. Whenever people will complain about neopronouns, I want to ask them if they have ever, in their real life, met anyone who uses neopronouns? The chances are almost nonexistent. I’ve met a handful of non-binary people, mostly through work, and all of them use “they.” People will say things like “soaring numbers” or “explosive growth” about trans kids, and the actual numbers will be 161 (number of kids prescribed puberty blockers in a year) or 3,000 (the number simply referred to a gender clinic), out of a population of 14 million. So no, those groups are significantly less common that people think. We should just leave them alone to live their lives.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What were the initial reactions to the Acolyte's twin idea?
Answer: I thought the idea that they were identical twins was very silly and very soap opera, consequently the longer I thought about it, the more I liked it. Particularly since the show doesn’t drag out that element for very long. We find out almost immediately that Osha and Mae are identical twins. Jedi Master Sol insists that Mae is dead, so the only suspect in the murder mystery has to be Mae. And then when Osha is in custody, Mae commits another murder. Then they see each other and confirm that both are alive. A lesser show would have dragged out the identical twins plotline for the entire season. We know the sister is alive and the killer if not exactly at the end of the first episode, definitely by the end of the second. Rather than pad out this as a mystery (which already exists inside another mystery), we can get right to the emotional core of how they relate to each other as sisters. Which we are already starting to get, Osha deliberately misses firing a stun blast at Mae. My big problem is that Amandla Stenberg isn’t really giving a strong enough performance to carry this conceit. Osha is just being played as nice and helpful. While Mae doesn’t have the level of menace she really needs to pull this off. But on the whole it is extremely goofy and silly and I like it.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What are your thoughts on George Lucas addressing the critics who think Star Wars is "all white men"?
Answer: He’s being both very dumb and very disingenuous. “They would say, ‘It’s all white men,'” Lucas said of the films’ critics. “Most of the people are aliens! The idea is you’re supposed to accept people for what they are, whether they’re big and furry or whether they’re green or whatever. The idea is all people are equal.” It’s just objectively not true. In A New Hope there is an alien, Chewbacca, that could be considered a main character. There are also two droids, but he is ignoring them. Everyone else, hero or villain, is white. And everyone aside from Leia is a man. Who is the second most important alien character in that film? Greedo? It’s insulting to the audience to say that Chewbacca is representation for anyone not a white man. And it is lying to the audience to claim Chewbacca represents most of the people in the film. And Lucas tacitly admits this with what he says next. As for the issue of race, Lucas said, “In the first one, there were a few Tunisians who were dark, and in the second one I had Billy Williams, and the [prequels], which they were also criticizing, I had Sam Jackson. He wasn’t a scoundrel like Lando. He was one of the top jedi.” I could not even begin to tell you what characters those Tunisian actors played, if any. This was a flaw in the film that Lucas recognized and fixed in 1979 when he created Lando. There’s really no reason for him to be defensive over choices made fifty years ago, particularly when he, by his own admission, noticed and corrected them already. He went out and found someone with more charisma than Harrison Ford! I think Star Wars, under George Lucas, was inarguably about white people. The seven most important characters in those films are white people. I don’t think there is an argument to be made that any other character is more important and prominent than Luke, Leia, Han, Palpatine, Anakin, Obi-Wan and Padme. And that group is mostly men. We can acknowledge basic reality here. I think the themes were applicable beyond race and gender, and I think the characterization of Leia was amazing, and that Lando is a great character and a wonderful addition. All that can be true too. I actually think it is great that kids can relate to Chewbacca, Yoda, or R2-D2, but that’s not representation and it’s insulting to claim that it is. I think George Lucas is being defensive and over inflating certain things and making excuses. Rather that just acknowledging it was the ‘70s, he was doing his best, and he recognized certain flaws and worked to fix them.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Do you like or dislike the movie "A Deadly Adoption" based on its trailer?
Answer: I not only saw the trailer for A Deadly Adoption, I watched the entire movie. The joke of A Deadly Adoption is that Will Ferrell and Kristin Wiig are doing a Lifetime movie, and playing it completely straight. And it is not even a good Lifetime movie. The only time that either of them gives into the urge to play something for comedic effect is when Wiig falls into the lake, which is what causes her to miscarry and then be unable to conceive, leading to the titular deadly adoption. In that scene Wiig just goes ham with over acting and flailing ridiculousness. Now your enjoyment of this film is entirely dependent upon how much you like Lifetime movies. The script has a level of authenticity that lets you know this was genuinely an overly serious thriller that was written to be nothing more than made-for-TV schlock. It was pulled from a stack of nearly identical scripts because it so clearly typified the concept of a Lifetime movie. As someone who loves bad Lifetime movies, I enjoyed the hell out of it. Jessica Lowndes gives the perfect subdued and sober performance for a Lifetime villain. Jake Weary is in the film, and I love him. He’s always great for playing some kind of dirtbag lowlife. But obviously the stars are Wiig and Ferrell. Who are going out of their way to not give comedic performances. If you can’t get the joke of why they doing a Lifetime movie, then you probably won’t enjoy it. It’s just one made-for-TV movie length joke. And either that appeals to you, or it doesn’t. I certainly appeals to me.

Question: Why has LGBT become much more of a staple in mainstream cinema?
Answer: Because… If your media product features characters born between 1997 and 2012, 20% of those characters should be something other than straight. If your media product features characters born between 1981 and 1996, 10% of those characters should be something other than straight. Name: Johan Torres
Question: What are the reasons for the negative reception of "The Foundation" TV series and is it worth watching until the end?
Answer: Foundation is a really bad adaptation of one of the greatest sci-fi series of all time, that is also, somehow stapled onto a really good show of entirely original material. If you reedited the entire series so you cut out everything except for the Empire and Cleons you would have an amazing show. The Foundation novels are premised on the concept of psychohistory, which is the idea that, while you can’t predict what any individual is going to do, you can predict what large groups of people will do. Harri Seldon, who developed psychohistory, used it to predict the fall of the great galactic empire. But he set up two Foundations to be the core of a new empire to shorten thirty thousand years of chaos down to just one thousand. The central theme of the novels is that violence is the last refuge of the incompetent. This is stated many times. And the key to the Foundation’s success is that they trust psychohistory to show them the bright path to follow. The Foundation is made up of forward thinking people and scientists and they solve problems by being clever, not through violence. But, inevitably, there really was only one solution. The books are also structured so that there is a calamitous event, which is resolved by people rising to the occasion, and then time jumps forward. So the cast changes frequently. So, the TV show. The TV show is, for at least its first season, split into two parts. The first is the events taking place on the Foundation, on the far edge of the galaxy. The second is the heart of the Empire on Trantor. Because the books continuously jump forward in time, the show has to come up with all sorts of bizarre ways to keep its cast present and basically the same age despite huge gaps in time happening. The best way is how the empire is handled. When Cleon the First became emperor he decided that there was no reason for anyone else to rule. So he instituted the Genetic Dynasty. The Empire would be ruled by three clones of him, which would be continuously rotated. So there would always be a Brother Dawn who was a youth, a Brother Day who was middle aged, and a Brother Dusk who was elderly. This is all original to the show and is not from the novels at all. These three clones are trying to preserve the Empire, while also engaging in complex political moves. All of which reveals the utterly hollow core of the Empire leading it to die. Everything in this part of the show is brilliant and riveting television. The characters are great, and the actors playing them do a fantastic job. And the show is really good at figuring how how the ruling triumvirate, which technically has unlimited power, has to work within failing and diseased system. Also the second season is great for showing how the kind of extreme narcissism that makes a person decide that three clones of himself should rule an empire in perpetuity probably means their other choices will be pretty poor. The other half of the show is set on the Foundation home world, Terminus. And it is just a mess. Sloppy and inconstant writing. Characters making baffling choices. Everything undermines the central theme that violence is the last refuge of the incompetent. It just is unmoored from anything real. And the ways they came up with to have the same main characters regardless of how many time jumps occur get real silly. Some of this improves in season two, but then we get another narrative split and a third of the show becomes engulfed in this ludicrous plot about a planet of psychics. And it is genuinely hard to reconcile that you are essentially getting two shows at once, one which is very good and the other which is very bad. I think the good show is worth sitting through the bad show. The good show stars Lee Pace! but I can’t make that determination for you.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Has Marvel Studios lost its touch?
Answer: I think, really, it has lost its ability to surprise. And the tone has become so consistent and so oppressive that it just feels banal. The MCU set itself up, starting right from Iron Man, that every character was Spider-Man. Every character is a fast talking wise guy who makes the funny quips. Iron Man, in the MCU, got a personality transplant from Spider-Man, except that the switch previously set to “self-deprecating” got flipped to “arrogant.” By the time Joss Whedon got his hands on The Avengers every character was now just Spider-Man. Every MCU movie is going to be a fantastic romp where the characters make the funny quips and darkness will always be undermined with a joke. Which is fine for a superhero movie. But it is just Spider-Man. Doctor Strange is just Spider-Man with magic. Iron Man is just Spider-Man with money. Shang-Chi is just Spider-Man but Asian. Ant-Man is just Spider-Man but with ants. It's all Spider-Man. With a few notable exceptions they are just giving us the same Spider-Man movie endlessly. Again, with some notable exceptions, the audience just watched the same Spider-Man movie 40 different times. Which will, inevitably, result in diminished rewards from that movie. The MCU exists to be a conveyor belt on which IP gets cut up and stuffed into a box and then sold as content. Really good directors can still wring gold from that process. Most notably James Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy and Ryan Coogler on Black Panther. But it is designed to produce the same consistent product. And that said let me give you the best scene in the entire MCU: Yes, it is the hallway fight scene in the Netflix Daredevil TV show. In fact, the first season of Daredevil might be the best the MCU has ever been. But if Daredevil had come first and been a hit, then I would probably be complaining that every MCU movie is just Daredevil… the way Warner Bros. tried to make every DC movie Batman (until they course corrected by making them all Spider-Man). The next phase of the MCU is going to focus on the Fanstastic Four and the X-Men, the two Marvel properties closest to my heart. And I am kind of dreading them because they will be crushed into the gruel of the MCU. The Fantastic Four, I think, can survive that. The X-Men just can't. Possibly the best thing Marvel has ever done is X-Men ’97 and it does not resemble the MCU at all, even at its silliest. I do not trust the MCU is capable of giving a moment as honest and raw and ambitious and subversive as Val Cooper's “Magneto was right” speech. The degree that the MCU has lost its touch is the degree that it has just naturally diminished due to forcing the same story out over and over. And, regardless, whatever MCU movie anyone currently thinks is terrible will, inevitably, be defended in the future as strongly as people now defend the Star Wars prequels.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: In your opinion, was Luke's character ruined in Star Wars: The Force Awakens?
Answer: Not particularly, but if you have qualms about how Luke was portrayed in The Last Jedi… The Force Awakens forced those choices upon the narrative. "He was training a new generation of Jedi. One boy, an apprentice turned against him, destroyed it all. Luke felt responsible… He just walked away from everything." - Han Solo, The Force Awakens J.J. Abrams, by his own admission, had no clue what to do with Luke. So he just… didn’t. The trouble was a simple case of upstaging. “It just felt like every time Luke came in and entered the movie, he just took it over,” Arndt said. “Suddenly you didn’t care about your main character anymore because, ‘Oh f–k, Luke Skywalker’s here. I want to see what he’s going to do.’” Abrams made the choice the Luke’s new Jedi order was destroyed and then Luke abandoned the galaxy. And that nothing, not the rise of the First Order, not the death of Han, not that planet blowing up, was going to get him off that island. He just hangs out until Rey shows up. Luke’s storyline in The Last Jedi is just… following through on all the choices that Abrams made in The Force Awakens. That and trying to make them make sense. Luke is holed up exactly like Obi-Wan and Yoda both were. Luke is cut off from the Force, which is why he didn’t react to his best friend’s death. Luke doesn’t want to train Rey because he watched all his new Jedi get slaughtered by his own pupil. It is all logically and emotionally consistent. It’s really funny the amount of shit Rian Johnson got for being stuck with the ball Abrams punted. Abrams couldn’t figure out how to integrate Luke into his story, and so just reduced him to the status of MacGuffin. Honestly Abrams wasn’t even consistent with himself. Luke is supposedly searching for the original Jedi Temple, but also there is a map that leads directly to him. So Luke is simultaneously searching but also staying still. And honestly, the more you think about the map, the stupider the conceit gets. Luke creates a map to be found, but does not give it to anyone he might want to find him. You can just email Leia your location, Luke. You don’t need to put it on a thumb drive and just hope it gets passed around to her at some point. Once more, everything people were mad about Rian Johnson doing in The Last Jedi was actually something J.J. Abrams did in The Force Awakens.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Are there too many female characters in Star Wars now? Why or why not?
Answer: Well there’s Leia, whose actor died. There’s Padme Amidala, whose character died. There’s Jyn Erso, whose character died. There’s Doctor Aphra, who is comics only. Then there’s Mon Mothma, Rey, and Ahsoka. And it feels kind of disingenuous to put Mon Mothma here, even if she was effectively the second lead of Andor. Then there are the B through D tier characters: Rose, Vice Admiral Hodo, Captain Phasma, Mother Talzin, Asajj Ventress, Andor's mother, the Twi’lek pilot and the teen Mandalorian and that one Imperial funky in Star Wars Rebels (I only watched the first season and that was awhile ago), there's that blonde imperial officer in Andor (I like her), that law officer played by that woman who went on to make movies for the Daily Wire, there's poor dead Aunt Beru, there's poor dead Anakin's mother. Oh, and that Inquisitor who was fighting ol’ Ben Kenobi. Doesn't Starbuck play a character in one of these shows? Also that giant worm thing Han Solo was working for in Solo. And, of course, beloved Star Wars character Daenerys Targaryen. Wait… is the Acolyte female? With the exception of Ahsoka and Rey (and Jyn, but that was just the once) there are no female leads in all of Star Wars. And you could probably name two to three male characters from any given series for every single one of the female characters important enough to actually remember. So no, I don't think there are too many female characters. I think there are not enough female characters. There is no female character in all of Star Wars with a name as silly as “Savage Oppress” or “Count Dooku.” Which is just downright sexist if you ask me. Everyone knows the Mandalorian and Baby Yoda, they don't remember that lady who went on to do Terror on the Pairie. Sure you know Rey, but there is also Finn and Poe and Han Solo and Chewbacca and Kylo Ren and Luke and Hux and somehow Palpatine returned.

Question: Are there any hotter characters in the Star Trek franchise than T’Pol?
Answer: Vulcans are known for being hot. Vulcan is a desert planet, and in “The Deadly Years” Spock had to increase the temperature of his room to 125 degrees. This is probably why Vulcans seem relatively rare in Starfleet, standard human temperature is likely quite cold for them. However Tholians are much hotter than Vulcans. Tholians are crystalline life forms. And their standard temperature is 404 degrees. So any time you see a Tholian, for example Loskene from “The Tholian Web,” they will be much hotter than any Vulcan you might see.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Who are the main characters in "Star Trek" and "Star Wars"? Which character is more popular among fans of both franchises and what makes them stand out?
Answer: The protagonist of Star Wars is Anakin Skywalker. The secondary protagonist is Luke Skywalker. The tertiary protagonist is Rey Palpatine. Anakin is the protagonist of the prequel trilogy. And the nature of the prequel trilogy retroactively made the original trilogy also about him and his journey as a character. He is also one the four or so main protagonists of The Clone Wars TV show, and probably the most important, aside from Ashoka (who over the course of the series takes a more and more central role). Luke is the protagonist of the original trilogy. And, to a large extent, the prequel trilogy is about how he came to be born. And he is the secondary protagonist of The Last Jedi. At least two of the numbered films refer to him by title. Rey Palpatine is the protagonist of the sequel trilogy. She is also the only Star Wars protagonist to have a numbered film refer to her by name, as opposed to title. And her existence (and “somehow Palpatine returned”) kind of makes the entire original trilogy about her, if not the entire prequel trilogy too. All that stuff in The Phantom Menace was part one of a billion to get to her. Those three are the main characters of Star Wars, in descending order of their importance. Star Wars is about them. The protagonist of Star Trek is Spock. The secondary protagonist is James T. Kirk. The tertiary protagonist is Jean-Luc Picard. Star Trek is a bit more of a tricky beast, as there is just more of it and it lacks the strict hierarchy of importance that Star Wars has. With the exception of Discovery and Lower Decks, the captain is the main character of every Star Trek series. Nonetheless, despite Spock never being the main character of any particular Star Trek series, he is the main character of the franchise as a whole. He was a series regular on four different shows. He has major appearances in The Next Generation. He is in nine movies, including two where multiple actors are playing him. He’s the only Star Trek character to ever get named in the title of a film. And if you look at Star Trek as a whole there just isn’t any other character who is as important to so much of the franchise. Much of what is true about Spock is also true about Kirk. He is, inarguably the main character of the original series, and the protagonist of all the TOS movies, as well as all the reboot movies. He’s in one of The Next Generation movies, and he is a recurring character on Strange New Worlds. Picard is the star of two different TV shows, and is the only Star Trek character to ever be named in the title to a TV show. The Next Generation was more successful than the original series, it also drastically departed from it in tone and style in a way that all Star Trek shows are still drawing from. Every captain since Picard is, in some since, a response to him (far more so than Kirk). I think that any honest appraisal of Star Trek as a whole would come to these three being the main characters. I can see arguments for ranking them differently than I ranked them. Out of these characters, if there is a Star Wars character that both Star Wars and Star Trek fans like the most, it would be Luke Skywalker. He is in the most consistent and beloved movies. He has the best character arc. Everyone loves Darth Vader, but you had to be a certain age to not loath Anakin. And Rey is… let’s just call her divisive. But everyone loves Luke. If there is a Star Trek character that both Star Wars and Star Trek fans like, I think it would be a toss up between either Picard or Spock. I don’t think Kirk is winning that race. I want to say Picard would win, but Spock would be loved enough for it to be extremely competitive. Picard is the eloquent statesman of Star Trek, played by beloved actor Patrick Stewart.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Can someone with superpowers become immune to their weaknesses?
Answer: For a really long time, Green Lantern’s powers were useless against anything colored yellow. We lamped him out! At a certain point the writers of Green Lantern decided the yellow weakness was just extremely stupid. And so Green Lantern simply no longer was bothered by yellow. Originally this was that his will was so great it overcame the yellow weakness. And then they just got rid of it all together. I would argue that, with the exception of kryptonite, this is the normal course characters take. Writers will carefully set up a limitation, and that limitation gets demolished because the most satisfying narrative choice is to overcome the limitation. Iron Fist, for example, could originally only use the Iron Fist once per day. Now he can use it whenever he wants. It’s just the way stories work.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is K'un-Lun?
Answer: K’un-Lun is one of the Seven Capital Cities of Heaven, in the Iron Fist comics. Each of the seven cities is lost, as they exist in a pocket dimension which only intersects with Earth at a certain rotation. Every eighty-eight years this rotation synchs up, and all the cities merge, creating the Heart of Heaven. Each city then sends its greatest warrior (known as the Immortal Weapons) to the Tournament of the Heavenly Cities, the outcome of which determines the next celestial order. K’un-Lun, and its immortal weapon the Iron Fist, is the preeminent city and consistently wins the tournament. This allows it to appear most frequently on Earth, once every ten years. The access point for K’un-Lun exists in the real Kunlun mountains in Tibet. The original inhabitants of K’un-Lun were sentient plants called the H'ylthri. About a million years ago a spaceship carrying humanoid aliens of an unknown species crashed into K’un-Lun. These aliens built the city of K’un-Lun and pushed the H'ylthri out into a much more precarious life on the cliffs, leading to an enormous degree of hostility. The most important inhabitant of K’un-Lun is Shou-Lao, the Undying, a massive dragon. At the dawn of the civilization of K’un-Lun Shou-Lao went into a rage and attacked the city. A man named Quan-St'ar saved the city by slaying the dragon by cutting out its heart. But the dragon was revived, and its heart was melted and placed into a brazier. The only way to defeat the dragon is to physically block the flow of chi from its heart to its body, an act that leaves a distinctive brand on whoever is successful in doing so. Then the victor can put his or her fists into the molten heart of Shou-Lao and access its chi in order to make their fists like unto a thing of iron. The first to ever do this was a woman named Fan Fei, who had left K’un-Lun and showed the primitive hominids that lived around the city the sacred art of Kung Fu. When this was discovered she was sentenced to execution by Shou-Lao, but managed to defeat him and become the first Iron Fist. She eventually joined the Avengers of 1,000,000 BC. As important as Shou-Lao is the Tree of Immortality. The fruit of the tree renders whoever eats it immortal. They are still able to die of accident or illness, but not from old age. K’un-Lun is ruled by Yu-Ti, the August Personage in Jade. Yu-Ti is a title, and not a name. The actual individual is Nu-An, the son of the original Yu-Ti and the adopted brother of Wendell Rand, the father of Danny Rand. Nu-An was extremely corrupt and fairly evil. And almost anything he said should be assumed to be a combination of half-truths and lies. Technology is strictly forbidden in K’un-Lun, except for the fact that underneath all those ancient buildings is a vast network of advanced computers. The final step of becoming the Iron Fist is called the Challenge of the One where the candidate has to defeat a seemingly undefeatable opponent, which is revealed to be a robot. Furthermore the robot is actually undefeatable, it can only be beaten when Yu-Ti chooses it to lose. Despite the fact that no outsider is worthy of being the Iron Fist, the One is specifically programed to maim or kill any naturally born citizen of K’un-Lun to ensure only outsiders are able to become the Iron Fist. Even though K’un-Lun only appears once a decade on Earth, there are wholly technological gates underneath the city that allow people to come and go as they please. Provided you know of their existence and can gain access. The principle trainer in K’un-Lun is entitled the Thunderer. His role is to ensure that K’un-Lun always has an Iron Fist to act as its protector. Although every Iron Fist is, seemingly inevitably, drawn into the greater world of Earth. K’un-Lun is extremely sexist and women are forbidden from learning Kung Fu. But the Thunderer Lei-Kung secretly trained women. Also slavery is still practiced in K’un-Lun. Yu-Ti is assisted by four Dragon Lords who… are lords who turn into dragons. The Iron Fist is referred to as “The Immortal Iron Fist” because there will always be an Iron Fist. The position is immortal, not the person. Iron Fists actually die quite frequently. The Iron Fist comics are really good (the show… less so…). Particularly the original comics from the ’70s and the Immortal Iron Fist series. K'un-Lun is a really interesting location. It is a lot “mystical east” orientalism, which occasionally borders on racist. But there are also all these sci-fi and steam punk elements. And while the entire Iron Fist canon is an example of a (white) outsider becoming the champion of a people, better than they, themselves, are… it’s also a fascinating deconstruction of that trope. And all this strange dichotomies go back to those original Kung-Fu comics from the ‘70s. K’un-Lun is a land of enlightened monks… but also violently pushed out the indigenous people. K’un-Lun is a sexist society that doesn’t teach women martial arts…. but also they absolutely do. K’un-Lun is a mystical society that shuns technology… but also there are robots and the entire city is built on top of highly advanced machinery. K’un-Lun only appears for one day every ten years… but also there are all sorts of ways to get there. Danny Rand is the champion of K’un-Lun… but is he, though? K’un-Lun isn’t a Potemkin village that exists just for Danny’s benefit… but also it kind of is. Danny wasn’t the best, he was the one Yu-Ti wanted. Also, that they are aliens comes from a Marvel Handbook entry, and I have never seen it in any of the comics. The Avengers of 1,000,000 BC is a terrible nonsense retcon. But, in Iron Fist’s case there actually is an explanation for how K’un-Lun could exist a million years ago.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Who currently owns the rights to Tarzan? Has Disney acquired the rights through their multiple movie adaptations?
Answer: Sony currently has the trademark rights to Tarzan. The first thirteen Tarzan novels are in the public domain, along with twelve movies. So the copyright is owned by everyone. Based on my understanding, this means that Disney could make a Tarzan movie… they just couldn’t call it “Tarzan” in any advertising without violating Sony’s trademark. And there’s no real value in making a Tarzan film that can’t be advertised as Tarzan. If you look on the Disney Store or Amazon, there’s no Tarzan merchandise, because they don’t own the trademark.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why is the lost city of Punt not a commonly discussed topic?
Answer: The biggest reason is that there isn’t a really good story attached to it. For most of Western human history the two big lost civilizations were Atlantis and Troy. Those came to us from stories written by Plato and Homer, two of the most important writers in human history. And they were stories, full of narrative drama. Troy turned out to be real, Atlantis didn’t. While Punt appears in stories, most of our information about it comes from descriptions of trade or state visits between it and Egypt. We know it was somewhere south of Egypt. We know that it was rich in gold, spices, and wood. We know that it was the source for much of Egypt's perfume ingredients. We know it lasted at least 1,500 years, stretching from 2500 BC up until 1100 BC, if not later. And we know that it was so important that Egypt, with reasonable regularity, sent import political figures to Punt as a state visit. Queen Hatshepsut made a visit to Punt that was considered so important that her tomb has reliefs depicting it. We know that wherever Punt was, they had Secretarybirds because the only depiction of them in ancient Egypt comes from Hatshepsut’s tomb depicting her trip there. But for everything the Egyptians recorded about Punt… they didn’t actually record where it was located. It’s just somewhere south of Egypt that can be sailed to from the Red Sea. The most likely place is that it is somewhere in Eritrea. And that’s based on, of all things, DNA analysis of mummified baboons. Punt was the source of Egypt’s baboons. So there is a fantastic lost civilization somewhere south of Egypt that lasted for over a thousand years. Anything we could recover from Punt would be a treasure for all of humanity. There might not even be much to find, as sad as that might be. Their building materials probably weren’t stone, and the climate where Punt is located is a lot less conducive to preservation than the deserts of Egypt. But finding Punt would be up there with Göbekli Tepe as one of the most important archeological sites humans ever produced. But there isn’t a story associated with Punt. Egypt traded with Punt for 1,500 years and then just stopped mysteriously. We don’t know when Punt started nor do we know when it stopped. We only know when goods from Punt started appearing in Egypt and when Egypt not longer seems to mention them. The story of Atlantis is really good. The story of Sodom and Gomorrah are also really good. The story of Troy is really good. There’s no story to Punt. And, let’s be honest, Punt was absolutely an African civilization. Egypt, the African civilization that gets the biggest pass, still gets hit with the “Aliens built the pyramids.” For most of the history of archelogy, white Europeans and Americans are not going to spend a huge amount of time looking for a lost African civilization. If anything, a lot of them would consider the concept an oxymoron. There are a lot of African civilizations we know tons about, much more than Punt, and almost no one talks about them. The Ghana Empire lasted for 500 years and was hugely important. No one ever talks about it. Personally I find Punt fascinating. I hope I live long enough for someone to find it. I wish more people talked about it. Not just because every detail we have of it is important in its own right, part of our shared history as humans. But also because the more people who are interested in finding it, the more likely archeologists will be able to get funding to go look for it. Of course the place they would want to start looking for it is Eritrea, which has its own, unique political problems. Where is Punt? Where is it?

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What's a historical mystery or unsolved question that you wish you had the answer to?
Answer: Where’s Punt? Punt was a trading partner with Egypt from at least the Fifth Dynasty (and there’s evidence of items from Punt even earlier from the Fourth Dynasty) in 2500 BC up until at least the Twentieth Dynasty in 1150 BC. Egypt received gold, ivory, ebony, incense, aromatic resins, animal skins, live animals, eye-makeup cosmetics, fragrant woods, and cinnamon in trade with Punt. The historical record is, obviously, extremely spotty for anything this old, nonetheless there is a relatively huge number of attestations to trade between Egypt and Punt, as well as expeditions to Punt, and even state visits. The Pharaoh Hatshepsut has reliefs of her travel to Punt on the wall of her tomb. But… for all that they did write about Punt, the one thing the Egyptians didn’t write was where, exactly, it was. It was somewhere south of Egypt, and they traveled there by boat on the red sea. But no one knows where that was. There’s actually a pretty vast region where people have guessed Punt might be, covering everything from Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Eritrea, and Yemen. Traditionally it is has been placed somewhere in the horn of Africa. But one of the things we know Egypt got from Punt were baboons. And DNA analysis on mummified baboons has shown they came from Eritrea and Ethiopia. Of course its boarders might have changed a great deal over its long history. The fact that the most probable location for it is Eritrea is… distressing. Eritrea is a closed off military dictatorship known as “Africa’s North Korea.” Although it seems to be even more repressive than North Korea. So there’s no going in to look around for Punt. But this is a genuine lost civilization. One possibly as old a Egypt, and one that lasted for at least 1,500 years. Finding Punt would be a more important to archeology, anthropology, and human history than when Troy was discovered. I really don’t understand why there is so much obsession over Atlantis, when Punt really does exist…. somewhere. Where is Punt? WHERE IS IT!

Question: How come no X-Men or Fantastic Four characters appear in the video game Lego Marvel Super Heroes 2, unlike the first Lego Marvel Super Heroes game?
Answer: In the mid-2010s, when the MCU was cresting to its peak, real life super villian Ike Perlmutter got irrationally angry at Fox, believing they owed Marvel (and thus him) money. “Owed” is a much stronger word than is accurate, Fox was following all the contracts it had signed with Marvel when it bought the film rights to the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Perlmutter simply believed the rights were under sold, and so he deserved more money. Perlmutter was the CEO of Marvel, and thus it was in his power to kill the X-Men and the Fantastic Four stone cold dead as brands. Perlmutter's motivation seems to be that if he did as much damage to those two brands as he could, then Fox would be willing to renegotiate the contracts. So Marvel entered a period where the X-Men and Fantastic Four were persona non gratta by Marvel. There has always been a rumor that Perlmutter went into the Marvel offices and saw someone with a Fantastic Four poster on their cubicle and he ripped it down and then ripped it up in front of them. Normally I am not one to give much credence to rumors, but that story is in line with every other story I have heard about Perlmutter. There is a long list of news items that came out over those years about the X-Men and Fantastic Four being dropped as characters. And in a rare spirit of unanimity, CBR also confirmed that the Fantastic Four comics were to go on "hiatus". Mondo Posters confirmed they were unable to make Fantastic Four posters anymore. Gazillion execs say they got in trouble for including the Fantastic Four in Marvel Heroes game update. The Marvel Heroes ID posters lost the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Statue lines featuring the Fantastic Four or the X-Men were cancelled in mid-sculpt. Trading cards could no longer be reprinted. Fantastic Four was snubbed in 'Marvel's Greatest Collections'. They were not part of the Star Wars Welcome Home posters. There were no Fantastic Four or X-Men T-shirts anymore, and such characters were removed from group shots. Marvel pulled permission for an art show — but only for the Fantastic Four characters. Foreign comics saw Fantastic Four characters removed from strips, and it was confirmed to me that Panini was not allowed to publish translated Fantastic Four comics. This all culminated in the straight up cancelation of the Fantastic Four comic. But in this period there were no toys, no cartoons, and no video games. Marvel strictly forbid its licensees from using those two properties. I will also say that Marvel spent this entire time period lying. I don’t think I have ever seen a corporation put so much effort into gaslighting its own customers as Marvel did. Marvel had many, many employees insist that this wasn’t happening and that the fans of the X-Men and Fantastic Four were being paranoid for claiming it was. Tom Brevoort, who is about to become the X-Men editor, straight up lied to retailers claiming the Fantastic Four comic was not going to be canceled only a few months prior to the announcement it was canceled. I have an extraordinary degree of contempt for him. Lego Marvel Superheroes comes out in 2013, and is filled with X-Men and Fantastic Four characters. Nearly thirty playable characters are from those two franchises, and the mansion and the Baxter Building are both important locations. Lego Marvel Superheroes 2 comes out in 2017 and there are zero. And, wow, the game developers made some deep cuts to fill out the games roster, making the absences that much more obvious. No Storm or Thing, but it does have Arizona Girl, a character from Wild West #1 in 1948 and only has ten appearances in her entire existence. Surely you are aware of beloved Marvel character Arizona Girl and are excited to see her in a video game as opposed to a minor character like *checks notes* someone named “Doctor Doom.” Given the development cycle for video games, I bet Lego Marvel Superheroes was one of the last times Marvel agreed to let a licensee use those characters. But, since we are talking about video games and Marvel declaring the X-Men and Fantastic Four forbidden, the absolute most bananas example was Marvel vs. Capcom Infinite. Where Capcom’s people were stuck trying to explain why characters who had been in every incarnation of the franchise were not included without just saying Marvel was out of its gourd. There was recently a leak about the characters, and people picked up on the fact that a lot of classic characters aren't there, specifically the X-Men characters like Magneto and Sentinel. How do you guys feel about people being hung up on that? Peter Rosas: If you were to actually think about it, these characters are just functions. They're just doing things. Magneto, case and point, is a favorite because he has eight-way dash and he's really fast, right? So our more technical players, all they want to do is triangle jump and that kind of stuff. Well guess what, Nova can do the same thing, Captain Marvel can do the same thing. Ultron can do the same thing. Go ahead and try them out. It's just the function that people are associating with the character, and there's no shortage of that. We made sure that all proper play styles can be represented with our current roster. The design team has been looking at that very closely. We wanted to make sure that if a legacy character doesn't happen to make the roster this time, that play style would still be represented. That somebody who has associated themselves with Magneto wouldn't be lost coming into this title. Michael Evans: The other thing is, you mentioned returning characters right? If you look at the returning characters and you play with them, you'll notice that they're quite different from their previous iterations. Iron Man, he plays completely different. He has new special moves. Obviously we wanted to keep fan-favorite characters, but since you have the new system they're gonna play differently. In addition to that, new special moves, new hypers, new level threes in some cases, these breathe new life into these characters even if they are returning. So we did definitely make an attempt to do that. The X-Men stuff, [I] can't talk to. But I do want to talk about the character-selection process because I think it's important. There's three things we're looking at: Gameplay first and foremost of course. The Capcom R&D team and us, we get together and we talk with Marvel about what characters we want to put in. From a character-type perspective, we want our big brawler characters, our characters that can fly, our small characters or whatever. Just from a creative side, gameplay, here's the characters we want. That plays a part. One of the first things we did was sit down to write the story. When we were thinking about the story we wanted to tell, as fans ourselves on both sides, on the Marvel side there's Mike Jones, an ex-Capcom guy. We're big Marvel fans, so we're sitting down to just like, "What crazy interactions do we want to see? What would happen if Docket, Dante, and Rocket came together? What would happen and who are these pairings that we want to see?" So from a storytelling perspective that also played into the character selection. Then the third one is obviously the popularity of these characters. X was one we had to get in there. A lot of fans wanted to see X, so we brought him back. Then also we talked with Marvel very closely about their future roadmap, about what's gonna be happening. Your modern Marvel fan, maybe they don't even remember some of the X-Men characters, but they know some of the Guardians characters or Black Panther. You know what I mean? Captain Marvel may seem like a strange pick, but she's fantastic. She fits the gameplay. She fits the story, and they're gonna be really pushing her as a strong female lead all the way up into the movie. We're trying to take everything into account and choose the best characters. The characters are just functions, man. They do stuff on the screen, like dash! Capcom is spending all this money to license these characters from Marvel because you can’t, like, make a stick figure that dashes. And any wany, obviously no one even remembers the X-Men in the first place. This remains one of the most ludicrous examples of corporate human speak I have ever seen. Any way, that’s why the X-Men and the Fantastic Four were missing.

Question: Do you believe that the movie industry will eventually become centered around streaming platforms like Netflix?
Answer: They tried that and essentially failed. Which resulted in the complete immolation of the entire entertainment industry. The profits of the media companies fell by 90% over the course of a decade as they decided to pursue streaming, just setting every means of making profit on fire in the hopes that maybe they can figure out something down the line to make money for them. Streaming swiftly killed the home video market, DVD and Blu-Ray sales collapsed by 90%. Then it slowly killed the theatrical release and television industries. This… this disaster is entirely because the movie industry centered around streaming. Everything bounced back from the pandemic… except the entertainment industry. They trained their own audiences not to spend money on their product. Which is a hilarious self-own. And 2024’s box office is looking like it will be even worse. Every disfunction in the entertainment industry right now is directly attributable to streaming. Warner Bros. complete collapse as a company is due to streaming. Streaming is just not a profitable system. Which was first learned by the music industry and then the movie and TV industry. There is no way to make a $150 million dollar movie profitable through streaming. In any other situation, Netflix would be considered a disaster, it’s profits are lower than Paramount’s was a decade ago. It’s actually never paid out a dividend to its shareholders, and most of its stated profits seems to be made up of interesting accounting and aggressive spin. And it is doing better than everyone else. In 1974, HBO launched with a price point of $6.50. That would be $41.34 in today’s money. And that seems like about the right price to make streaming as profitable as TV was. And even then it would not be able to budget $100 million plus movies. Game of Thrones was only like $15 million per-episode. I don’t think there is a solution to this. Every entertainment company chased a dragon believing it would supplement their existing revenue. And it wound up eating all their sources of revenue, while producing something far more anemic. They’re stuck. We’re stuck. And, eventually, everything will be adjusted to the reality that all profits will have to be eked out from a business model that is objectively significantly less profitable than everything that came before it. Prepare not for Netflix, but for YouTube dominance.

Question: What's your review of The Strangers: Chapter 1?
Answer: The Strangers: Chapter 1 is the first part of a trilogy of Strangers movies that were all filmed concurrently. Due to this, it might either be better or worse in hindsight, depending upon where the next two movies go. On its own, The Strangers: Chapter 1 is a decent horror movie, but far too derivative of the original. Ryan and Maya are two rich New Yorkers, moving to Portland, Oregon after a job opportunity. They wind up in a small rural town full of creepy people. And their car beaks down. There is no hotel in town, but there is an Airbnb, in the middle of the woods. From that point on it is the standard Strangers plotline. A girl knocks on the door asking if Tamera is there. People in masks are already inside the house. And then lots of violence. The big thing this movie does correctly is that it really makes you care about the central couple. They are really fun, funny, and sweet. I really enjoyed their interactions. I was scared for them. I felt sad when something bad happened to them. They are two of the dumbest horror movie protagonists I have seen in awhile, but I still really liked them. And Maya, at least, is going to have to carry this trilogy to its conclusion, so that’s a good thing. But the film as a whole relies heavily on all The Strangers’s tricks. There are so many scenes that only work because the Strangers have a preternatural knowledge of the exact range of vision of Ryan and Maya. They are somehow always able to find their prey, even when the area expands into a giant woods. And the whole film is lacking in surprise because this is the third film in the franchise and is just doing what the others did. The problem The Strangers faces is that there really isn’t anywhere to take the franchise. It really shouldn’t be a franchise, as opposed to terrifying original film. Most horror movies transition the antagonists into the position of the protagonists (as happened to Freddy and Jason). But the whole point of The Strangers is that the audience does not know who these people are of why they are doing this. Every Strangers movie features the protagonists asking the Strangers why they are doing this and the answer is always “because you were home.” Which is chilling and evocative. But also means the franchise is simply going to repeat the same beats over and over. Which The Strangers Chapter 1 does. But then again, this might be the new trilogy establishing that it can do a The Strangers film. And the next two films might be more interesting and experimental. It is a kind of cheap trick to get me invested in seeing what Chapters 2 and 3 might be. But since I really enjoyed Madelaine Petsch and Froy Gutierrez as Maya and Ryan, I am going to stick around to see if their story resolves well.

Question: How do the new Disney-made 'Star Wars' movies compare to the original episodes 1-6?
Answer: They are extremely messy. They are better than the prequels, because while being extremely messy they at least are competently made (the prequels are messy and incompetently made). But they aren’t anywhere as good as the original trilogy. The biggest flaw was that Disney wanted a Star Wars film in theaters every year from now until forever. There would only be two years between films, as opposed to the normal three years of both previous trilogies. And in between would be spin off films. In order to accommodate this punishing schedule, Disney decided to farm out each film to a different director who would be in preproduction with his film prior to the other film’s being released. This is a completely nuts way to make a trilogy of films. If you are making a sequel, you should be able to see the previous film. Disney made the terrible idea to hire J.J. Abrams. Abrams writes in a style known as “mystery box.” You can even find a Ted Talk he gave about this. He creates a mystery, which will lead to audience speculation and engagement. And then he leaves the project before he ever has to pay off those mysteries. That’s someone else’s job. The Force Awakens is an empty, hollow film. That is specifically designed only to function as a receptacle for audience speculation. It is just a banal retread of the original trilogy. It is a film that is all red herrings. The new characters of Rey, Finn and Poe are fine, but very quickly you understand they aren’t well thought out. And enjoy the start of nonsense erratic character arcs, since three people are at the steering wheel. Everything that is wrong with the sequel trilogy is traceable back to this film. The Last Jedi is the best film of the bunch. It pays off most of the completely empty promises of The Force Awakens in the only way they could possibly be paid off well. It does a bunch of annoying things, though. And the fact that it has to be a grand Star Wars numbered film hurts it a lot. If you just stripped it down to its core chase narrative, it would be a much better film. The Rise of Skywalker is incompetently made. It is a complete mess. Clearly no one had any idea what was going on when making it. If someone claimed it was the worst Star Wars film ever, I wouldn’t argue with them. And when Rey and Kylo Ren kiss I started laughing uncontrollably in the theater. “Somehow Palpatine returned” is the most iconic line in all of Star Wars and I will be quoting it until the day I die. The sequels are a bad trilogy that does not work at all. But they at least have enough interesting ideas that supplemental material could hammer them into something interesting. Which is what happened with the prequels.

Question: Do you think Lucy MacLean is the best new character in Prime Video's Fallout series?
Answer: She is easily my favorite character. I assume there is a big contingent of fans who like Walton Goggins’s Ghoul better. But Lucy is just the best. During one of these every three years exchanges, Raiders break into Vault 33 and kidnap Lucy’s father, who is the current overseer. Pretty soon she is cutting the head off a corpse and destroying robot doctors. Lucy’s catchphrase is “Okie dokie.” Which is just so perfect. Lucy is silly, funny, and bad ass throughout the entire season. She is such a great character, and such a perfect encapsulation of what Fallout is about. Question: What do you think of the argument that no improvement can last and progress is an illusion in X-Men comics?
Answer: It’s true. It’s entirely true. We’re living through the absolute evidence of it right now. The Krakoa era featured mutants forming their own nation, free of poverty and want. They undid the many, many previous genocides. They explored space, colonized a planet, rescued millions of mutants from a dimension that was (technically) not hell. They were functionally at peace with humanity. They had co-opted or neutralized all their enemies. They had achieved something that while neither Xavier nor Magneto’s precise dream was a hybrid of both. It was the single longest period of uninterrupted progress for mutantdom in the history of the comics. And we are literally in the middle of the fall of Krakoa. In fact, from the very first issue of “House of X” we knew this would happen. The most interesting Krakoa stories were about how unprecedented success was ultimately a bitter fruit, but no matter how great the success would be… we all knew it would not last. This is a line from Asher Elbein’s brilliant essay, “The Judgement of Magneto” which was recently quoted by IGN. Read enough X-Men comics, and you’ll notice that the fundamental feature of the franchise—the idea of mutants as eternal stand-ins for Jews, or black people, or queer people—is its essential pessimism. In X-Men, minority life is wholly defined by oppression. No improvement can last; progress is always an illusion; as figures in an ongoing, eternal piece of intellectual property, mutants must always be hated and feared. This enforced, recursive Marvel-Time unwittingly echoes what we might call Jewish-Time: the idea that Jewish people were, are, and always will be oppressed by antisemitism, cast as the same villain in different costumes. Persia is Rome, Russia is Germany. Rather than discrete historical occurrences—contingent, contested, complex—they are foreordained, essential, and inescapable. There is only the pogrom, forever. It should be noted that Elbein is a Jewish writer, writing specifically about the Jewish nature of Magneto. If the X-Men are able to secure Xavier’s dream, or even just enough of it, then the stories are over. They no longer have a reason to exist. The X-Men aren’t people, they are corporate intellectual property whose existence is predicated upon being hated and feared by other people in their fictional universe. Progress exists only to be set back. Prior to Krakoa the longest period of uninterrupted progress for mutants was immediately after the destruction of Genosha. That ended with the Decimation and the United States government putting them into a concentration camp. The moment improvements last and progress is not an illusion is the moment the story is over. And so long as the story can’t end, improvements can’t last and progress needs to be an illusion.

Question: What is the "female" equivalent of "phallic"?
Answer: It’s “Yonic.” “Phallic” comes from Latin by way of Greek. “Yonic” is a Hindi word by way of Sanskrit. The first usage of “yonic” to mean a stylized representation of female genitalia in English comes from 1799. Now when I asked about this in college, the story I was told was that the cultural establishment considered the concept too tawdry for the unsophisticated masses, and so specifically chose a word that only people with an upper class education could piece together what it actually meant. This does broadly fit in with other stuff of that time, like the first two English translations of One Thousand and One Nights being private editions for subscribers only. I have actually encountered “yonic” in the wild more and more frequently in recent years…. But it is still an at most once every three months thing for me to see the word “yonic” used by anyone. One of the more recent examples was someone on Twitter commenting about how DC keeps forcing Wonder Woman to use the phallic sword as opposed to her yonic lasso. That was exciting. But the word you are looking for is “yonic.”

Question: What were the issues with the new Ghostbuster's film? In your opinion, what could have been improved in its creation?
Answer: If I had to make a guess, too many people were making too many decisions creating a bloated, creatively bankrupt product that failed. This image of nine different characters is not even the full cast There are some basic ideas that are pretty good in this film. There’s a strange brass orb with a demonic god inside that they are investigating, that’s a great idea for a Ghostbusters movie. The containment unit is also old and at capacity, and they have to get the ghosts to a new facility. Also a good idea. And Phoebe makes a ghost friend, who might not have the purest of intentions. She’s a good character, but it is really funny to compare her to her brother Trevor and what he’s up to the whole movie. There’s a ghost in the attic, Slimer obviously, who he is playing Tom and Jerry with whenever the movie feels like cutting to a comedy bit. Phoebe meets a ghost named Melody, and they become friends. But Melody is working for Garraka, the movie’s main villain, and is attempting to free him in exchange for meeting her family in the afterlife. And this is all a gay thing. Like… this is all obviously about a vulnerable queer youth desperate for connection getting taken advantage of. But because we live in America in 2024 none of this can actually be stated or talked about directly. So it is this stilted, awkward mess of a story with characters doing weird things for unmotivated reasons. The entire plot hinges upon Phoebe doing something that really only makes sense if it involves the kind of kissing the film adamantly refuses to acknowledge. Also it is extremely overly convoluted and implausible. Now I say Phoebe Spangler is the only character in the film the movie cares about…. but that’s not strictly true. The film is deeply invested in Nadeem, a random loser who happens to own (and then sell) the brass ball that drives the entire plot of the movie. Nadeem is a Firemaster, the child of an ancient order of fire controlling mystics who guard this one specific demon in case he gets out and tries to destroy the world. Nadeem just consumes screen time. He’s like a piranha eating away at the script. When Nadeem first showed up, I thought it was a funny cameo by Kumail Nanjiani… and then he just doesn’t leave. Just endless focus on Nadeem and his “journey” to be a Firemaster. Was this supposed to set up a spinoff? Nothing about the film is particularly compelling. Nothing about it hangs together well. There are logical failures and plotholes all over the film. There are so many characters, and almost none of them do anything worthwhile. It feels like there was no editing on the script. Maybe do a few more drafts, absolutely cut some stuff. Make things more streamlined and tighter. It’s just way too many ideas, too haphazardly slung together.

Question: How come the biology I was taught back in school was wrong according to woke liberals? What changed?
Answer: When you were in school you were taught there were five senses: sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste. But we also have our sense of balance (Equilibrioception), and our sense of where your body is in relation to itself (Proprioception). Our sense of “warm” and “cold” and “pain” might not be one sense, but instead three separate senses. Lots of different schemes have been proposed for how many senses humans have, sometimes up to 53. The biology you were taught in school about the five senses was wrong. It’s a lot more complicated and messy. However, you were a child and a lot of this stuff is particularly abstract, or based on new material. If I wanted to explain Proprioception to a child I could (“close your eyes and touch your nose, that you can do this is called ‘Proprioception’”). But not everything could be explained that easily. And, generally speaking, all most people need to know is that there are five senses. Teaching kids that there are five senses is not a bad way to teach them, just an incomplete one. And all teaching is inherently incomplete. But if you, as an adult, encounter that there are more than five senses, you can react to that knowledge by understanding the biology you were taught in school was simplified for your benefit and that life is more messy and complicated (and perhaps more importantly more interesting) or reject the new information and dogmatically believe in the five senses because that’s what text book written for children from 1982 told you. The biology you were taught back in school was objectively wrong. We know more about every aspect of biology than we did when you were in school, so your knowledge is outdated. What you were taught was simplified, so it was both incorrect and incomplete. You can either take in new information, incorporate it into what you already know, and marvel at what an amazing universe we live in… or view such information as a personal attack. It’s up to you.

Question: What's up with all these New Gay movies?
Answer: I have seen sixteen movies this year and only five of them have any gay content at all: Mean Girls, Monkey Man, Challengers, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes. And some of these are extreme stretches. Truly extremely stretches. In the adaptation of the musical Broadway adaptation of the 2004 film Mean Girls, the character Damian is openly gay just like he was in the original film. In this revenge film set in India, the main character, who is unnamed but calls himself “Bobby” at times, is saved from drowning in a river after his first attempt at revenge goes wrong by Alpha, the keeper of Ardhanarishvara, a local temple whose hijra community is being targeted by the police/politicians. Ardhanarishvara is a form of the Hindu deity Shiva combined with his consort Parvati. Ardhanarishvara is depicted as half-male and half-female, equally split down the middle. Hijra would be the equivalent of transgender, intersex, and eunuch people. Bobby heals at their temple, spiritually and physically, and trains there too, again spiritually and physically. And then gets them the money they need to continue to exist. And, in the end, they help him with his revenge. This is all stuff that is extremely specific to India, and all pretty fascinating. It is a look into a culture that most Americans are unaware of. If you don’t know that this is a film by the director of Call Me By Your Name, then I can see someone going to see the Zendaya tennis movie and being very confused by the product they are watching. My friend went to see it with her grandmother and reported that, yes, it was awkward. It’s a film about three tennis players, a men’s pair and a female prodigy, who spend the entire film wanting to have sex with each other in every possible combination. And Patrick and Art, the two men in the film, do make out while Zendaya watches. If you think this is a tennis movie and not a movie where tennis is a metaphor for sex, then I can see being surprised. The team behind the film does try to prepare audiences for what they are going to see by putting “Luca Guadagnino’s Challengers” in all the advertising… but what percentage of the population are going to realize he directed Call Me By Your Name? Also both Art and Patrick spend the whole movie having sex with Zendaya. It’s a single exchange: Gus: If that’s how you fight, I’d hate to see you love. Anders: You don’t have to worry about that, you’re too pretty for me. Freddy, on the other hand… Freddy: You’d have to catch me first. Anders: I do love to hunt. Freddy: You’d be lucky. Anders: I’m really getting quite hot. It is… unclear if this is supposed to be taken as a literal confirmation of a character’s sexual orientation or a joke between a bunch of guys who like killin’ Nazis. Or possibly both? They’re laughing the entire time they are saying these lines. It’s a fifteen second gay joke in a film where a huge portion of the film is spent on a female spy seducing a Nazi. The chimpanzee protagonist Noa crashes into the home of orangutan Raka. Raka is, at the moment, holding a funeral for his partner in the Order of Caesar, who he refers to as “his tribe.” That’s it, it’s like four words. Four ambiguous words. There are some soldiers in Civil War that you could maybe think are indicated to not be straight. I’m sure there is something in Lisa Frankenstein I am forgetting. And at the very least Argyle can be interpreted as having gay elements. The idea that there’s “all these new gay movies” is just not true. In the pre-summer blockbuster period of the year, when all the art films are released, it’s still only like a third of films have a gay character at all, and half of those are just ambiguous lines of dialogue.

Question: Is it necessary to have strong female characters in media, or are well-written female characters enough?

Question: How does Gwenpool's power compare to that of Spider-Man or Daredevil?
Answer: They are completely different powersets, and Gwenpool’s fluctuates wildly. Gwenpool started off as just a girl who came from our reality (or something basically identical) where Marvel was just an entertainment company. And, being a huge nerd, she read all the comics. When she was transported by unknown means into the Marvel universe, all her powers were just an encyclopedic knowledge of minutia of the Marvel universe and deep understanding of all the tropes of superhero stories. But, as her story progressed, her status as an outsider aware she was in a comic book allowed her to start manipulating the comic book medium. In particular the gutter space that exists as the white edge of the page. She has essentially unlimited godlike powers to do whatever she wants. Travel through time, teleport, manipulate reality. As long as it is feasible to do in the comic book medium, she can do it. A particular favorite of mine is when she retcons in, via flashback, Tony Stark giving her a bunch of money that she can use as the prize in a fighting tournament. But her powers depend entirely upon context. In her own books, on her own adventures, they are phenomenal godlike cosmic abilities. But when she joined the West Coast Avengers she lost them, believing herself to be “rebooted” into a version that better fit with the team. So how does she compare to Spdier-Man and Daredevil…. well she’s sometimes so laughably more weak then they are that it would like them punching any teenage girl they meet. Other times she is so much more powerful than they are that she can twist their continuities pretzels around them or toss them outside reality itself. Although even at her most powerful there are hard limits to her abilties. Marvel editorial will not allow her to kill Spider-Man.

Question: What is Dead Boy Detectives on Netflix specifically about?
Answer: This is one of those cases where the title just doesn't lie. It is about dead boy detectives. Very accurate title. Edwin Payne died in 1916 at a boarding school in England. He was subsequently condemned to hell accidentally. Charles Rowland was attending this same boarding school in 1989 where he was killed by bullies. When the assault of Charles was going on, Edwin had just escaped from hell. Edwin's soul sat with Charles while he died, keeping him company. Rather than move on to the afterlife, Charles just decided to hang out with Edwin on Earth. They start the Dead Boy Detective Agency, where ghosts can hire them to resolve whatever earthly matters are keeping them tethered to this plane, allowing them to move on. While the show has lots of multi-episode and season long arcs, every episode is centered on a specific case where a supernatural mystery is resolved. So what the show is about, specifically, is about the dead, who are both boys and detectives. Or boys who are both dead and detectives. Or detectives who are both dead and boys. Very honest title.

Question: Do you think Kristi Noem's story about meeting Kim Jong Un was a mistake?
Answer: No. There are only two possible reasons for a story about a fake meeting with Kim Jong Un to appear in South Dakota governor Krist Noem's book. Neither of them could be classified as a “mistake” in the sense of an accident. And while both are a “mistake” in the sense they are an error of good judgement, neither is a mistake in the sense that a simple accident of human error explains them. Looking at those two options, the only one that makes sense is that she was just lying. I have no doubt she is very lazy to collaborate with, but no professional ghost writer would come up with something this ridiculous. And… she narrated the audio book herself, and it includes her entirely fictitious meeting with Kim Jong Un. We know this wasn't some error on the publisher's part. If the ghost writer had just misheard the name, or a passage from a different book somehow wound up in this one… she would have said something when she was literally reading it outloud into a microphone. Even if she is so lazy she didn't bother reading the manuscript, she would have noticed at this point. I remember when I met with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, I'm sure he underestimated me having no clue about my experience staring down little tyrants. I've been a children's pastor after all. This passage absolutely sounds like an incredibly practiced story she has told many times. That she drops this anecdote at parties and in Republican meetings. There's no other explanation that makes sense. This lie only lasts until someone askes themself, when could she ever have possibly been in the same room with Kim Jong Un? There's no possible way that this happened. And yet… she would probably have gotten away with it if she didn't include the passage where she shot her puppy. That was a bananas passage to include (but, apparently, in South Dakota people called her “dog killer” behind her back, so it would inevitably come out if she moved onto the national stage, as she clearly had ambitions to do). And one bananas passage meant the media smelled blood in the water and went looking for more. Which they found. No puppy killing, probably no one would have bothered pressing her on her obviously fake meeting with the dictator of North Korea. If you listen to the excellent podcast Behind the Bastards, lying is like breathing to the worst people in human history. I don't mean normal political lying, like fudging a number on an economic report. I mean lying on the level of claiming to have been made a member of a Native American tribe when you never left Germany, or lead a revolution in a country you weren't even in at the time, or claimed to sunk a Japanese submarine in the Pacific by Oregon when you were really just bombing rocks. And the amazing thing is that it always seems to work. A person just brazenly lie for a surprisingly long time without anyone ever calling them on it. Even now, in the era of the internet. I think she told this obviously fake story a lot, and told it to her ghostwriter without thinking twice. I think her ghostwriter then put it in the book, because that is their job. And I think the publisher didn't bother fact checking. They kept the puppy killing story in the book, so they weren't exactly attempting to protect her. Also people aren't really meant to buy these books. They exist to be published and then bought in bulk by think tanks, which then just pulp them. It is an ass backwards (and wasteful) system to just give politicians money indirectly.
