Question: The media pushed hard on Arron Hernanadez being “gay”, but only one (possibly attention seeking ?) guy made that claim, all other evidence was jokes or gossip . Does the media like to put the gay label when they have a villain?
Answer: More than one person made the claim Aaron Hernandez was gay. The people who claim he was gay includes his brother DJ, his mother Terri, his ex-girlfriend Alyssa, his attorney George Leontire, and numerous other friends and acquaintances. Aaron Hernandez was a football player for the New England Patriots who murdered multiple people, and eventually committed suicide in prison. Just in case you don’t know the story. Both before and after his death, rumors that he was gay circulated. Those rumors have, by this point, been very much confirmed by multiple people. The Boston Globe has a recording of him explicitly saying he was attracted to men and that it “made him angry all the time.” Aaron’s brother Jonathan wrote a book about Aaron, which contains many passages explicitly about his sexuality. Jonathan interviews many people who knew Aaron at different stages of his life in different cities, and all of them have the same experience that he did. Aaron was deeply in the closet, but also extremely bad at hiding his real desires… and also would react with violent anger if anyone attempted to talk to him about it. The next morning as we gathered in the lobby to leave, Aaron and his two friends were nowhere to be found. I went back to his hotel room door and knocked—no answer. I walked the casino floor. An hour after we were scheduled to leave, I finally got a key to his room from the front desk and opened the door. Aaron was tucked under the covers of the king-size bed with his two friends, their shirts off, even though it was a luxury suite with multiple beds. “Hey, what the hell are you doing?” I asked. “We’re all waiting for you so we can leave.” Aaron popped up. “Uh, we’ll be right down,” he said, as the other two began to stir. Once we got home, I shut my bedroom door in my apartment so Aaron and I could have privacy, away from the other guys in my living room. I asked Aaron if he was gay. “If you are, I don’t care,” I said. “I love you. You are my brother.” “Don’t you ever ask me that again,” Aaron said. “If you say that again, I’ll fucking kill you.” Hernandez, Jonathan. The Truth About Aaron: My Journey to Understand My Brother (pp. 77-78). HarperCollins. Kindle Edition. Many such passages. If you read any of the deep dives into Aaron Hernandez, in particular the Boston Globe’s fairly exhaustive reporting, then the fact that he is gay is never vilifying. It is always presented as tragic. Hernandez suffered from some pretty extreme child abuse, both physical and sexual. Jonathan Hernandez mentions numerous truly horrific incidents in specific detail. And part of that child abuse was subjecting him to vile and continuous homophobia. As we walked back to our car, I heard my dad say, “Aaron, why do you stand like a faggot—with your hands clasped on your stomach and your elbows glued to your ribs? It’s feminine. Are you a faggot? Only faggots stand like that. There are no faggots in the Hernandez family.” Aaron put his head down and he placed his hands straight down by his sides. This wasn’t the first and wouldn’t be the last time our father grew angry over what he called Aaron’s feminine posture. Aaron didn’t even want to be a football player, he wanted to be a cheerleader. But that was not acceptable to his father who made sure to beat that idea out of him. The actual vilification is football itself. Aaron’s brain was essentially mush, noted to have the most severe case of chronic traumatic encephalopathy that researchers had ever even seen in someone his age. His specific kind of severe brain damage is known to cause paranoia, lack of impulse control, anger and aggression, all of which Aaron exhibited for most of his life. He was also very much addicted to drugs and alcohol. And, again, this is where the fact that he was gay is tragic, not vilifying. Aaron said that in order to become intimate with a woman, he needed to be extremely drunk. He loved Shayanna, but it had crushed him that he couldn’t give her the intimacy that she deserved. Aaron said he would stay out late with his friends, hoping that she would be asleep when he returned. “I hated living a secret, and I hated all the lies, but I felt like I had to do all those things because people wouldn’t accept me,” Aaron said. “There was no way I could come out as an NFL player. So much of the dysfunction that characterized his entire life can directly be traced to his inability to accept himself. The only time I have ever seen him vilified over his sexuality was when the prosecutors in his murder trial wanted to put forward the idea that the murder of Odin Lloyd was due to a pick up not reciprocated or that Lloyd had discovered his sexuality and Aaron was afraid of being outed. This was, seemingly, because no one has ever been able to come up with a motive for the murder that Aaron undoubtably committed. In fact, the crime doesn’t make much sense. But, personally, I don’t really think there was anything like a motive. I think a deeply paranoid drug addict with severe brain damage isn’t going to have particularly clear reasoning for committing a spur of the moment murder. Aaron Hernandez was not a good person. But he was a person, and he was the product of the world in which he was raised. The more you learn about him the more you realize he never had a chance. He was a monster who murdered multiple people, but that was a path that he was forced onto.

Question: If Disney and Warner Bros. are working together and their rivalries has ended, what are the consequences of collaboration?
Answer: They aren’t “working together” so much as they are reinventing cable. Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery are combining to release a new streaming bundle featuring Disney+, Max, and Hulu as both companies fight heavy losses. The new bundle, which will be available in ad-supported and ad-free versions, will combine of the most popular streaming shows available today, including The Bear, Shogun, House of the Dragon, and of course, Bluey. The official release highlights "ABC, CNN, DC, Discovery, Disney, Food Network, FX, HBO, HGTV, Hulu, Marvel, Pixar, Searchlight, Warner Bros., and more more" as part of the offering. This bundle has a name. It’s called “cable.” See in the long, long ago, the before times, you didn’t have to bother to figure out what content was on what streaming service, because instead all the content was piped directly into your home and you only paid for one service. It was called “cable.” You might have to figure out the time and the channel something was on, but thanks to the magic of cable, it was all there. Mad Max enjoys some cable with his friends. When the streaming revolution started, I said it was entirely unsustainable to expect people to individually pay for half a dozen different services, and then hunt through each one in an effort to find the one thing they want to watch. Inevitably the only option was to just reinvent cable. And now they are reinventing cable. This isn’t some magical world where Disney and Warner Bros. have put aside their competition for a new era of cooperation. This is the end product of streaming essentially destroying both companies, necessitating an attempt to rewind the clock out of sheer desperation.

Question: What did you think of the movie Challengers (2024) with Zendaya, et al.?
Answer: Sex is like tennis: a competitive sport with one winner and a lot of losers, and the only thing that matters is being in the top 125 in the world. Challengers is about the champion juniors doubles tennis team of Art Donaldson (Mike Faist) and Patrick Zweig (Josh O'Connor) who both become infatuated with up and coming tennis star Tashi Duncan (Zendaya). Ten years later Art and Tashi are in a loveless, joyless marriage coasting on what fame Art has left despite clearly being over the hill. Patrick is so destitute that he can’t afford a hotel room (or even a sandwich) and has to, essentially, prostitute himself for a bed. Art and Patrick both enter the same challenger tournament. Most of the film tells the story of how three people on the way to tennis super stardom got so waylaid, and how none of them can stand each other yet, also, none of them can give each other up. It’s also about sex. For the entire movie tennis is a transparent metaphor for sex. This is a movie filled with phallic and yonic symbolism. Bananas, glasses, strategically placed tennis rackets. There’s a bit with churros that is so on the nose I almost laughed. There’s a whole thing about sticking a tennis ball in the throat of the tennis racket. The same music plays over sex scenes, charged dialogue scenes, and tennis match scenes. Despite how sexually charged the entire film is, it does leave the audience with a pair of blue tennis balls. The threesome that the entire movie builds up to never materializes. But then again, I suppose what they could put on screen would never be as satisfying as what the audience imagines happening literally seconds after the final match ends. The film is also kind of hilarious for how little it attempts at trying to make the characters look like they aren’t in their late 20s/early 30s even when playing teenagers. Whoever made the decision that all that was needed to show Zendaya aging was to just a cut a few more inches off her hair whenever there was a time jump deserves a raise. It’s a fun, extremely horny movie about tennis people who are mostly, pretty awful to each other. And yet, somehow, you care about the relationships in the film. Really could you ask for anything more?

Question: Why have Star Wars fans ruined Star Wars and why do they keep ruining the franchise?

Rowling committing rape, which is an actual thing actual Star Wars fans did about George Lucas. Name: Johan Torres
Question: What did Valerie Cooper mean when she said "Magneto was right" in the latest episode of "X-Men '97"?
Answer: The brilliant writer Asher Elbein wrote an entire essay on Magneto and Judaism, which basically answers this question. Read enough X-Men comics, and you’ll notice that the fundamental feature of the franchise—the idea of mutants as eternal stand-ins for Jews, or black people, or queer people—is its essential pessimism. In X-Men, minority life is wholly defined by oppression. No improvement can last; progress is always an illusion; as figures in an ongoing, eternal piece of intellectual property, mutants must always be hated and feared. This enforced, recursive Marvel-Time unwittingly echoes what we might call Jewish-Time: the idea that Jewish people were, are, and always will be oppressed by antisemitism, cast as the same villain in different costumes. Persia is Rome, Russia is Germany. Rather than discrete historical occurrences—contingent, contested, complex—they are foreordained, essential, and inescapable. There is only the pogrom, forever. The essence of “Magneto was right” is pessimism. It is the idea that better is not possible. There is only the pogrom, now and forever. The eternal pogrom. She was on Genosha when it was attacked by Sentinels. And, as she says, she felt a lot of emotions. But the one emotion she didn’t feel was surprise. That giant machines would genocide Genosha out of existence is, in fact, the least surprising possibility. “Magneto was right” means that the pogrom is eternal, is foreordained, essential, and inescapable. Peace is never an option. The fight can never be won. Coexistence is lie. Magneto’s path is the only morally (and, in fact, practically) acceptable path foreword if you believe those premises. And within the X-Men, and our real world, society points you to that conclusion. The same tragedies happen endlessly, the same battles are fought. Rights are always precarious and about to be rolled back. One of America’s law wizards decides to stay on the bench despite multiple rounds of cancer and dies at the wrong time. The pogrom is eternal. That’s the central tension between Xavier and Magneto within the X-Men. Xavier believes a better world is possible, despite all evidence. While Magneto believes the only rational response to the world is dominance, that is the only way to achieve security.

Question: What is your review of The Fall Guy (2024 movie)?
Answer: The Fall Guy is a really lovely romantic comedy, with a surprisingly high number of murder/suicides and boat explosions for the genre. Ryan Gosling plays Colt Seavers, a Hollywood stunt performer who, after an accident, broke his back. After a year of rehab, having completely dropped out of the movie industry, he is asked to work on the film Metalstorm by big shot producer Gail Meyer (Hannah Waddingham). He only agrees because his ex-girlfriend Jody Moreno (Emily Blunt) is directing. But Gail has an ulterior motive for hiring him, the star of the film has gone missing, and she wants Colt to, quietly, investigate what might have happened. The film follows two major plotlines, which very heavily intersect. The first is the investigation, which is filled with high stakes action and excitement, lots of car chases and fist fights. The second is Colt and Jody working out their relationship issues and potentially coming to a place where they could get back together. This is also filled with high stakes action and excitement, lots of car chases and fist fights. It’s a very funny movie that absolutely does not take itself too seriously, very much in the vein of big, dumb ’80s action movies. Both Gosling and Blunt give incredibly affable performances, that really makes the audience care about the core relationship. I was actually surprised at how prominent the love story was to the film. And the stunt work is amazing. It is a film made by people who cherish stunt work and stunt performers. It will take any excuse to set someone on fire or have them get hit by a car. It currently holds the world record for largest number of cannon rolls for a car. It’s a really solid, charming film.

Question: Are you surprised by the 40% drop in sexual content over the last two-plus decades in Hollywood movies?
Answer: No. It was both obvious that that was going to happen, and obvious that it was happening. The moment internet pornography became widely adopted, there was, essentially, no longer any utility to including sex scenes in movies. Or, rather, not including them and getting a PG-13 rating is significantly more profitable. Much of the history of art is wrapped up in plausible deniability for not being pornography. In order to get pornography prior to the internet, you had to go to a specialty store, or go to your local video store and risk someone you know seeing you in the porn section. And then there is a clerk. You have to have someone physically check out your porn and potentially judge you. It’s an extremely high bar to overcome the level of internalized shame and humiliation. So, instead, you can just get Friday the 13th: A New Beginning, and say you are really there for the art, and not the many, many gratuitous sex scenes. But now we all have access to an endless stream of pornography, featuring every fetish ever imagined, from our phones. Thirty seconds of boobs in a film is not going to significantly impact sales. And I can say that with a lot of confidence because Scarlett Johansson did full frontal nudity in the film Under the Skin and no one seems to have noticed or cared. While including nudity and sex will potentially limit sales. So it was very, very obvious that internet pornography was going to kill the movie sex scene, and that’s exactly what it proceeded to do.

Question: What other animated shows do you feel are underappreciated and carry high stakes and weight such as "X-Men: The Animated Series"?
Answer: Have you heard about Exosquad? Exosquad was a toyline and someone was really like “what if we did all the brutality of World War II but as a Saturday morning sci-fi cartoon?” The basic premise of Exo Squad is that humanity has terraformed Mars and Venus and is expanding out into the outer reaches of space, thanks to developing powerful mechanized Exosuits. In the back story to the show, humanity decided to genetically engineer a slave race called Neosapians to be their workers on Mars. But the Neosapians revolted and eventually were freed, however they continue to face significant discrimination. In an effort to crush the pirate clans which operate on the fringes of the solar system, the Earth Congress dispatches the entire Exofleet to attack with overwhelming force. The Neosapian governor of Mars, Phaeton, uses this opportunity to stage a Neosapian coup, taking control over the inner solar system. The general structure of the two seasons track closely with World War II, even down to specific battles such as the Battle of the Bulge. The main characters in the show are Able Squad. People die frequently on the show, and it tries to present a realistic look at the psychological toll of war. And there are just weird and creepy elements. Phaeton gets a disease that causes his body to liquify, requiring him to always remain in his suit. Whenever Phaeton gets disappointed in one of his generals, he kills them and replaces them with a clone. At one point they spend several episodes talking about how the Neosapian government is putting all dissidents into workcamps on Venus. Then an episode comes where they discover that this is all a ruse and Phaeton is simply having them fired directly into the sun. That’s an episode that has stuck with me for literally decades. It’s a show where they discover Phaeton cloned himself, and then spend time arguing about how the clone both is and isn’t completely innocent. They can’t release another Phaeton into the world, but the clone never actually did anything wrong. Several of the people who worked on X-Men the animated series also worked on Exosquad. Tonally, they are quite similar, focusing on darker and more mature storytelling and complex and nuanced ideas. It is one hell of a toy commercial.

Question: Can you recommend any good movies to watch on an airplane? How was your experience watching these movies while flying?
Answer: I watched The Peanuts Movie on an airplane. Now, I saw The Peanuts Movie in theater, and watched it many times since. It is a wonderful movie, filled with heart and really does capture the magic of Charles Schulz’s work. But it is a great movie to watch on an airplane. It’s a kids movie, so there is nothing in the film that would be weird or embarrassing for someone else to see. You should absolutely not watch Basic Instinct on a plane. But the film is also very much pulling from the original medium of Peanuts. It has an overarching plot in only the loosest sense. Charlie Brown wants to impress the Little Red Haired Girl, but embarrasses himself or gets sidetracked consistently. But structurally the movie is mostly vignettes. There’s a set up and resolution to a small story, and then the movie moves on to the next one. It’s the perfect film to watch when you are in a busy atmosphere and can’t perfectly concentrate on what you are watching. If you miss something, you will probably get the gist of what’s happening, and even if you don’t, then that part will be concluded relatively rapidly and the next story will start. It’s a cramped seat, there’s people getting up to go to the bathroom, there are kids talking, you have to make sure to get your drink order in with the flight attendants, you have to be paying attention to any announcements. And in the midst of all that you can fill your heart with Charlie Brown and his friends.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Which TV shows were first rejected before becoming smash hits?
Answer: In 1984 children’s entertainment producer Haim Saban was staying in Japan where he came across a show called Super Sentai. It was a show where colorfully costumed individuals fought monsters. In that show, he saw the opportunity to create an action adventure show for kids that could be made cheaply, as they could just license the expensive action scenes from the original show, as the characters were all wearing helmets. That meant they only had to film half the show with new material, and what would be the least expensive material. He pitched this for eight years, with every network rejecting it. All thinking it was too cheesy. But in 1990 Fox was launching the brand new Fox Children’s Network, hoping to expand into the lucrative Saturday morning/weekday afternoon space. To run this, they hired Margaret Loesch, who formerly worked for Marvel Productions. Loesch is one of the most important people in the history of children’s entertainment. Because she had worked with Marvel Productions, she knew a lot of the people she was suddenly in a position to hire personally and trusted their creative visions. This resulted in a string of hits including the Batman and X-Men animated series. And because of her familiarity with both Saban and the Sentai series, she greenlit the show that Saban had been trying to make for nearly a decade. Mighty Morphin’ Power Rangers didn’t just make a lot of money, it made all the money. To call it a smash hit, does a disservice to it. It was a success like nothing else. It was making over $1 billion a year in merchandise sales. A meet and greet with the cast caused an eight mile long traffic jam in LA. It was viewed by seven million people daily. “When it premiered 20 years ago, it went on to redefine what was possible in a kids’ show in terms of ratings, global appeal, pop-culture relevance,” Dekel says. “All those things kind of reset when Power Rangers got to the marketplace.” It was the show no one believed in, and it was the most successful children’s show of the era.

Question: Would Carmen Sandiego defeat Batman if she ever encountered him just by outsmarting him and using other villains like The Joker or Penguin as pawns to help her?

Name: Johan Torres
Question: How does the character of Captain America's stance on tolerance and compromise in X-Men '97 reflect real-world political dynamics?
Answer: The episode is drawing directly from Martin Luthor King Jr.’s, “Letter from Birmingham Jail.” So much so that I think the episode quotes from it at points. But, with regards to Captain America (and President Kelly), this passage seems to be the most appropriate. I have never yet engaged in a direct-action movement that was "well timed" according to the timetable of those who have not suffered unduly from the disease of segregation. For years now I have heard the word "wait." It rings in the ear of every Negro with a piercing familiarity. This "wait" has almost always meant "never." It has been a tranquilizing thalidomide, relieving the emotional stress for a moment, only to give birth to an ill-formed infant of frustration. We must come to see with the distinguished jurist of yesterday that "justice too long delayed is justice denied." In X-Men ’97 the creators of the Sentinels go missing from government detention and then massive Sentinels genocide the mutant population of Genosha. In response to this, the United States government withholds aid to Genosha, and the president worries about the optics of looking like he is too favorable to mutants. But, don’t worry, this is actually for mutants! Because what if someone worse got elected! So the most important thing to understand about Captain America in the show is that he is unbelievably full of shit. Genosha wasn’t just a mutant tragedy, it shames us all. But rampaging across the country dishonors those who were lost. It is telling that Captain America calls hitting two government black sites a “rampage across the country.” Her targets are, in fact, well chosen as she finds the exact information trail she needs to proceed. And, Captain America is being emotionally manipulative here. How would attacking two military instillations from the country that was supposed to be holding the Sentinel makers and lost them, dishonor the people who died by the Sentinels? What does dishonor them, withholding action. Finding Bolivar Trask and Henry Peter Gyrich is a real, tangible thing that is literally the least that the people tasked with holding them could be doing. Captain America: This uniform shows up in Mexico bashing heads with you… it sends a message. Rogue: Damn right, that you stand with mutants… unless you don’t now. Captain America: Gotta do this by the book, Rogue. Right now, my hands are tied. Like I said, full of shit. This is a common tactic where people obfuscate their real concerns with legalities. If you attend a lot of protests, or read a lot of coverage of protests, “I would support this protest, but they didn’t follow the proper permitting process” is something you hear weirdly frequently. “I can’t do anything about this mass murderer on the lose because America and Mexico haven’t worked the proper extradition procedure” is a completely bananas thing for Captain America to say. Particularly as, by Captain America’s own admission, no one actually in the government is attempting to extradite Gyrich to the US. And I realize that, as of now, Bucky doesn’t exist in this continuity. But we all know that Captain America would throw out any concern about legalities if Bucky was at stake as opposed to the genocide of mutants. Captain America’s initial statement is about messaging, and we should just assume he is telling the truth. He doesn’t want to visibly show solidarity with mutants, and when pressed on that point, he retreats into legalism. To turn it back to Martin Luthor King, Jr. he is the white moderate. I must make two honest confessions to you, my Christian and Jewish brothers. First, I must confess that over the last few years I have been gravely disappointed with the white moderate. I have almost reached the regrettable conclusion that the Negro's great stumbling block in the stride toward freedom is not the White Citizens Councillor or the Ku Klux Klanner but the white moderate who is more devoted to order than to justice; who prefers a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice; who constantly says, "I agree with you in the goal you seek, but I can't agree with your methods of direct action"; who paternalistically feels that he can set the timetable for another man's freedom; who lives by the myth of time; and who constantly advises the Negro to wait until a "more convenient season." Shallow understanding from people of good will is more frustrating than absolute misunderstanding from people of ill will. Lukewarm acceptance is much more bewildering than outright rejection. Captain America is considerably more concerned with order than with justice. Hence why he is bothering Rogue about her “rampage” and not the people who let Bolivar Trask vanish from custody. Why he privately agrees with Rogue, but doesn’t want to take a public stand in solidarity. Why when it comes to mutant mass death he is very concerned about following all the appropriate legalities, when we know he doesn’t actually care about them. And the fact that we can see these play out in real world politics all the time. We’re literally seeing them play out in the news this past week. So, in conclusion, Rogue did nothing wrong the entire episode. And definitely didn’t do anything wrong by taking Captain America’s shield and throwing it into a mountain.

Question: Is comic book reading still popular? If so, what makes people continue to read them despite the availability of more detailed and interesting novels?
Answer: I think people really don’t understand how unpopular reading, in general, is. How utterly niche it is. The preeminent list to track sales of books is the New York Times Bestsellers List. And we usually hear about the very top of the list, where the authors who have become brand names sell millions of books. But that’s not the whole list. The one year sales distribution of all bestsellers indicates that the majority of bestsellers sell between 10,000 and 100,000 copies in their first year The majority of books on the list are only selling 10,000 to 100,000. The median book on the list only sells between 4,000 to 8,000 books in a week (it’s a weekly list), or 16,000 to 32,000 books a month. If you look at any given month, the top fifty highest selling comic issues would probably all make it onto the New York Times Best Seller List. Comic book reading is not popular. However it isn’t because people are choosing to read novels instead. If you compare comic book reading to novels, then comic book reading is crazy popular. But reading, in general, is an extremely niche interest.

Question: Cassandra Nova is having a moment in the world of X-Men adaptations, but who is she?
Answer: Cassandra Nova is Charles Xavier’s twin sister, and also an alien. There are elements to her that are overly confusing. Cassandra is a Mummudrai, which is a bodiless psychic parasitic creature. They are an anti-self that you encounter and must overcome in the womb before birth as your first experience with the other. However, becoming entangled with a mutant as powerful as Xavier allowed Cassandra to grow a true body. In their conflict, he psychically aborted her, but she lived on as simply a clump of cells until her body fully regrew over decades. This is all very Grant Morrison being Grant Morrison. I always hated the Mummudrai explanation and think the better explanation is just that she is Xavier’s twin sister. Because of the violent nature of her birth, Cassandra is under the mistaken impression that she and Charles are still in the womb, fighting for dominance. That they are the only two “real” things in existence. And she is still trying to destroy him. To that end, she was the one responsible for actually sending the Sentinels to Genosha. She took psychic control of Lilandra, empress of the Shi’ar and Xavier’s lover, and wreaked havoc across space, and she tried to destroy the X-Men, multiple times. Her only motivation is to harm Charles Xavier in as many creative and brutal ways possible. Charles really didn’t have much luck with siblings, did he? So that is who she is. I can’t say anything about the performance which will probably be good, but Emma Corrin is way, way, way, way too young to play Cassandra. Part of Cassandra’s whole deal is that she is the same age as Xavier, she is an old woman who rips through whole teams of X-Men absolutely humiliating them.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Is it true that the whole world only watches Hollywood movies? If not, why do some people say this?
Answer: There is considerable truth to this. If you look at the highest grossing movies of any given year there will probably be a movie you have never heard of. In 2021, due to disruptions from covid-19, there were several. The Battle at Lake Changjin is a Chinese language film. It was released in only seven markets. It made $562,000 outside the Chinese market, and $902,000,000 inside it. Hi, Mom is a Chinese language film. It was released in four markets. It made $700,000 outside of the Chinese market, and $822,000,000 inside of it. Detective Chinatown 3 is a Chinese language film. I don’t think it was released outside of China at all. But it did make $700,000,000 in China. RRR is the third highest grossing movie from India of all time. It was released in ten markets. It made $37,000,000 outside India, and $130,000,000 inside it. Godzilla Minus One is the only recent international film I can think of where its foreign box office is significantly stronger than the domestic one. Meanwhile Minions: The Rise of Gru was released in seventy-six markets and made $370,000,000 inside the US and $570,000,000 outside of it. Top Gun: Maverick was released in forty-two markets and made $718,000,000 in the US and $780,000,000 internationally. The pattern that exists across the whole planet is that people watch their domestic films, and they watch English-language movies almost exclusively produced by Hollywood. If a nation has a large enough domestic market, and the obvious example of this is China, then they can have wildly successful films. Successful on the level of any Hollywood film. But there is a steep drop off outside the domestic market. If we are talking movies with truly global impact… then yes, the whole world only watches Hollywood movies.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is the plot of Yellowjackets?
Answer: Yellowjackets has multiple plots taking place in parallel. The two main ones are one taking place in 1996 and the other in the present. In 1996 a girl’s soccer team from a high school in New Jersey was heading to the national tournament, their plane crashes and they are lost in the wilderness for nineteen months. In the present, the survivors are living their lives, but each receive a postcard with a reference to events that happened in the woods. The very first thing we learn about their time in the woods is that over the winter some of them hunted, killed, and ate their teammates. As they were wearing masks made from animal skins, which of the main characters were involved is left a mystery (though one is revealed right away). Everything about the show either builds to this moment or from this moment. The show then shows the events of the day before the flight, including how the girls believe one of their team members to be weak player and make an agreement to keep the ball away from her at the tournament. But then, at practice, one of them deliberately breaks her leg to ensure she can’t compete. The show is, obviously, about how much this experience changes them… but also how it didn’t change them at all. It is a really interesting approach. The plane crashes and, very quickly, some of them adapt to their new circumstances. While others struggle a lot more. All of the adults die, except for an assistant coach whose leg gets crushed and has to be emergency amputated. As these events unfold, the show flashes forward to the present where we meet who these girls eventually become. Shauna is a mom with a failing marriage. Natalie is an alcoholic who is in and out of rehab. Misty is a rather cruel aid at a nursing home. Taissa is running for state senator. They are all approached by a journalist offering them book deals for the true story of what happened to them. A core part of the show is that when they were rescued they gave the most evasive and minimal account of the events that transpired and none of them have ever talked. They start receiving postcards with a specific reference to the experience. And then one person who survived is discovered having killed themselves, but in a highly suspicious way. While much of the show is given to the puzzle of who is bringing this back up, much of it is also just how badly they have all been coping with the trauma and stress of the experience. It’s a really great show.

Question: What is the origin of the term "mutants" in X-Men comics? Is it based on Darwin's theory of evolution or something else?
Answer: It is based on the fact that “mutants” were a fairly common trope in ’50s sci-fi. The reason why radiation does all those wacky things in Marvel comics is that the people making the comics were directly inspired by pulp sci-fi of the era. And pulp sci-fi was filled with post-World War II nuclear paranoia. Radiation leading to bizarre new life or radical biological changes was a staple of the genre. Think Them! where giant radioactive ants attack New Mexico. Often those radical biological changes would manifest in the children of people exposed to radiation. And sometimes no radiation was involved at all. Just someone being born different. Mutants were such a staple of sci-fi of the era that you can find whole anthologies of stories just about mutants. In particular the Foundation trilogy from Isaac Asimov was inspiration for the X-Men. That book series has a mutant named “the Mule” with amazing psychic powers. It was clearly such an influence that Beast would occasionally directly quote the most famous line from the trilogy, “Violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.” If you read the first handful of issues of Uncanny X-Men, then you realize the main conceptual thrust is that it is a school for superheroes. The school is the primary thing they focus on. Rather than come up with unique origins for the characters in the book, which would detract from the school elements, they came up with a uniform origin which was pulled from sci-fi of the era: they’re mutants. Mutation is a concept directly pulled from the theory of evolution. But the creators of the X-Men didn’t read The Origin of Species and decided to base a concept on them. They were reading contemporary sci-fi of the era and pulled from it. There is a long chain of influence from the actual biological theory of mutation to the X-Men with many steps along the way. Interestingly enough, Charles Darwin is a really important character in the X-Men comics. Charles Darwin shows both compassion and horror towards Mr. Sinister As the comics have developed, Victorian era London as the birthplace of the theory of evolution has become incredibly important. Mystique, Destiny, Apocalypse, the Hellfire Club, and Mr. Sinister were all active at that location and time. Cyclops and Jean Grey time travel to it. Mr. Sinister even attends Darwin’s funeral procession. But this is all working backwards from the real sources of inspiration for the X-Men.

Question: If you could have one positive thing to say about "X-Men: Apocalypse," what would it be?
Answer: I think the ending, as in literally Apocalypse’s end, is really good. This message is for one reason alone, to tell the strongest among you, those with the greatest power, this Earth will be yours. Apocalypse’s whole thing is that the strongest, by right of their strength, should have dominion over all that is beneath him. And the ending he is confronted by Jean, a being much stronger than he is. “All is revealed.” The impossible power of Jean has been released, showing the one who styled himself a God what a real God is. And, it sets up Dark Phoenix perfectly. Apocalypse is vindicated, he was right all along. He fought a bunch, and then someone stronger came along and supplanted him. From his perspective, Apocalypse was beaten by his own philosophy, not Xavier’s. Did Jean use her strength to protect the weak, as Xavier asked, or did she take the Earth, as Apocalypse proclaimed? That is a perfect launching pad for Dark Phoenix. Which, of course, is never followed up on. Here is the temptation a brilliant movie could be built on. Jean gave into the Dark Side to kill Apocalypse and got the victory she wanted, she got the love and admiration of all her friends and teachers as a savior. She crossed a moral line and not merely didn’t suffer consequences, she was lauded. How easy would it be to push her to do so again, one little flick of a domino? But yeah, Apocalypse’s death is very much the highlight of the film.

Question: What sparked your interest in Kaiju movies?
Answer: The 1998 Godzilla film came out when I was a child, and even then I realized it was bad. But it did make me want to watch the original Godzilla. And so I started looking out for any time the Godzilla films showed up in the TV guide. I distinctly remember watching Godzilla, Rodan, Ghidorah the Three-Headed Monster, Invasion of Astro-Monster, Destroy All Monsters, and Godzilla vs. the Smog Monster on basic cable. Frequently my dad would watch them with me. Those are actually some very fond memories of mine. I was, naturally, extremely tolerant of camp, bad dubbing, and lower quality special effects because I watched Mystery Science Theater 3000 incessantly. I could see past any cheesy elements to see what makes those movies truly wonderful. When I was around college age I decided to make a list of every kaiju movie I could think of and and watch them in order of release. There are some kaiju movies that are really bad. Some that are really great. Some that are really interesting historical and cultural projects. And the original Godzilla is one of the best movies ever made.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: How did the producers of "X-Men: The Animated Series" handle the voice actor for Storm to ensure accurate representation of the character?
Answer: X-Men the animated series recast Storm twice prior to the episodes airing. The realized, weirdly deep into production, that the actor who the originally cast for the part was white, and decided to recast her. Well, as excitement grew towards the big American series premiere, it finally occurred to someone that the series might be a hit and could get a lot of publicity – and that our only X-Man of color, our regally African, very Black Storm, turned out to be voiced by a White actress. Oh no. Much scrambling and panicking. I guess they felt it would be quicker to find a Black American voice-over actress to redo the work. They quickly recorded Iona Morris, and whew, a major political incident was avoided. Anyone else would have left it at that. But Haim Saban had budgeted for Canadian actors – who don’t get immediate, endless “residual” payments when episodes have repeated airings. So, to avoid the bookkeeping and the modest continuing fees that the American actress would be owed for voicing Storm, he later took the time and eventually found an excellent Black Canadian voice-over actress (Alison Sealy-Smith) to replace Ms. Morris. I have been told that Ms. Morris’s voice played the first year of the first season episodes and perhaps on some VHS tapes. Then every run after that, it was Ms. Sealy-Smith. Saban had just saved himself 25 years of residual payments. Lewald, Eric. Previously on X-Men: The Making of an Animated Series (pp. 90-91). Jacobs Brown Press. Kindle Edition. I am sure the original actor, and Iona Morris are both terrific voice actors who turned in great performances… but damn if Alison Sealy-Smith is not outstanding in the role. She has so much gravatas, and is able to make the extreme purple prose that is Storm’s dialogue work. I would argue she gives the best performance out of anyone in that voice cast, and it is a strong cast. Sealy-Smith has said she wasn’t attempting to do any kind of West African accent, and instead was going for Shakespeare preformed in front of a thousand people, which is her own background as an actor. I can absolutely say that I hear her voice as Storm when I read the comics.

Question: How many issues are typically included in a Marvel Omnibus?
Answer: It varies significantly from omnibus to omnibus, but you can expect around 30 to 60 issues. I have a lot of omnibi from Marvel because it is by far the best way to read most comics, and I can tell you just from my collection there are massive variations in amount of content depending upon which omnibus you aee looking at. From my collection, going from smallest number of issues to largest: She-Hulk by Peter David: 22 (this is by far the shortest omnibus I have, and also by far the cheapest) Annihilation: 30 Rom: The Original Marvel Years: 30 A.X.E. Judgement Day: 35 The Immortal Iron Fist and the Immortal Weapons: 37 Guardians of the Galaxy by Abnett and Lanning: 40 Thunderbolts vol. 1: 41 Young Avengers: 43 Thunderbolts vol. 2: 45 Moon Knight by Huston and Finch: 45 Guardians of the Galaxy by Brian Michael Bendis: 48 Gwenpool: 49 Thor by Matt Fraction: 49 Thunderbolts vol. 3: 50 Wakanda: World of Black Panther: 57 Immortal Hulk: 62 (this is also, by far, the most expensive one) There is no set number of issues. You just get whatever number of issues it makes sense to put into an omnibus. Additionally there are omnibi like Captain Britian, Miracle Man, and all the Aliens and Predator omnbi where large chunks of the collection simply aren't issues. The median number, though, is 45.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What elements of Grant Morrison's New X-Men run do you see in X-Men '97 Episode 5, "Remember It"?
Answer: “Remember It” is a sharp turn for the series, as prior to this episode the show mostly focused on storylines from the latter half of Chris Claremont’s run in the ‘80s. But this episode was a lot of New X-Men mixed in with a little bit of Krakoan spice. It’s really fun! So reporters interviewing the X-Men is from New X-Men #123 and there continue to be reporters there until #125. This is throughout Cassandra Nova’s second attack on the mansion, with the Shi’ar Imperial Guard. Trish Tilby is Beast’s longtime girlfriend, and she was there as one of those reporters. I think this is the first time Trish has appeared in the show, whereas in the comics they were freshly broken up. And instead of flirtation… well… something else happens. Beast decides to get revenge on Trish by lying and telling her he is gay. Trish then immediately leaks that to the tabloids. Which begins a weird running joke where Beast is extremely self-congratulatory about how progressive he is for letting people think he is gay. Also, that last bit is going to be important latter. Genosha is ruled by a Council, which is an obvious reference to the Quiet Council from the Krakoa era. Particularly when you see some of the people on it. Madelyne Pryor is on the Council because “They wanted an X-Man, and luckily you could spare a Jean.” Jean was on the Quiet Council at the start of the storyline. Nightcrawler is here. And he is on the Council to “help work with Genosha’s communities of faith.” That’s why he was put on the Quiet Council. This is a reference to New X-Men #117 when Jean and Wolverine kiss. In the comics it marks the start of the Jean and Scott infidelities plotline. And this episode is themed around infidelity. I know the bit about Jean holding back the water in the lake is a reference to a training sequence in a body of water, but for the life of me I can’t remember the specific issue. It wasn’t in New X-Men. It’s also probably a reference to X2: X-Men United. Yet more Quiet Council references. Emma and Sebastian Shaw are both on the Quiet Council and are essentially in control over the Krakoan economy. Moira MacTaggart is also on Genosha’s Council. In the comics she is not on the Quiet Council, but she is the hidden third founder of Krakoa. And much of the first half of the storyline involves keeping her existence a secret. I really wonder if we are going to get an evil Moira arc, because wow did her villain turn go to dark places. They want to make Magneto king or, more officially, “Chancellor.” That is in reference to an earlier storyline where the UN gave Genosha to Magneto as a way to placate him. In the original cartoon, they, very frustratingly, don’t explain all that. And so in the final episode Genosha is just stated to be a mutant homeland, with Magneto in charge. I don’t mind X-Men ’97 eliding some of that in order to make things a little more straightforward. This is a reference to New X-Men #139. Prior to that issue Scott had asked Emma for telepathic therapy to deal with his depression, and it had turned sexual. Jean is informed of this, and catches them. Which leads to a giant telepathic fight between the three of them. Here Scott is with Madelyne Pryor instead of Emma. So all of this is in reference to a period of time Rogue and Magneto spent together in the Savage Land in Chris Claremont’s run where they definitely had sex. That’s why Rogue is wearing this weirdly tattered outfit even though they are just in a villa together. The original outfit was obviously too sexy, so they give her shorts. So the party is called a “Gala” which is an obvious reference to the annual Hellfire Galas in the comics. But to my mind it looks a lot more similar to the party that is thrown at the end of House of X #6 than any of the Hellfire Galas. It has the same circular dance floors and multiple levels as that party. Plus the fireworks. And while everyone is dressed up in the cartoon, they aren’t wearing couture high fashion, and while Valerie Cooper is attending, there isn’t the emphasis on inviting influential and powerful humans. This design for the Master Mold is identical to the designs from New X-Men #115. Yeah, they are identical. Gambit saving the Morlocks is a reference to a storyline that ran in the late ’90s in the X-Men. They discover that Gambit had been hired by Mr. Sinister to recruit and train the Marauders and was the one that led them into the Morlocks tunnels during the Mutant Massacre. So, despite different continuities, this is an act of redemption for Gambit as a character. They keep telling people to take the injured to the “Gardens” which is a reference to the Healing Gardens, which is where Krakoans go for medical attention. They are overseen by the Morlock healer. Just to break away from the comics lore for a moment… “E is for Extinction” (the storyline this is adapting) was published only a few months prior to 9/11. And I have talked to people who were in New York City at the time who found that storyline very moving. Beau DeMayo who was the executive producer of the series and is the credited writer for this episode specifically, has said that it was based on 9/11, the Tulsa race massacre, the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, and Pulse Nightclub Shooting. He regularly went to Pulse. This episode is written with a greater degree of personal hindsight in what these kind of events are like, and what they mean than the original comic storyline. Magneto dying is a reference (again) to New X-Men #115 where the X-Men believe he is dead. In the cartoon he says “Have no fear” in German, as German is Magneto’s first language. The Sentinels refer to him as an “Omega Level Threat” because… well… he is an Omega level mutant. So this is a visual taken directly from New X-Men #115. This is extremely graphic and devastating for a kids cartoon. With people being vaporized on screen, and so many corpses. However the Sentinel attack is no where near as bad as the one from the comics, which took Genosha from a population of sixteen million to under a thousand. And it wasn’t actually stopped, the Sentinels simply turned themselves off when they had killed all the mutants they could find. What a great episode. In any scene set in Genosha, if you pause the the episode, you will find at least one (and likely many) obscure X-Men characters.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why hasn't Thanos fought the X-Men in the Marvel Universe? Why didn’t he just go to their school and defeat them all at once instead of searching for the Infinity Stones?
Answer: Thanos has fought the X-Men, many times in fact. Whenever Thanos comes to Earth, there are usually several X-Men on hand to fight him. But the X-Men don’t really care about Thanos, and Thanos doesn’t really care about the X-Men. Thanos is a distraction to the X-Men, almost an irritant. Thanos is irrelevant to their mission as a team, and so while they will fight him if he shows up, they are uninterested in being sucked into his drama. From their perspective they have more important concerns than the arcane schemes of some guy who wants to bang the concept of death. Leave that to the Avengers who have nothing better to do with their lives. From Thanos’s perspective, there isn’t anything the X-Men have that he might want (aside from occasionally the Phoenix Force and that one time Xavier had the Mind Gem). And Thanos could not care less about human/mutant relations, or the internal intricacies of mutant politics. He just wants to kill everyone. Thanos could go to the mansion and kill everyone there… but why would he? Thanos doesn’t need a reason to kill people, but why bother going to the mansion when he could just kill all the people wherever he already is? Ironically, now that the X-Men have figured out how to negate death, Thanos has more reason to go kill them all, as he would consider that an afront. But instead all the Eternals except Thanos went to kill them.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is the current status of the Gambit franchise, which began development over a decade ago but has not made any progress?
Answer: It’s dead. It officially died in 2019, but all evidence indicates it was dead long before then. Disney officially killed it when the acquisition of Fox was finished, along with basically all the rest of Fox’s in development X-Men projects. As near as I can figure from the trail of wreckage of this project, Channing Tatum wanted to play Gambit and Fox simply said, “Okay, we’ll do that!” The original announcement in 2014 was that Gambit would be X-Men: Apocalypse, followed by a solo movie which would be released in late 2016. Multiple sources say that Tatum will get a stand-alone spinoff, with his version of Gambit being introduced in X-Men: Apocalypse. The stand-alone film is still in development, however, and no director has been attached. When asked what kind of an actor she was looking at to play Gambit, Shuler Donner said, “It’s Channing.” In October of 2014 it was announced the Gambit film (entitled Gambit) was going forward with a script by Joshua Zetumer based on a treatment by X-Men comics writer Chris Claremont. Question: When and how did X-Men's Gambit first appear? How much did it sell for and what were its notable features?
Answer: Gambit’s first appearance was Uncanny X-Men #266. And the most notable thing about it is that it is Gambit’s first appearance. Gambit was the legendary X-Men writer Chris Claremont’s last major contribution to the X-Men universe. He would leave the title in around a year, if not less. So Gambit is really his final crowning glory, but one he never actually got to do what he wanted with. This issue takes place in the middle of the weirdest Storm arc of Claremont’s tenure. When the X-Men had their secret base in Australia (known as the Outback Era) Storm had been thought to have been killed in a helicopter crash. But that was actually a S.H.I.E.L.D. life model decoy. The real Storm had been abducted by the villain Nanny and had been de-aged into a child, and then Nanny lost her in Cairo, Illinois. Storm winds up robbing a house belonging to the Shadow King… which Gambit also happens to be robbing. He saves her from the Shadow King’s hounds and then they fly down the Mississippi to New Orleans. Also Gambit shoots energy out of his eyes, which is green. And, for some reason, when using his powers his face turns green. These are not features that will stick around. Soon Gambit’s color will uniformly be pink. But aside from this, most of Gambit’s notable traits are already fully formed, including that he is a thief, his over-the-top Cajun accent, and the gratuitous use of French. In 2022 Chris Claremont revisited this time period with an entire Gambit miniseries which is set inbetween pages 14 and 15 of the following issue, #267. As for how much did it sell for? $1.00

Question: Why does Sinister, in X-Men '97, want to cut ties with the Nasty Boys in favor of a newer, deadlier team of mutant villains called the Marauders?
Answer: Have the Marauders been announced as part of X-Men ‘97? But, regardless, on to the Nasty Boys. X-Men the animated series debuted in 1992 and is extremely reflective of that specific moment in the comics. All the X-Men’s costumes are the Jim Lee designs that were created in 1991. The lineup is a combined and modified Blue/Gold line up, again from 1991. Obviously (OBVIOUSLY!) X-Men the animated series was pulling from many classic stories from the franchise’s three decades of history. But equally obviously they were pulling from the most recent stuff that had only hit the stands a year or so before being put into the show. Because they were so heavily influenced by the most recent comics, they did not have the luxury of knowing what stuff was going to stick and be important and what stuff was going to be discarded. Mr. Sinister first appears in the Inferno crossover event at the end of which he is presumed dead as Cyclops blasted him down to his skeleton. Sinister does not appear again until X-Factor in 1991, in Peter David’s retool of that title. Mr. Sinister was neither a major nor an important X-Men villain at the time. He was in a handful of issues and was extremely under developed. He didn’t even have an origin. X-Men the animated series made Sinister so important to their stories, that his current position as one of the principle X-Men antagonists is largely due to the show. “Inferno” was big and important, but so was “Fall of the Mutants” and you don't see the Adversary getting something like five full movies of foreshadowing before never appearing because Disney bought Fox. Jubilee and even Gambit also owe a hell of a lot to that cartoon with regards to securing their position as characters. Mr. Sinister’s team are the Marauders, which is who he employed to commit the Mutant Massacre and has largely used ever since. But Peter David introduced a second team in X-Factor in 1991, the Nasty Boys. When they were making the cartoon, Sinister had two teams they could pick to use. And they went with the brand new one. They couldn’t know that the Nasty Boys would have six (JUST SIX!) canonical appearances. While the Marauders would still be around and be used regularly. The Nasty Boys were part of a trend in the ’90s to give the X-Men's old villains new hench men. So Magneto got the Acolytes, Apocalypse got the Dark Riders, and Mr. Sinister got the Nasty Boys. The Acolytes are the only ones who really stuck around, and even then mostly due to individual members becoming important. If X-Men ’97 is bringing the Marauders in, it would be because they are the important hench men for him. And the Nasty Boys are just not. The Marauders the ones in “Messiah Complex” not the Nasty Boys. But it really would be a shame, I like the Nasty Boys. They are great characters who just need some love. Really Marvel needs to integrate the two teams.

Question: What is your review of X-Men '97 episode four, "Motendo / Lifedeath – Part 1"?
Answer: I think this episode was the weakest so far, but still really strong. “Motendo” got about as much out of its premise as possible. But “Lifedeath Part 1” was far too short to convey everything it needed to cover. It was still excellent, and I can understand the desire not to have two full episodes as ponderous and devoid of action as the two “Lifedeath” issues were. I assume Gambit is the one that baked all those muffins. “Motendo” is an homage to all the 16 bit X-Men video games. In particular it seems to be an homage to the 1992 X-Men arcade game, which was based off the failed pilot “Pryde of the X-Men.” It is also a game I have never played. I did however play a lot of the 1993 X-Men Sega Genesis game and its sequel X-Men 2: Clone Wars (yes, they got that name a full decade before George Lucas). The episode starts out with everyone chatting about Jubilee’s 18th birthday. Magneto, of course, wants her to train instead of focus on having fun. Morph makes an joke about his dad, which results in Magneto being the ultimate buzzkill by telling everyone about how his entire family was murdered in a genocide. I have to give Morph a pass on this one as they were dead when the X-Men first met Magneto. But it really feels like someone should have explained all this to Morph. Jubilee wants to go to the arcade, but Magneto finds that too undignified. The very first scene we ever see of Jubilee in the cartoon is of her in an arcade destroying a game. Jubilee is the gamer superhero, and always has been. She also does an amazing Magneto impression, which is delightful. So this is called a Motendo but it is obviously based on a Sega Genesis. But the cover art for the cartridge is based on the Super Nintendo game X-Men: Mutant Apocalypse. Also Jubilee has had enough experience to know this is obviously a trap. But she still goes ahead with messing with the Motendo anyway. The villain is eventually revealed to be Mojo, which Jubilee… you should have called that one. If there is one thing I love, it is the Mojoverse. I love everything about the Mojoverse. It’s delightfully wacky, it’s why you can just stick your characters into a video game homage. Anyway, Mojo has realized television is dying and so he is pivoting to video games. Because the only thing more evil than a TV executive is a Twitch streamer. Mojo is also a frequent boss in many X-Men video games, and there is an infamous level where after you beat Mojo you have to reset your console. Jubilee mentions that Mojo has been dieting, and he tells her he has had a little plastic surgery. This is a reference to the fact that Spiral’s side hustle, when she is not producing all of Mojo’s TV programs, is to be the multiverse’s premier plastic surgeon. Spiral created Lady Deathstrike. She is also responsible for swapping Betsy Braddock and Kwannon’s brains. And she… well she made some enhancements to Rachel Summers. Mojo mentions that he picked Jubilee because Dazzler already had a gig. In the original cartoon Dazzler shows up on Mojoworld as a cameo before her introduction in “Dark Phoenix Saga.” Mojo also mentions he wants to dominate the 18–45 age demographic, which is the prime demographic for television. See, X-Men ’97 is educational! I’d watch all these shows. The game’s possible players are Jubilee, Colossus, Sunspot, Magik, Longshot, and Cable. Which is a game that I would love and no one else would. The plastic surgery did not take. In addition to being an homage to all the old X-Men video games, this is also an homage to the legendary storyline, “The Crunch Conundrum” from Wolverine #51–53. This episode has elements of that story, but they are too minor to really count as an adaptation. But in “The Crunch Conundrum” Wolverine, Mystique, and Spiral work together to defeat a time traveling Mojo who has abducted Jubilee. One of the characters at the end of that storyline is revealed to be an older Jubilee due to time travel shenanigans. The ending of the episode is extremely anime. As is the magical kiss. So I guess Jubilee and Sunspot are an official couple as opposed to two friends hanging out platonically. Although it is kind of funny that it has taken them this long, considering neither Jubilee nor Sunspot is exactly a reserved character. But I like it. Then we switch to “Lifedeath.” In the comics “Lifedeath” is the follow up issue to Storm getting shot with the neutralizer. She is rescued from the river by Forge who takes her to his home in Dallas. This is way more rustic than his original high tech skyscraper. They start a romance which ends when she learns that he was the one who built the neutralizer gun. The outfit Storm is wearing here is the same one she was wearing in the comics, but desexualized. S She’s just straight up only wearing overalls in the comics, while the cartoon made sure you saw there was a shirt under there. If there is one thing you have to know about Forge it is that he loves short shorts. I am glad the cartoon made sure to keep this character trait. X-Men ’97 is clearly showing a younger Forge than the one from Bishop’s future. The original X-Men cartoon puzzlingly used the same character model for both stuff set in the present and stuff set in the distant future. It is very funny that Forge has this shirtless photo of himself up on the wall. Over the course of the ’90s Forge began to take on more and more Fabio-esque. I swear he was sometimes drawn just as if he was on the cover of a romance novel. Forge reveals he was the initial person who made mutant control collars possible. I don’t like this for a couple of reasons. The first is that “Lifedeath Part 1” is only ten minutes long and this comes at the five minute mark. They just haven’t had enough time for it to really feel like a real relationship is crumbling. Also it is reality breaking because now anyone could make neutralizer gun, so obviously they would. In the comics, only Forge is capable of making it. It also elides that Forge wasn’t really attempting to make a neutralizer gun in the first place. In the ’80s Marvel held the license to make comics about a Parker Brothers toy called “Rom” who was a space cyborg. Rom’s enemies were aliens called “Dire Wraiths” who could shapeshift, and were impersonating various high level people in the government. Rom had various guns which would create various effects, one of which was a neutralizer which would revert the Dire Wraiths to their original forms. Valerie Cooper had Forge attempt to recreate that gun, which became the neutralizer gun. But Marvel lost the Rom license and then could never republish any of those stories, so the entire reason why Forge built the neutralizer gun essentially became lost. Marvel is just now republishing Rom for the first time since it was originally published, and I have the first omnibus but I haven’t gotten to the Forge stuff (and it might not even be in these issues) so I am going off summaries. But all this is should be more tragic than it comes off in the cartoon. Also Forge mentions that a “scientist in Scotland” created the actual mutant inhibitor collars. Which could be Apocalypse. But also could be Moira MacTaggart. Moira has been on one hell of a villain arc recently. She did some real messed up things. Storm rips into Forge because, “you of all people should know the perils of trusting those in Washington!” This… seems a little racial Storm. Although it has always been an… interesting choice to have a Native American character consistently working for the American government. This is one of the benefits of having lots of diversity. There are quite a few native X-Men, from lots of different tribes, who all have very different personalities and histories. There are Native Americans who have worked for the government, and Forge is a really complex, nuanced and interesting portrayal of what that actually means. So the villains in “Lifedeath” are the Dire Wraiths. In that storyline, one of the Dire Wraiths kills Forge’s mentor Naze, and replaces him. And then the alien posing as Naze gets possessed by Forge’s ancient enemy the Adversary, resulting in the Adversary looking like a Native American warrior. X-Men ’97 skips past all that complexity, and just has the Adversary as an owl monster. I thought X-Men ’97 was going to build to “Inferno,” but “Inferno” was last episode. We might wind up having “Fall of the Mutants” as the finale. It’s interesting that X-Men was really deeply interested in what was on the stands when it was being produced, they did classic Chris Claremont stories, of course, but the bulk of the show was the contemporary ’90s stuff. X-Men ’97 is, ironically given the title, really delving into those ’80s stories that the original cartoon was uninterested in. This is an episode that could have used an extra ten minutes for “Lifedeath.” But still it is an impressive outing. X-Men ’97 is succeeding beyond my wildest dreams when the project was announced.

Question: Is it not extremely racist for the new Dune movie to use African Americans to represent the tribal uncivilized fremen who perform ritualistic sacrifice and murder? Movie always seem to use African Americans in these roles.
Answer: The Fremen were uncivilized? The Fremen were the most civilized society in the film. They were certainly a harsh society, but no harsher than any of the other civilizations depicted. Paul Atreides engages in ritual combat to secure his position on two occasions, not one The Fremen culture survives under extreme conditions, and has completely adapted to those conditions. Everything they do makes absolute logical sense when you place them in an environment where water is as scarce as it is on Arrakis. So what is the excuse for barbarism of the Harkonnens? Of the Corrinos? Of the Bene Gesserit? Or, indeed, of the Atreides? None of them are without sin. The entire plot if Dune is about barbarism. It is about the richest people in the entire universe plotting to murder each other (and kill a lot of other people in the process). Everything that might be considered uncivilized about the Fremen is just as true about the wider Empire. It is just that the Fremen look uncivilized to us, while all those noble houses don't. There is a tendency, going at least back to Rome, and likely much further, to divide the world into the civilized and the savage. And the savage’s violence is proof of their barbarism, while our civilized violence is justified a thousand different ways. Even if our violence is many, many times greater than any of the so-called savages. One of the great tragedies of Dune Messiah is that, over the course of the Jihad, Fremen culture completely collapses. There are a lot of passages bemoaning this. A few Naibs had come out to observe the treatment accorded a fellow Fremen. They’d brought on the clamor, exciting Korba to protest his innocence. Alia moved her gaze across the Fremen faces, trying to recapture memories of the original men. The present blotted out the past. They’d all become hedonists, samplers of pleasures most men couldn’t even imagine. It is fair to say in Dune Messiah the Fremen are uncivilized, or less civilized. Not Dune. They went from engaging in a massive, multi-generational terraforming project to killing sixty billion people and plundering hundreds of planets. As far as using black actors to play Fremen, they didn’t solely use black actors. But using people of color was a necessary precondition of the story. The Fremen are a group of people the Harkonnens consider insects. Who the Bene Gesserit view as easily manipulated rabble. Who the Atreides view as a useful tool. The racial politics that are right there in Dune in the original novel necessitate that the Fremen be a non-white civilization. Not to mention that everything about the Fremen is meant to evoke Arabian civilizations.

Question: Do you think X-Men '97 was made by fans, for fans?
Answer: Not entirely, but we know for the most part it was. "My [line producer] was the first hire, and he brought along all the amazing talent that followed. My general rule was you had to be a fan. No questions," he said. "I've been on a show -- namely Witcher -- where some of the writers were not [fans] or actively disliked the books and games, even actively mocking the source material. It's a recipe for disaster and bad morale. Fandom as a litmus test checks egos and makes all the long nights worth it. You have to respect the work before you're allowed to add to its legacy." The staff isn't entirely made up of fans, Eric and Julia Lewald, who co-created the original cartoon, are consulting producers on X-Men ‘97. Before they were hired for the original X-Men cartoon that had never even heard of the X-Men. But they have done a lot to preserve the show's legacy, including publishing two books on its history. Also acting as a consulting producer is legendary animation director Larry Houston. Houston was a huge X-Men fan before the original cartoon, and he was consistently pitching a revival of the series. He also once drew Wolverine for me This is something I will treasure for my whole life. But, for the most part, yes, everyone who was hired was someone who grew up watching the original cartoon and loved it. Actually I am surprised the show is this good considering that fact. There is, in fact, almost no fan service. It is extremely respectful of the original series but is also intent upon making new stories and pushing this specific portion of the franchise forward.

Question: When do you think Jean Grey was replaced by Madelyne Pryor in 'X-Men '97'?
Answer: It is sometime after season two. And he was, at least, at the stage of cloning Jean by the time the season four finale “Beyond Good and Evil” begins. Throughout season two, Mr. Sinister has a lot of irons in the fire. He’s a very busy guy. But the main thing he is after is the genes of Jean Grey and Scott Summers. But, by the time “Beyond Good and Evil” rolls around he is willing to personally hand Jean over to Apocalypse. Which means that by that point he had everything he wanted from her. The X-Men even comment on this directly in “Beyond Good and Evil” part two. Cyclops: Jean and I were both in the car when the blast hit. Sinister's always wanted both of us. Why was she taken and I left behind? Xavier: I have been wondering the same thing, Scott. X-Men ’97 retroactively made Sinister’s actions in “Beyond Good and Evil” make more sense and answer this specific dialogue. The problem with narrowing it down further is that Mr. Sinister is just not in many episodes between season two and “Beyond Good and Evil.” I think the most obvious place for the swap to occur is around the start of season four. The only other real place for it to happen is between seasons two and three. Season three begins with the “Out of the Past” two parter, which leads directly into “The Phoenix Saga” five-parter, and then the “Dark Phoenix Saga” four parter. Jean could not be replaced anywhere durring or between the two Phoenix Saga stories. And while there is a gap between “Out of the Past” and “The Phoenix Saga” it is not one where I would slot much time in. Adding to all this is that Mr. Sinister is shattered at the end of season two. So I think the obvious place where the switch occurred is in season four.

Question: How do you think Marvel could have handled its Pride Allies variant covers better?
Answer: They could have just explained what they meant when they published the solicitations. This is one of the more idiotic news stories to happen in the comics industry. On March 21st Marvel published it’s June solicitations, which included a bunch of solicitations for “PRIDE ALLIES VARIANT COVER[S]” for various books. But they didn’t explain what that actually meant. So a website called “Popverse” decided to hop in. Marvel Comics will be celebrating Pride Month this year by looking beyond those of us in the LGBTQIA+ community and focusing on those who support them: the allies. Which, naturally, riled some people up. Doing, “let’s think of straight people,” for Pride month is… not great. Then Marvel released its actual announcement about the covers. The premise of the covers is that there will be a queer character and a straight character (who is presumably the star of the book). Which is… perfectly fine. There is really isn’t a legitimate complaint for the star of the comic to be on the cover. And I actually hate variant covers that are completely unconnected to the books they appear on. And Marvel does this a lot. If Marvel had just announced what they meant by “Pride Allies,” either before or with the solicitations, then no one would have cared. In fact, no one would have cared if they did do covers of characters who are just allies, if they didn’t make a thing about it. DC does that. People actually loved this cover. By now Marvel should know that sites will farm clicks off them and so they need to be on top of things. Anywho, and now I will get to the actual thing I think they should have handled better. Marvel…. has Daredevil even met Rachel Summers? HAVE THEY MET? These two are not allies, they are strangers. My friend made the joke that they both wear red, and apparently Marvel thought that was good enough. If Daredevil is going to be an ally, it feels like he should be allied to someone who is, like, his actual friend. Does Daredevil have any gay friends? Is Daredevil homophobe coded? I demand a list of comics that Daredevil has shared with Rachel Summers to prove there is a genuine friendship here! Now Spider-Man has met Northstar, because Spider-Man has met everyone. But they are not particularly friends. In fact, I would be surprised if Spider-Man didn’t irritate Northstar. Why isn’t Spider-Man’s cover with Iceman! As my friend said, they are amazing friends! It just feels like we are throwing random characters together rather than highlighting actual allies. Artistically the better choice would be to showcase characters who have deep and profound connections to each other. I assume Black Cat will be on the cover of her own book, which sort of defeats the point of these covers. Hercules, I assume will be on Hulk, which will be a fun throwback to The Incredible Hercules (which is extremely good). Either Rūna or Loki could be on Thor, though I would hope it is Loki. And Hulkling would probably be on Scarlet Witch, which would be very funny that she’s on the cover with her son-in-law and not her son. But, honestly, I think I put more thought into this than Marvel did.

Question: Why did the Marvel films initially get built around white male characters?

The ten Marvel characters in the arrangement are Captain America, The Avengers, Nick Fury, Black Panther, Ant-Man, Cloak & Dagger, Dr. Strange, Hawkeye, Power Pack, and Shang-Chi. Each film is expected to have a budget of up to $165 million dollars and a rating no more restrictive than PG-13. Although the financing allows for the production of animated films, Marvel currently intends to use the financing to make only live-action films. Black Panther, Shang-Chi, and Cloak and Dagger were supposed to be among the first films they planned on making. While Iron Man and Thor weren’t even considered. So… what happened? Real life super villain Ike Perlmutter. It’s actually in Bob Iger’s autobiography. "I’ve been in the business long enough to have heard every old argument in the book, and I’ve learned that old arguments are just that: old, and out of step with where the world is and where it should be," he writes in The Ride of a Lifetime. "We had a chance to make a great movie and to showcase an underrepresented segment of America, and those goals were not mutually exclusive. I called Ike and told him to tell his team to stop putting up roadblocks and ordered that we put both Black Panther and Captain Marvel into production." (Former) CEO of Marvel Entertainment Ike Perlmutter is possibly the most hated individual in the comics industry in its entire history. In my entire time following the comics industry I have never once heard a single positive story about him. Ever. He’s notoriously racist, he’s notoriously sexist. He threatened to shoot one of his employees with a gun he keeps in his desk. He is personally responsible for canceling Fantastic Four, and all the licensing rights to the X-Men. He continuously prevented Marvel from making Black Widow toys. He’s in the Sony email hack telling Sony to not make female led films. He is the reason a Black Widow film didn’t get made when the character was, you know, alive. This is one of those rare cases where there really was a single bad person who was responsible for everything. Perlmutter personally killed any attempt to make a film about anyone who wasn’t a white male. A lot of stuff, obviously, happened between Marvel’s announcement in 2005 and when they first released Iron Man in 2008. But Black Panther almost certainly would have been a Phase One film without Perlmutter personally killing it.
