Question: I stopped reading X-Men comics in the mid 90s. What is the best way to get back into the comics and catch up on what I've missed?
Answer: All you need is this one specific book: New X-Men by Grant Morrison. You missed out on a lot of good stuff, and a lot of bad stuff. But only New X-Men can really be considered a foundational text of the franchise. Everything that has happened in the last twenty years has been, in some sense, about these stories. This is both the best starting point for X-Men comics, in general, as well as the first place to go to catch up on them. After reading New X-Men you can skip directly to the Krakoa era with House of X/Powers of X. Or the entire line is about to be rebooted. So you can just wait a few months to skip directly to the reboot. Known as “From the Ashes.” IF you want to fill in the parts that you missed, you can read Joss Whedon’s Astonishing X-Men which is direct continuation of New X-Men. Also the Mystique solo series. Skip House of M, all you need to know is that a bunch of mutants got depowered. Read Mike Carey’s X-Men (which is retitled X-Men Legacy) and Peter David’s X-Factor. Also X-Men: Endangered Species. Read the Messiah Complex, Messiah War and Second Coming crossovers. Necrosha is fun, but inessential. Then read Matt Fraction’s Uncanny X-Men followed by Kieron Gillen’s Uncanny X-Men. Skip Avengers vs. X-Men, it’s terrible and all you need to know is that mutants are back. Then you can hit Krakoa directly. Starting with House of X/Powers of X and then working your way through Dawn of X.

Question: What was the most chilling moment in "The Zone of Interest" for you?
Answer: There are a lot of them, but this moment, this is the one that really stuck in my mind. HEDWIG:Aniela! Aniela enters from the kitchen. HEDWIG (CONT’D) (gestures to Linna’s uneaten breakfast):Take it away. (as Aniela picks it up) Was that here to spite me? ANIELA (perplexed): No, Mrs. Höss? HEDWIG (eating, as Aniela takes the plate away): I could have my husband spread your ashes across the fields of Babice. The film is about how the comfortable, aspirational upper middle class lifestyle of the Höss family is can't be extracted from the horrors it is predicated upon. The horrors going on right behind the wall that their yard bumps up against. Even more then that they can’t unwind their life from the genocide it is based on, they don’t even try. They aren’t ignoring it, they are indulging in it. The character of Hedwig is fascinating in how she is unflinching about what their position is. She is fully aware that their life is based on a death camp, and intends to take advantage of that fact, strictly for the most mundane comforts. She isn’t Ilse Koch, she’s too provincial and stuffy for that. But she does call herself “the Queen of Auschwitz” and is willing to threaten to kill her slaves over the most insignificant of perceived slights.

Question: Have any members of the X-Men ever joined the Avengers? If yes, who were they and what was their role?
Answer: A bunch of them have joined the Avengers. It is not too terribly uncommon for X-Men to, essentially, take a break from mutant issues to join the Avengers. But no matter how much they to be an uncomplicated hero, it catches back up to them. The first member of the X-Men to migrate to the Avengers was Beast. And Beast is really the only character to really get treated as having both teams co-equal. This was after the All New All Different X-Men debuted. And after his solo title got canceled. But before he joined the Defenders, and long before X-Factor. Anyway In Avengers #137, Thor felt the Avengers were understaffed and so made a TV commercial asking for people to join. They didn’t have American Idol back then and so didn’t know how that would actually go in real life. Beast shows up and joins the team. Beast really gets his fun loving goofy personality here. As opposed to the overly erudite studious one in X-Men (though, honestly, frequently silly there too) and his tortured monster routine in his solo title. He becomes really good friends with Wonder Man. And he is on the team for an extremely long time. He eventually leaves in Avengers #211, so it was a good seventy-four issue long stretch. Nearly twenty-five years will pass before the next member of the X-Men joins the Avengers, Wolverine. In New Avengers #6, the New Avengers have a fun little romp in the Savage Land where they run into Wolverine who is also there for some reason. And they ask him to join the team because he will kill people. No, seriously, that’s the reason. This is deeply silly for multiple reasons. And it begins what is one of the more bizarre deconstructions of Wolverine as a character. Where the loner who doesn’t get along with people joins every team he can. In fact, he becomes a cop. You sort of really see how pre-mind wipe Wolverine worked for every single evil government agency that would hire him. New Avengers was a weird book, and not very good. The next X-Man to join was Storm. This is Avengers vol. 4 #19. She’s only there because T’Challa askes her to be there, and he only askes because he wants her to stay in New York where he was at the time. She’s possibly the least committed member of the Avengers ever. Her stint as a member of the Fantastic Four was far more obviously something she actually wanted to do. Then we have the Uncanny Avengers recruits. Havok, Sunspot, Cannonball, Rogue and Sunfire. And, eventually, Cable. Hahaha. No. Cannonball and Sunspot would go on to a much better stint in the Avengers in Johnathan Hickman’s run. That’s where Cannonball meets his wife. Sunspot sticks around even longer with his own Avengers team, culminating in the USAvengers. Which is really fun. So far there has only been one Avenger to make the opposite trip, and that Namor. Namor was established to be a mutant in X-Men #6. And no one did much with that information for decades. But during Dark Reign he and Emma Frost formed an alliance against Norman Osborn, which eventually became an alliance between the X-Men and Atlantis. Namor joins the various X-Men teams for a quite long time.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is your review of X-Men '97 episode two "Mutant Liberation Begins"?
Answer: What a really great episode. This would have ranked as one of the best episodes of the original cartoon. It just so perfectly encapsulates everything the series is about while also filled with propulsive action. So this is the big Magneto showcase. It is very explicitly an adaptation of X-Men #200, “The Trial of Magneto.” The tragic death of David Hemblen, who was a fantastic Magneto, means that Matthew Waterson has stepped into the role. And while the change in voice actors is noticeable, Waterson really nails all the different shades Magneto requires: his majesty, his charisma, his pathos, his anger, his sadness. This episode lived or died on his performance, and he did a fantastic job. Magneto’s final speech is chilling for how good it is. While the first episode of the season reintroduces the X-Men after a (in our time) twenty-five year gap, this episode really lays out what the season will be about. The season, at least so far, keeps treating Xavier as if he is really dead, even though obviously he is just in space with his wife. This is weird, but it gets us to where Magneto is in this episode. He isn’t actually reformed. However he has decided to honor Charles by putting in as good faith an effort into his dream as possible. He might not truly believe in the dream, but he will genuinely put in the effort. Magneto doesn’t half ass anything. But to start off the episode we get some changes to the credits. First Magneto gets his own title card. But then we get Storm and the Morlocks, Bishop time traveling from the episode “Beyond Good and Evil,” Asteroid M, and the Dark Phoenix. I am curious if they are going to keep switching up the opening to accommodate all the episodes in the series. The opening scene has Magneto rescuing people from a ferris wheel, which is hilariously the perfect situation for him, specifically, to do rescue operations. And everyone on the planet begins speculating about Magneto rescuing humans. But then we get Magneto rescuing the Morlocks from the Friends of Humanity. This establishes Magneto’s new attitude perfectly. He doesn’t kill the hate group members, even though he obviously could have easily. But he does heap contempt on humanity for their actions. Not these specific humans, all humans. He is still Magneto, even if his behavior has changed. Rogue talks about how plenty of the X-Men have had rather sordid pasts. Rogue’s past as a super villain really only comes up in the episode "A Rogue's Tale," so I really hope we explore that more this season. Also I am so glad that the show is giving her completely bananas Southern expressions (that are so homespun that I don’t even know if they are expressions!). But keeping that episode in mind let’s the audience understand why Rogue is so quick to believe Mangeto has reformed. Also explains the surprise twist at the end of the episode! Magneto shits on Xavier for letting the Morlocks live in the sewer, and then announces he is sending them to Genshoa (that… seems ominous). It is fair to criticize Xavier for that, but also if I recall correctly the Morlocks didn’t want to move. And the last time we were in Genosha, you were in charge, Erik. You could have done that any time. This scene also really emphasizes Magneto’s distaste for what he is doing. He basically spits out the word “co-existence.” This is such an interesting character arc. When they talk about scanning Magneto’s mind to see whether he is going to betray them, Jean brings up what is a really great point. She can only assess his intentions at the moment she scans him. Which only tells them about right *now* and not the future, when he could just as easily change his mind. This really interesting, very true, and something I haven’t seen brought up with telepathy much before. “My intentions here were not to cause drama or discord” says the most dramatic person the X-Men know aside from maybe Apocalypse. Jean delivers some exposition about the Dark Phoenix Saga, which is surely just some nice color. And is not foreshadowing that, say, she has been replaced by a clone who is going to go real evil real soon. This is an interesting conversation because Storm reveals she sometimes wants to be human, but also loves her life in the X-Men. Which is probably also not foreshadowing. Jean reveals she hopes her child won’t be a mutant… which we probably shouldn’t linger on. By the by, at one point Jean read Cable’s mind and so explicitly knows his parentage, however she never told anybody what she saw. Not sure why I am bringing that up. It’s probably not relevant. Ahh, the Trial of Magneto. This is great because Magneto views it as a shortcut to earning the X-Men’s trust, submitting to a form of justice he doesn’t actually believe in. Magneto obviously can’t be compelled to stand trial, the episode itself shows that. He is doing this because it aligns with his goals. And if he doesn’t get a fair trial with a reasonable verdict, then he proves Xavier wrong, and discredits humanity to the X-Men. This is a high risk gamble for Erik, but one with a lot of upsides. He also gets some real potshots into the United Nations, pointing out the Sentinel programs and the control collars. One of the judges claims they need to protect themselves, but their actions demonstrate they think of mutants as a problem to solve rather than a people to co-exist with. But this is all cut short because rioters break into the UN. Some really snappy points by Magneto that just treating him as a person, giving him that small dignity, places them on the side of mutant rights in a way that marks them as the enemy. X-Cutioner is a very minor villain in the comics. He uses alien technology to hunt down mutant criminals. Making him a member of the Friends of Humanity is much cleaner. As is having his technology being old Sentinel and Genoshan tech. I think having him win against five X-Men is pumping him up a bit much. But it is really funny that he just straight up does the “white privilege doesn’t exist because my life is hard!” whine. Except with mutants. “Well now who does she think she… “Do not think. Be silent. Heed my commands and you shall survive.” Damn, Ororo, you didn’t need to go that hard, but I am glad you did. Scott and Jean dealing with this bigot doctor really hits on some of the themes of the show. Bigotry isn’t some super villain attacking, but rather a constant stream of indignities that make life measurably harder for people. And I like that the resolution allows the show to reestablish more of Rogue’s powers. As I knew they were adapting “Lifedeath” parts ones one and two, I knew this storyline was coming. I can understand the economical reasons to make this the X-Cutioner’s gun. But in the comics this gun was made by Forge, and that is was really drives his need for atonement. And it was Valerie Cooper who ordered it made. And she was actually shot by Henry Peter Gyrich. It is a really complex point, the government is a huge entity, and everyone who got their hands on the gun had more malicious intent than the previous person. Ultimately the US government doesn’t care that it depowered Storm, she was merely an acceptable casualty in a weapons test. Which is a very different story from she got shot by a member of a hate group. I really don’t see how “Lifedeath” part one can be adapted, though, as it is entirely about Storm discovering Forge was the one who built the gun. Also, the show is introducing the fact that anyone could have built the gun, when in the comics only Forge could have built it. This is such a tragic moment and it lands so well. Magneto’s speech is so good. So beautifully written. The sentiments so perfect. I can’t do justice to it. Just go watch it. Or watch it again. Many people don’t know that Rogue and Magneto had a whole thing when they were stuck in the Savage Land together. Two Jeans?!? What could this mean? Could they finally be resolving the Jean-Scott-Logan love triangle? Such a good episode. I highly recommend it. This is really strong, really confident show.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Do you believe Cyclops made the right decision to abandon Madelyne Pryor and their son in favor of reuniting with Jean Grey in the comics?
Answer: Yes. Obviously it was the right decision. The one thing we know about the relationship between Scott Summers and Madelyne Pryor is that she was physically abusive. If the genders in this story were reversed, it would be a tragic story of a person getting out of an abusive relationship. We know that to be true because every Hank Pym story is still about the one time he hit Janet. It is absolutely baffling to me that people give Maddie a pass on her physical abuse, or even applaud her. Additionally Madelyne Pryor was extremely psychologically abusive. Madelyne Pryor regularly goes behind Scott’s back to his friends and co-workers in order to talk shit about him. She consistently attempts to poison his entire social circle against him, with her ultimate goal being to isolate him in Alaska thousands of miles from his entire support system. It’s incredibly manipulative, incredibly malicious. She will do things like blame Scott for when the Beyonder abducted him, something he has no control over. And let’s talk about the infamous scene where he “abandons” her. All she knows is that Warren needs to see Scott. Warren, not Jean. Hearing that Warren, one of Scott’s three oldest and closest friends needs to see him causes her to end the relationship. Her. Not him. Stop to think about how manipulative this is. How cruel this is. How possessive this is. She won’t even let him see Angel. She is threatened and lashes out to the point of ending her marriage because Scott wants to see Angel. She can’t allow him any relationship with another person. In fact, this pretty much proves that Scott was right to not tell her about Jean. It would be unreasonable to expect him, in this situation, not to see Jean. But she can’t even handle him going to see Warren. It’s so abusive. And none of this includes her selling her soul to a demon, trying to sacrifice her child to a demon, or telepathically manipulating Scott to keep him in the marriage. Or how she cheated on him with his brother. She was always a monster. Long before any of those revelations/retcons. Scott never even wanted to be in the relationship in the first place. He spends the entire time they dated trying to get out of it, and then when they get married keeps trying to end it. The sole reason he stuck it out with her is because everyone kept gaslighting him into staying in what is an obviously toxic relationship with an obviously abusive person. I wish Scott had taken lil’ baby Cable with him. But that’s not something that we can really say is on him, he was getting out of a profoundly abusive relationship. Like I said, I have been baffled by this for years. I do not understand how anyone can think Scott did anything wrong in this relationship, aside from staying in it. We’re literally shown physical abuse on pannel.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is your review of X-Men '97 episode one "To Me, My X-Men"?
Answer: This is an extremely strong opening episode that reflects a creative team really understanding the original X-Men cartoon. While it had its weak points, it confidently demonstrated everything the original show excelled at, the humor, the heart, balancing so many different characters. And it really understood the core themes of the series. The original series chose to start with the Sentinels, and quite wisely the new series also starts with them. The episode focuses on the Sentinels, Bolivar Trask, the Friends of Humanity, and Henry Peter Gyrich. Not only does this tie into the original series, as Gyrich was the one who shot Xavier, but thematically in the original series episode “The Final Decision” Xavier told Master Mold that it was the antithesis of his dream. In fact, Gyrich sums up the anti-thesis of the X-Men perfectly in this episode when he says, “…normal people know the more room we make for your kind the less we leave for ours. So we might wear tolerance on our sleeves, but we know the naked truth: tolerance is extinction.” In the episode we watch the villains perfectly encapsulate everything the X-Men stand against, and then get the absolute crap kicked out of them. In fact, the Sentinels they fight at the end of the episode are rusting junk, violent and dangerous… but also decaying. It’s works so well. The real weakness of the episode is that it has to remind everyone who all the characters are, what their deal is, and what their relationships are. It’s a very thin plot so that a lot of exposition can happen. Apparently not everyone has spent the last twenty-five years obsessively rewatching the original cartoon. For the most part, the original opening titles are lovingly recreated in the original art style. However there are some interesting changes. Jean is moved from second to last to second. And Morph and Bishop both get their own title cards. Morph is now rendered in the style of the character from the Exiles comics, which is the most successful version of Morph. Morph also gets this very evocative shot with Mr. Sinister. I really loved this shot. Magneto’s Brotherhood has also been updated. Juggernaut, Pyro, Mystique, Sabretooth, and Avalanche were there in the original. But Thunderbird and Alpha have been replaced by the White Queen and Lady Deathstrike. I know before hand someone intimated that Emma would have a big role to play in the season, but I would be so excited to see more Lady Deathstrike, who only appeared in one two parter in the original. This opening scene with Sunspot is really good. The Friends of Humanity were probably the most radical thing X-Men ever did because they are just a hate group. Sunspot has to learn the hard way that, to bigots, there is no such thing as “one of the good ones.” He doesn’t get much of an arc this episode, there’s way too much else the episode needs to accomplish. But learning the limits of respectability politics is a really great throughline for him. Very explicitly the people working on this show were all fans of the original. Which resulted in some really interesting things. They are huge Cyclops fans. Cyclops gets to do more bad ass stuff, and has more respect piled on him than any other adaptation. He uses his powers so creatively and just tears through these chodes. This show is extremely horny for Gambit. Also there are some truly amazing ’90s fashion choices going on throughout it. But it is deeply funny that Gambit is just cooking a massive amount of beignets for everyone, in case you didn’t know he is from New Orleans. Have you had beignets from New Orleans, because you should. HOW MANY BEIGNETS DID YOU COOK, GAMBIT? Jubilee askes Sunspot what his powers are when they are in the Danger Room. She says, “What can you do? Fly? Teleport? Shoot gold balls from your body? That’d be weird!” Weird, yes, but also very useful. This is why you don’t let Wolverine teach children. The original show did establish that these five were the first X-Men. Something I don’t think is really reconcilable with Archangel’s stories in that first season. But honestly, who cares? Embrace the continuity error. Valerie Cooper is supposed to be a big character this season, even supposedly going to be the one to deliver the theme of the show. In the comics she works for the government, and is the pro-mutant voice. But she more considers mutants to be a strategic asset. Question: What is the difference between a villain and a super villain?
Answer: A villain is simply someone who has malignant goals that knowingly cause harm to other people. Raise your hand if you have ever felt personally victimized by Regina George. An antagonist is simply whoever is preventing the protagonist from achieving their goals. But a villain is someone whose own goals are antisocial. The protagonist can, in fact, be the villain. A super villain is when the abilities of a villain cross the threshold of the possible. If whatever they are doing is no longer actually possible in the real world, that’s a super villain. If a character is a mob boss that likes to kill, that’s a villain. If a character controls all the crime in a major urban center and seemingly has infinite money to spend on conflicts with crime fighters, that’s a super villain. If a character is an immoral martial arts expert, that’s a villain. If a character has mastered a martial art to such a degree they now have magical powers, that’s a super villain. If a character uses technology to commit acts of larceny, that’s a villain. If a character builds a satellite that functions as a giant space laser, that’s a super villain. A super villain is a character who has harmful goals, and their abilities are not actually possible here in reality.

Question: In what ways is Dune a criticisms of capitalism?
Answer: It really isn’t. Frank Herbert was quite right-wing. He worked as a Republican speech writer. He was deeply mistrustful of the government, which is something that is all over the books in a way anti-capitalism is not. And, unlike a lot of works, the weird pseudo-feudal economy of Dune doesn’t really lend itself to much unintentional critique of capitalism. What critique there is of capitalism lies in the CHOAM corporation. CHOAM is an acronym standing for Combine Honnete Ober Advancer Mercantiles, and CHOAM has, essentially, monopolistic control over all trade in the Empire. The wealthy houses of the Landsraad, the Imperial House, the Spacing Guild and the Bene Gesserit are all partners in the corporation, and all view it as mutually beneficial. Much of the wealth of the great houses comes from securing directorships in CHOAM and then vacuuming up money. Before the final battle in Dune, the emperor raises the CHOAM flag over his encampment as a means to indicate he is siding with profit, and a reminder to all observers to do the same. This is the final stage of capitalism. One corporation that is inextricable from the government, being run by an anemic elite all of whom have permanent sinecures, and which exists solely to extract rents. It’s a nice bottomless cookie jar that the people who are already wealthy and powerful can keep sticking their hands in. While I think CHOAM is an interesting and important element to the story, it matters so little that every adaptation of Dune cuts it. And Herbert wasn’t laying out some grand philosophy of capitalism with it, so much as he wanted to demonstrate the petty corruption of governments.

Question: Which novel is recommended to read first: The Foundation Trilogy or Dune?
Answer: I would say you could read them in either order. Foundation is significantly shorter, and made up of short stories. Dune is more of a classic adventure story with an exotic location and strange alien life. Foundation is mostly conversations, frequently about how violence is stupid. I think thematically they are complimentary. Foundation is a series about an empire in terminal decline and the creation of the foundation on which its eventual replacement will rest. It’s extremely philosophical, with its often stated theme being that “Violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.” The characters always discover better ways to secure their goals than violence. There are stories about the use of religion and economics instead of conquest. The principle driving Foundation is that the actions driving groups of people is predictable, and because of this there is a path that, once set in motion, will be hard to deviate from. Dune is a series about a messianic figure appearing in the desert who takes control over the resource all transportation is based on. It is, much like Foundation, very philosophical. But it has more traditional action/adventure elements, such as wars and interpersonal fights. Dune is also interested in religion and economics, but comes to very different conclusions (and sometimes very similar) conclusions. Dune is also very concerned with fate and destiny, with psychic visions driving the entire series’ narrative. Like I said, they are more complimentary than competitive. I don’t think there is anything wrong with picking either series to start with. They are both good. They are both foundational sci-fi texts. If someone were to ask me this in real life, I would ask them what kind of sci-fi they like, if it is Star Wars, then Dune, if it is Star Trek, then Foundation. But that’s incredibly simplistic and reductive. Just in general, I would probably say Dune, as the first novel is largely what a person would expect from a sci-fi novel, while Foundation is very much its own thing. But read them both! I did, and I turned out fine!

Question: What do you think about the decision to avoid certain problematic traits of the Harkonnens in "Dune: Part Two" for modern audiences?
Answer: When I saw the first half of Dune, I was extremely skeptical about the aesthetic choices they made for the Harkonnens. The severe asceticism seemed to be rather contradictory to their nature as extremely corrupt wealth hoarders. It felt like subtraction, without any counter balance of addition. But then we got to the scenes on Giedi Prime in Dune Part Two and they were glorious. Some of the most amazing things in the entire duology. Frank Herbert was an extreme homophobe who rejected his son Bruce for being gay. He wouldn’t even let Bruce see his mother on her deathbed, according to Brian Herbert. Frank Herbert’s homophobia seeps into the Dune novels a surprising amount. There’s a whole conversation in God Emperor of Dune about how homosexuals are disgusting perverts, but that might be channeled into being good soldiers. But really the homophobia comes out with Frank Herbert making Baron Vladimir Harkonnen the most repulsive character he could imagine. He’s a fat, effeminate, gay pedophile. When we first meet the baron he’s described as covered in jewelry and sitting behind a giant pink desk talking to his nubile nephew and his effeminate servant. In all the films the suspensors that he uses to hold up his weight just make him fly around, that’s not the case in the books. In the books he is described as essentially dancing wherever he walks. Baron Harkonnen is the ugliest and most malicious possible stereotype that a mid-century writer could come up with for a gay man. There’s an entire subplot in the novel about a male sex slave who Feyd-Rautha attempts to poison the Baron with. It’s all right there on the page. And none of this is ancillary to the character. He isn’t a villain who happens to be gay, he is gay and therefore a villain. His homosexuality is demonized all over. Just like how his weight is demonized. The David Lynch movie leaned into this, even if indirectly. Sting is wearing bikini briefs after all. But Denis Villeneuve purges his version of all these plots and themes, which does reduce Feyd-Rautha to barely a character. And, at first I thought that was a mistake. If you watch all those Disney live action remakes they make their extremely gay villains not gay, and thus really boring. Just subtraction. I felt there were better ways to handle it. Just make some important person in house Atreides gay. But I came around to it in Dune Part Two. That harsh black and white visual dynamism convinced me it wasn’t simply subtraction, but rather clearing the way for what makes the Harkonnen’s villains. They’re villains because they are genocidal, murderous, sadistic slave owners. And there isn’t really any need to focus on other elements. Just show them in the harshest possible light. Which is exactly what the movie did.

Question: Are "filler episodes" in TV series a necessary evil to properly develop characters or would you prefer that they were completely removed from a show's storyline?
Answer: “Filler” means different things in different context. Within anime “filler” actually does have a specific definition. Usually anime winds up overtaking its own source material resulting in it needing to, essentially, kill time until the next story arc is complete. Filler is usually bad because, by definition, it can’t meaningfully affect the story in any way. All the characters have to be in the exact same position when the filler is over, without experiencing any growth. And it can’t explore the characters because that might need to be contradicted down the line. But, other times, shows do something interesting with their filler. There’s a great filler episode of Dragonball Z where Goku and Piccolo learn to drive. Filler doesn’t have to be bad, but most of the time it just is. But, like most terms that have a very specific definition in one context… it escapes that context resulting some nonsense. I think there is a fairly strong argument that, outside of anime, filler simply does not exist. There’s got to be TV show somewhere that overtook the book series it was based on, but I can’t think of it. A lot of people started using the term “filler” to mean any episode that doesn’t advance the plot. Which, in my opinion, stupendously fails to understand the point of television, as well as the concept of filler. Kurt Vonnegut said, on the subject of good writing, “Every sentence must do one of two things—reveal character or advance the action.” Revealing character is half the equation. Taking episodes that ignore ongoing plotlines in favor of adding depth and nuance to the characters is not filler. Those are always some of the best episodes I will say there are certain episodes I would consider filler, particularly in streaming series. They are usually heavily serialized shows with every aspect of production working under the belief these episodes will be binge watched, as opposed to watched in more discrete chunks as, say, episodes. Streaming shows tend to have episodes that just exist to fill out contractually mandated episode counts which are little more than plate spinning. Just wasting time until the finale. Hemlock Grove tended to have a lot of these. Netflix in general is notorious for extremely bloated seasons. So I guess I come down on the side that the filler should be good.

Question: How does Denis Villeneuve's decision to end "Dune: Part Two" on a cliffhanger impact audience expectations for a potential sequel or continuation of the story?
Answer: Dune ends with Paul Atreides having secured the throne as emperor of the known universe. Dune Messiah picks up with the jihad he unleashed being largely, if not entirely, concluded. And mostly deals with the fallout. The conclusion of Dune Part Two has the jihad starting. I don't known if we can accurately say whether this is a good or bad change until we get the third movie, but it will heavily impact the audience's view of the franchise. The ending of Dune Part Two is more elegant than Dune when considered in the context of the whole story. Paul has prophetic visions of the jihad across the novel, but Dune Messiah just casually dropping that sixty-one billion people were slaughtered between the books still comes from pretty far afield. So in that sense it is smoother. But the audience is going to expect to see the holy war the film just ended on having started. And that's not what happens at all. To anyone not familiar with the books, the war is what would be most interesting, and it would make little sense to skip over it to focus on post war political intrigue, assassination plots, and baby drama. The one way to thread this needle is to just set the events in the middle of the jihad, but I don't think that works. A lot of the justification for the messed up stuff in the Dune series is that that is just the way that it has to be. Which works a lot better as an excuse after the fact. As opposed to in the middle when Paul would have to say, “sorry can't do anything about my personal troops killing billions upon billions of people.” ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ Dune Messiah is incredibly important, but also a strange follow up to Dune. There is just no way the audience is going to go in and see the kind of story they expect, given the ending of Dune Part Two. I am excited for the Dune hot take industrial complex to try to grapple with Dune Messiah…

Question: How can Storm from X-Men be defeated? What are her vulnerabilities?
Answer: She’s just a person. You can just shoot her. In fact, that’s kind of what happened. It’s a high tech sci-fi gun that doesn’t use bullets, but it is still just shooting her. Storm is crazy powerful. Her ability to control the weather is unmatched by anyone except possibly Thor, and even Thor is starting to get a bit hesitant on that regard. Question: Is it true that many TV shows start off with their worst episodes and improve over time, or is this just a myth?
Answer: No, not their “worst episodes.” Those usually come at the end when a show is no longer capable of surprising the audience and is solely coasting. But the first episodes are usually quite weak compared to what comes later. TV is made on a pretty quick schedule. Those first episodes no one knows what works. They don’t have a firm grasp on what characters have chemistry, or even what their traits are. If it is a comedy, what kinds of jokes the show is going to tell. What plotlines are going to be important and what aren’t. And, if the show works, over the course of that first season, all this gets refined into a much stronger show. That’s why if you go back and watch the pilot episode of a series, people will often be acting slightly out of character. One of the more famous examples of this is that in the show Parks and Recreation, the character Leslie Knope was written to be very similar to Michael Scott from The Office in its first season. That’s…. not how her character stayed. In order to see this really happen, watch the TV show Happy Endings. Which is a brilliant, but largely overlooked, sitcom. And one of the greatest hang out sitcoms of all time. Happy Endings is about a group of six friends, two of which are getting married, Alex and Dave. Except Alex leaves Dave at the alter. The casting of the show was perfect, but everything else…. well, let’s just say there was room for improvement. The plot element of Alex and Dave is fairly rapidly dispensed with. It’s a big part of those early episodes, but as the series goes on all that is really important is that they used to be in a relationship. It’s never so bitter they can’t hang out. The character Penny was a sad sack Debbie Downer type character at the start, she got retooled to be more spunky and optimistic, despite keeping the trait of being extremely unlucky (particularly in love). Alex and Dave didn’t really have firm character traits at the start, because their main role was to facilitate the relationship break up plot. Alex eventually develops into being quite naive and, well, she’s pretty stupid. Dave becomes this try-hard hipster guy. Everyone in the show has these non-descript upper middle class office jobs at the start of the series, and the show slowly gives them all unique jobs based on their personalities. Dave runs a food truck, Alex has a failing store named Xela (it’s her name spelled backwards!), the character Jane becomes a used car salesperson. When Happy Endings debuted, it had pretty negative reviews from critics, but as the first season progressed, they started turning around on it. It ended its initial season with quite positive reviews. You may remember that I wasn't a fan of ABC's "Happy Endings" when it debuted last month, dismissing it as not only the last, but least, of this season's trend of sitcoms about young friends and/or relatives at different relationship stages. Then a funny thing happened: I kept watching the show, at first just as something to have on in the background while doing other things, but then because I realized I was starting to actually, somehow, enjoy it. By the time season two gained momentum it got rapturous reviews, favorably comparing it to 30 Rock and Arrested Development. If you want to understand what this phenomena is, then Happy Endings is a show where it is very clearly shown. You see this progression where things become more specific and refined. Where the stuff that doesn’t work is jettisoned, new stuff is brought in, and the stuff that worked is enhanced. But you will find that most shows have weaker initial episodes. And if you listen to DVD commentary tracks as much as I have, you frequently hear the people bemoan that they can’t just do six practice episodes in order to get the series to the level it gets midseason. There are plenty of series that are great out of the gate. But also so, so very many with weak initial episodes.

Question: What factors do you think contribute to the trend of TV shows being canceled after only one or two seasons?
Answer: The way television worked was that studios would license the shows they make to networks for what amounts to a relatively small amount of profit. The networks would then make money from the advertising shown while those shows aired. The big bucks for a studio came when a show entered syndication, because then the product has already been fully paid for, so it is literally just free profit. But the barrier to syndication is an episode count of around 100. It’s never been exactly 100, many kids shows top at around 65 episodes because you can then air the series four times per-year in syndication. But 100 is kind of the benchmark. So the studio is highly motivated to get its shows to 100 episodes. A new series, which has 13 to 22 episodes, inherently has less profit potential than a series three seasons in, with 66 episodes. So studios will work extremely hard to keep shows that are deeper into their run on the air. They will cut their fees down to the bone, sometimes even accept a loss. This is what happened with a show that I am borderline obsessed with, ’Til Death. Under traditional TV models, there is less incentive to keep a new show that has mediocre ratings on the schedule than a series in its third season. Not to mention that most shows are just not going to be hits. And certainly not hits out of the gate. So while all this applies to traditional TV… that’s not what’s going on with streaming. I’m just going to quote directly from an excellent Vulture article on the subject. To make up for the lost back end, streamers floated performance-based incentives. Schur describes a scenario in which a platform might promise a showrunner a $100,000 bonus for season one, $250,000 for season two, $500,000 for season three, and $1.7 million for season four. “So you’re like, Holy shit. This is great!” he says. There was a catch. Many seemingly successful series began to vanish after just a couple of seasons. “What no one saw coming was they’d just kill the show before they ever had to pay that money out,” Schur says. “They kind of tricked everybody. Now if you get to 20 episodes, it’s a miracle.” If the streaming industry seems aggressively ruthless with canceling its shows, that’s because it is. It promised that people would get skimpy pay for the start of a series, and big pay for its conclusion. So it makes sure that no series reaches that conclusion unless it is an astounding hit on the level of Stranger Things.

Question: Why is it when watching old TV series, we'd see some actors returning throughout the series playing different roles, but that's pretty rare to see in modern series?
Answer: Old television series were made with the understanding that the audience would regularly miss episodes. The only options the audience had was to see an episode where it aired, catch a rerun, or catch it in syndication. People could, theoretically, tape every episode of a series and watch them obsessively, but outside of Star Trek and Twin Peaks, how often was that going to happen? At the most, the audience was going to view one episode per day in syndication. There was no binge watching, there was no starting over from the begining. So, for the most part, no one will notice if one actor is going to play multiple. If you have 100 episodes airing one per day, who will notice that the same actor plays a character in episode 23 and a different character in episode 76? When the DVD player came into existence, it was suddenly viable to put a whole series onto a format where the audience absolutely would watch every episode. TV had been put on VHS before, but the limits of that format precluded the scale that DVD allowed for. This resulted in a revolution of how TV was made. TV could now be much, much more heavily serialized. It was now a lot more prestigious. People were now obsessively viewing these shows. The audience was now not only watching every episode, they were watching them back-to-back-to-back. And so things that were largely unnoticeable under the old system were now glaringly obvious. So, an actor playing multiple parts. Or, its inverse, multiple actors playing the same part. And so TV shows started minimizing those kinds of disruptions.

Question: What is the true potential of AI without its hype that's surrounding it?

So we are simply stuck accepting a world which is getting shittier in very obvious ways. Much like everything else in our lives.

Question: Is it necessary to have prior knowledge of the stories before reading major comic books like X-Men and Avengers?

You know Emma was a villain, and she did terrible things, including terrible things to a child. And you know why there is so much animosity between them. I look at them all the time. But they aren’t necessary. My advice to anyone wanting to read the comics of Marvel and DC is to simply pick up a book and start reading. Just accept anything you don’t know is irrelevant, and you will have a much better time.

Question: What is your review of the 'Madame Web' film?
Answer: Adam Scott plays Uncle Ben in Madame Web, which has a very extensive subplot about the birth of Peter Parker. And that is the level endless generosity of this film. This is a film that says what audiences want is to see Madame Web stare at the amniotic fluid left on the living room floor by Mary Parker giving birth, while considering the web of life and destiny. It was grand theft spider! But some spider-people in the jungle are able to save her unborn child, while also being bitten by a spider. Madame Web, now an adult in 2006, is a paramedic who seemly hates all of humanity, possibly except for her partner Uncle Ben. When she shows up 3/4ths of the movie still in the stolen cab I wanted to stand up and applaud. I guess they were all embarrassed to admit they got taken out by a spider-guy behind them, rather than the woman in handcuffs in front of them. So who is Madame Web? She is an icon. She is a contradiction. She saves lives and yet has nothing but contempt for every human she interacts with. She is a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma. She’s a bitch, she’s a lover, she’s a child, she’s a mother, she’s a sinner, she’s a saint, and she does not feel ashamed. She is GIRL to the MAXXX. And you know what, there’s a little Madame Web inside all of us, and we should all learn to be a little more like her. It is our responsibility. Is Madame Web good? How dare any of us ask such an offensive question! Madame Web gives, endlessly. Madame Web is the kind of movie where Madame Web will dump the three girls being stalked by a spider-guy who wants to murder them off onto Uncle Ben, while she flies to Peru for a week. That is the spirit of this movie, and I was in rapturous awe of it. Bravo, Madame Web, bravo! Question: What distinguishes an Omega Level Mutant from a regular powerful mutant in the Marvel Universe? Is it solely based on their potential or does it also involve their actual power output?

One Omega level mutant is Lactuca the Knower. Lactuca’s power is to know where things are. As in everything. In the entire universe. At all times. It is not possible to for anything else to ever know the location of more objects in the universe than Lactuca. Her power of simply knowing where things are is unsurpassable by anything else. As far as the power of knowing locations, she is the most powerful mutant ever born. The mistake everyone makes with Omega level mutants is assuming they are basically like Superman. They’re not. They are simply the most powerful potential version of whatever narrowly specific power they have. Some Omega level mutants are godlike reality manipulators. Others are just someone who knows the location of things. You can be an incredibly powerful mutant and still not be an Omega level mutant. Apocalypse is not an Omega level mutant.

Question: Why do some TV series get cancelled while others continue for many seasons? What factors contribute to this trend in the television industry?
Answer: Almost all TV is based on what advertisers are willing to spend to run commercials during a given show. Television exists to deliver commercials. The target demographic of TV are the ages of 18–49. That’s the age range considered to not have permanent consumption habits, as well as more likely to be persuaded to buy luxury goods. For almost all TV shows, the ratings are irrelevant, outside the demo. As TV ratings have gotten more sophisticated, they can be broken down even more by racial categories, gender, location, income, ect. Young, urban, middle and upper class white people are usually the demographic that is most valuable to advertisers. In 2011 Kathy Bates had a show called Harry’s Law which was watched by eight million people. It was canceled despite being watched by more people than The Simpsons, Glee, Family Guy, New Girl, and Law & Order SVU. But Harry’s Law was one of those cases of extremely lopsided ratings. It was watched, almost entirely, by people outside of the demo, while all those other shows were watched by the demo. NBC had a Thursday night line up of The Office, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, and Community. With the exception of The Office, these shows had garbage ratings. And even The Office wasn’t that great. In terms of general viewership, the highest it ever did was 41 out of all the shows airing in 2009–2010. But they smashed it out of the park in the demo, and even more importantly that young, urban, middle-upper class white demographic that advertisers crave. These were the shows the trendsetters were watching, and that’s why the internet is filled with gifs, memes, and references to them and not NCIS. There used to be an amazing website called TV by the Numbers which published the Neilson ratings every day. As part of the fandom for the shows above, it was always anxiety Friday while you waited for those numbers to roll in. But they all were renewed, year-after-year despite having objectively garbage viewership numbers. It’s more complicated than just the ratings, there are all sorts of esoteric edge cases and issues with network positioning, but it’s the ratings. And when you understand the ratings, it almost never becomes a mystery where any specific TV show is canceled or renewed.

Question: What is the reason for the increase in remakes and sequels in new movies compared to original stories in the past?
Answer: In the ‘80s, only one out of every twenty movies turned a profit when it was released in theaters. But that was that didn’t matter because the home video release was a second opening, and the TV premiere was a a third opening. Once a movie was made, it would be a perpetual revenue stream that would, eventually, be profitable. In order to actively lose money in this media ecosystem, a film had to be an extremely expensive bomb. Like Gigli starring Ben Affleck and Jennifer Lopez which cost $75 million to make. And honestly extremely expensive bombs from ‘60s, ‘70s, and ’80s probably mostly became profitable at some point. But in 2008, with the advent of Netflix streaming, the DVD market started collapsing. It declined by 86%. That completely changed the calculations for the entire movie industry. Now every movie had to be profitable in its theatrical release, which destroyed mid budget films. Everything released was either a microbudget film, which almost has to turn a profit or a blockbuster which was considered safer. A $200 million superhero film was considered safer than a $50 million period drama. In this environment, remakes and sequels, which already have brand recognition, are much, much safer than creating new films that need to build interest from scrap. And they are easier to marker internationally. So, we get a lot of remakes and sequels. And unless people start turning out in mass numbers for films like Babylon, that’s all we are getting.

Question: What are the best new movies of 2023 ranked?
Answer: Since I just completed my annual submission to the best movies of the year ranking list, I actually do have this ranked. I saw sixty-five movies this year, and there were a bunch of really great ones! Here are my top fifteen. Saltburn is black comedy thriller about an Oxford scholarship student, Oliver, who becomes best friends with one of his wealthy classmates, Felix, and is invited to spend the summer at his palatial mansion, the titular Saltburn. Oliver has to navigate the incredibly complex web of egos and needs that is Felix’s family in order to keep his indefinite stay going. And things start to get real weird, including a series of suspicious deaths. It’s a really fun, strange movie. The kind of movie where someone actually has sex with a grave. It is never really that big of a mystery why all these woes are befalling Felix’s family, but it is a fun, if bizarre ride. Alexander Skarsgård stars in this film as a struggling writer, James, in a failing marriage. They take a vacation in a third world country with a draconian legal system. Driving while drunk, James accidentally hits and kills a local man, the sentence for which is death. However the country has a loophole, for tourists who commit crimes, they can pay to have a perfect duplicate of themselves made and executed in their place. Rather than being horrified at the spectacle of seeing himself executed, it instead turns James on. And he winds up falling in with a group of tourists who commit murder and then get off on seeing themselves killed. It’s weird and dark, and really, really over the top. The Zone of Interest is a Polish movie that is entirely in German. Rudolf Höss, commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp lives right outside the camp in a house that borders the wall keeping the prisoners inside. The movie is primarily about the struggles of an upper middle class family to keep the lifestyle they have become accustomed to. While also being about the fact that no matter how hard they try to, they can’t normalize their absolutely monstrous existence. It is one of the most disturbing movies I have ever seen. It sat with me since I saw it, and every so often I ruminate on what it is saying. This is the exceedingly rare trilogy where the third entry is the best. Probably because it centers on Rocket, and his journey of self discovery. But the Guardians have to take on the High Evolutionary who is ruthlessly attempting to create a perfect race. And along the way all of them come to make peace with themselves. Also Cosmo is in it, and I love Cosmo. Based on the beloved Judy Blume novel, this is a lovely coming of age film about a young woman’s existential crisis of faith. Margaret is from a mixed Christian and Jewish family, and has been raised in neither faith, and after her family moves from New York City to the suburbs, she starts exploring religion as a means to understand herself. And along the way she learns a lot of life lessons, and grows up a lot, becoming a more empathetic person. It’s a really sweet, feel good drama. A Western noir about the real historical Osage murders, this is an excellent (if extremely long) film. The Osage people were moved onto a reservation which just happened to have a massive amount of oil under it, resulting in them becoming the richest nation on the planet. But this also resulted in an entire society that worked to extract money from them, including orchestrating over 100 murders to try to get the rights to their oil. Ernest Burkhart, the husband of an Osage woman named Mollie Kyle, winds up being a thief, hitman, and administrator of the murders on behalf of his uncle William King Hale. It’s dark and depressing, and unsparing in its look at how even wealth is not enough to protect some people. What an absolutely delightful fantasy heist movie. As someone who loves a good heist movie, the idea of using the Dungeons and Dragons IP this way is brilliant. It’s so much fun. It allows itself to be weird and esoteric, while also having so much heart. Chris Pine is absolutely delightful. It’s great. The third of Kenneth Branagh’s Hercule Poirot films, Poirot has retired to Venice where he is contacted to debunk a psychic on Halloween. While at its core, this is still a standard mystery film, it is filled with horror and supernatural elements. Adding in the exotic location, which the film makes the best possible use of, and it is a gorgeous film that is a great time to watch. An adaptation of the Broadway musical, it is the story of how one woman who was abused and mistreated her whole life was able to rise through her simple good nature and loving spirit. The songs are amazing. The visuals stunning. When it needs to be brutal it is unflinching, but it still rises up to a glorious ending. Greta Gerwig managed to make a toy IP cash grab into one of the most interesting and provocative films of the year. Barbie, who lives in Barbieland where everything is wonderful all the time, is plagued by uncontrollable thoughts of death. And has to travel to our world in order to find the person who is playing with her and fix her life. Along the way Ken discovers the concept of the patriarchy. It’s extremely funny, while also being profoundly deep. And also working as the most basic introduction to feminism. Not to mention how incredibly stylish and lavish everything looks. The sets alone are amazing. Who knew a three hour movie about security clearances could possibly be this enthralling? Utilizing multiple timelines, as he does, Christopher Nolan explores the life of Robert Oppenheimer and how he become the person who coordinated the Manhattan Project. Visually it is an impeccable film. The explosion of the test bomb is glorious. And the performances were spectacular. Just a great movie. A horror comedy about a group of college friends who have a reunion at a cabin in the woods, and are forced to play an extremely racist board game by a crazed killer. It’s just really funny. Really, really funny. When his mom is diagnosed with dementia, a literary professor writes a parody of inner city ghetto fiction, under an alias, which winds up being a stunning success. Far more successful than any of his other books. It’s a fascinating film about both the need to sell out, and being resentful of selling out. Every time he attempts to derail his own book, which is something that happens frequently, it only makes him more successful. And he really does need the money. Alongside that story is a really heartfelt family story about tragedy, growth and acceptance. And the ending is brilliant. This film set a new bar for what animation is capable of. I watched a lot of gorgeously animated films, several of which barely missed out on this list… but nothing was this creative and astounding. And the story is so grim, and sorrowful. Once more the characters really shine as some of the most humane portrayals to ever grace a superhero film. It’s just brilliant. The original Godzilla is one of my favorite films, it is nothing short of a masterpiece. And Godzilla Minus One is as good as it. It’s so good. It’s a very profound movie about the effect that war has on both a person and a country. As well as a rebuke of governments who hold human life with little value. While also being an amazing Godzilla film. It’s unbelievably good. And there you have it. That’s me and my extremely eclectic taste.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What are your thoughts on the trailer for "X-Men ’97"?
Answer: I am very excited about it. I have some things I am more tentative about. But I am cautiously optimistic about the show. It is a good trailer, giving away exciting moments and giving you a hint of what storylines are going to come, while still keeping most things close to the chest. The trailer opens with an extended bit showing an old school TV playing the series finale of X-Men the animated series. From everything I have heard about this project, it is being helmed by people who were all fanatical fans of the original cartoon. And this opening is very much attempting to convey that while the animation transition might not be seamless between the fifth season and X-Men ‘97, the writing transition will hopefully be. It recaps where things stood in the finale, setting up the new status quo for the season. Our first real shot is Calisto and Leach huddled in an alleyway. Part of the problem of doing allegorical stories about racism is that they usually collapse into nonsense. The Morlocks were introduced early in the first season, and the show used them very effectively to be the victims of various mobs. Not every mutant is Jean Grey. Lots of references to Spider-Man in this shot. I think attempting to fit in a cameo from the Spider-Man the animated series in the first season might pull too much focus, but really hope it happens in a potential season two. Okay this is the Hellfire Gala, which they are calling “The Hellfire Gala.” In the original show, the Hellfire Club was only ever referred to as “The Inner Circle.” This shows that they are going to do storylines from the more recent X-Men comics, which I am a little weary of. But we can see Banshee, Dust, and Nature Girl, along with two others that I am a little unsure of. There is a bunch of “Xavier is dead!” stuff, even though Xavier is absolutely not dead. So I assume the X-Men are going to fake Xavier’s death. This is classic X-Men the animated series. That show loved anti-mutant mobs. Out of every adaptation of the X-Men ever made, X-Men was the one most overtly focused on being a show about the poisonous nature of bigotry. And there is a Friends of Humanity sign! The Friends of Humanity were probably the most radical thing the show ever did, as even if they did get wrapped up in sci-fi nonsense, they were just a group of bigots. This is some sort of United Nations group, coming to the mansion, probably to arrest Magneto. This is “The Trial of Magneto” from X-Men #200. I am curious to see where they go with it, as a lot of the stuff that happened in the trial doesn’t apply to cartoon Magneto. Magneto has certainly blown up a lot of stuff but he hasn’t killed anyone. There are several shots of this compound in the trailer. It’s absolutely not the mansion. It’s in a valley. I would think it is the Savage Land. Hey! It’s the team! Morph is here. Morph was never really supposed to be around for longer than his death. He was based on the character “Changling” who died way back in the silver age. But kids loved him. If Morph is elevated to main character status, it will be entirely because the kids are now in charge. Morph’s design is the Morph from Exiles, as opposed to the animated series. Bishop is also here, and Bishop appears a lot in this trailer. Whoever they got to voice Cyclops is really good. I am not sold on the pseudo-mohawk hair design for Storm, but damn, it is exciting to have her back. Hey, it’s Jubilee! I hope they give her more to do than the animated series did. I also hope she keeps her radical ’90s ‘tude. Random dance break! I love that Wolverine is in his civilian clothes, while Gambit and Morph showed up in full X-Men costume. Jean is pregnant! They are finally resolving the Cable’s parentage storyline, which is one of the biggest dangling threads from the original show. X-Men ’97 released a toyline that includes the Goblin Queen, even if she doesn’t appear in this trailer. So I would say the most likely scenario we are looking at is that Mr. Sinister has replaced Jean with a clone. This is the only line of Lenore Zann we get in the trailer. I really, really hope they continue Rogue’s thing where she says absolutely baffling southern aphorisms all the time. Also I could not be more thrilled to see Rogue be super strong and fly again. X-Men the animated series really, really understood that the Sentinels and not Magneto were the X-Men’s archnemesis. It’s a show about bigotry. This is a mutant circuit. Like the Hellfire Gala, this is a modern concept, as opposed to a ’90s one. I suppose the adamantium can’t explode, but it feels like this is more likely to go bad. Will be cool though. Given that the X-Men will now say, “To me, my X-Men” at the drop of a hat now, it is shocking to realize how recent that phrase is. It’s really from the 2000s, and only became the X-Men’s slogan around 2012. This is pure Jim Lee “The X-Men are playing basketball.” Including several outfits lifted directly from Jim Lee’s X-Men playing basketball designs in X-Men #4. I really hope we get X-Men in civilian clothes, because Lee would put them in the most rediculous, over-the-top ’90s fashion. Magneto is taking over the school! I think this plotline is going to not work as well considering there is no New Mutants team in the animated series. With the exception of Jubilee, the X-Men are all fully grown adults, they don’t have to accept Magneto. They can just move out. I bet this is partially why Sunspot is supposedly a big part of this season. I hope this is a proper continuation of the series, and not just indulgent fan service. But I am very excited. I think there are some strong visuals here. I hope they can bring everything together.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Did Disney gain full control over X-Men and Fantastic Four after buying Fox? Is this the reason why there are no current plans for a reboot of these franchises at Marvel Studios?
Answer: Yes. Disney has full ownership of all rights to the X-Men and Fantastic Four in all respects. But that’s not the reason for the delayed plans to reboot them into the MCU. At least delayed until now. When Disney bought Fox, every contract Fox had signed was transferred to Disney. Those contracts are still valid and Disney has to abide by them. When Fox made Dark Phoenix it extended the contracts for all of the actors to, potentially, appear in future films. According to those contracts, Fox (now Disney) can not recast their parts, or even begin to plan a project that will recast their parts. Disney can only proceed with films where those roles are being played by the same actors. That’s why every time the X-Men have appeared so far, it’s been one of the original actors. They can have Patrick Stewart or James McAvoy play Charles Xavier as much as they want. But they can’t have anyone else. And James McAvoy might trigger another contract extension. Disney wants to get new actors under ten year contracts for its big X-Men MCU debut. So they have to wait it out until the original contracts with the original actors expire before they can even start developing a project.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is the general consensus on the quality of the new mutants comic book series?
Answer: It is very good, but the quality varies a lot. For a long, long time New Mutants just wasn’t republished, but now almost all of it has been published in the Epic format, with the final volume due to be published sometime this years. And I recommend getting them all. The New Mutants has a bit of a rough start. It is never actively bad, but never really quite good. It was written by Chris Claremont and is an attempt to get back to the X-Men’s roots as a school. It’s a very Chris Claremont comic…. so, so, so many accents. There are more women than men on the team, there are more people of color than white people on the team. It’s really what Claremont would envision as the team if he started from scratch. They get mixed up in this obscenely long adventure in Nova Roma, which is fake Rome in Brazil. Nova Roma is really over developed, apparently Claremont intended it to be the New Mutants version of the Savage Land or the Shi’ar. But it will never be important again. It just goes on for an interminable amount of time. But it did give us Selene so that makes it worth the trip. The book finally turns the corner when Illyana Rasputina, Colossus’s sister, joins the team in issue #14. That’s the point when everything comes together and becomes amazing. All the most beloved storylines in the New Mutants happens in this stretch of episodes. This is when the Demon Bear Saga happens. It’s when Magneto takes over the school. It’s when Magneto has to turn to Emma Frost to preform telepathic therapy. It’s when Bill Sienkiewicz was doing the most amazing art of his career on the book. The writing is amazing, the art is gorgeous. And it ends with a really fun storyline where the New Mutants attend a party at the Hellfire Club that most consists of people passive aggressively insulting each other. Claremont leaves with issue #54 and is replaced by his editor Louise Simonson who will finish out the hundred issues as the writer. Simonson seemed to struggle a lot. Her first story arc features this bird monster that the New Mutants call “Bird Brain” and they become completely obsessed with. Bird Brain was created by the Ani-Matter who was working for Simonson’s X-Factor villains The Right and Cameron Hodge. And in the process of this whole storyline Cypher gets shot and dies. It is extremely bad. There’s just no way around it. And it really starts the Simonson’s process to slowly disassemble the New Mutants. Simonson is one of the most brutal writers in comics. She can be very good, but her comics are noticeably quite violent and she does not mind absolutely destroying a character. She was the one who really initiated the Death of Superman storyline at DC comics (not her idea, but she was the one who pushed it as doable). And she is the one who turned Angel into Archangel in X-Factor. Simonson’s run genuinely has just about every storyline end with one of the classic New Mutants characters leaving the team, either by being killed off or just moving on. And she eventually replaces them all with characters from her X-Factor run. In X-Factor she had the team take on a motley group of wards who they were training, most notably Rictor and Boom Boom, all those characters were eventually moved to the New Mutants. Once she gets her new cast in place, the New Mutants becomes quite good again, if a very different book. Towards the end of her run Rob Liefeld is brought on as the new artist. He was hot and up and coming at this point, and he increasingly took creative control. This is, by far, the best art he ever produced. But there are pretty significant changes. Cable shows up and eventually takes over the team. They start fighting the Mutant Liberation Front and its leader Stryfe. And the whole book really feels like it is bracing for the switch over from the ’80s to the ‘90s. Sitting down and reading those 100 issues is a good time. You won’t regret it, even in the middle of the Bird Brain arc.

Question: Is Ulysses considered a mutant in the Marvel Universe?
Answer: No. Ulysses was an Inhuman who basically data mined reality in order to make predictions. I will just say upfront I do not like this character, and the event he was a part of, Civil War II, is one of the worst comics Marvel has ever published. The thing they were fighting over goes away so they have no more reason to fight. It sucks so much. Almost as much as Ulysses does. The only good part of the event is Civil War II: X-Men. Question: Which movies and TV shows would you recommend to someone who wants to see a relationship crash and burn?
Answer: The show you need to watch is Crazy Ex-Girlfriend. One of the relationships in that show crashes and burns so badly there’s an actual musical number about it entitled “It Was a Shit Show.” So darling let's not tiptoe This thing we had Was not just bad It was a shit show Crazy Ex-Girlfriend is the story of Rebecca Bunch, a hyper successful corporate lawyer working in New York City.
