Question: How come the Oscars nominate films that have not been released in the theaters that no one can see such as Rustin, short films, docs, and many foreign films? What is the point of nominating stream only films? Why can't anyone get films distributed?
Answer: Here is what the eligibility requirements are for the Academy Awards https://www.oscars.org/oscars/rules-eligibility In order to be eligible for consideration, Academy rules state, “feature films must open in a commercial motion picture theater in at least one of six U.S. metropolitan areas: Los Angeles County; the City of New York; the Bay Area; Chicago, Illinois; Miami, Florida; and Atlanta, Georgia, between January 1, 2023, and December 31, 2023, and complete a minimum qualifying run of seven consecutive days in the same venue. Feature films must have a running time of more than 40 minutes. To be eligible a movie has to play in a movie theater in a major market for a week. The line is blurry, but there are two different release models: wide release and limited release. Wide releases are going to try to be in as many theaters as possible. That's what is playing at your local cinema. Limited release movies target the specific markets that can support them. This is a marketing strategy I despise, but the genre that we can call “Awards Bait” works by very limited releases in order to secure a nomination which is then used as a springboard to a wide release. This year it was American Fiction and Poor Things. Last year it was The Whale and Women Talking. You probably saw The Whale after the nominees were announced and not before. “No one can see them” is actually a reasonably correct assessment. Moonlight famously played in four theaters and only grossed $402,072 prior to its nomination. It only surpassed 1,000 theaters right before the ceremony. Increasing the Best Picture category to ten nominees was a very calculated move on the part of the Academy so that some popular wide release movies people actually watched would get nominated. Meaning this year Barbie got nominated. Even if we all know it will never win. If you are not in one of the largest markets in the country, the Academy will mostly nominate stuff you have never heard of. Streaming films are ineligible for the Academy Awards. They are only eligible for the Emmys. And while, theoretically, an Emmy is as prestigious as the Academy Award, we all know no one treats them that way. If a streaming film is nominated, for example this year Maestro, then it was parked in some theater for a week prior to it debuting on the streaming platform. Maestro played in New York City starting on November 22nd prior to its Netflix debut on December 20th. I think this a bad system that renders the entire awards ceremony too insular. And kind of irrelevant. It obviously works, since it happens every year. But it is extremely condescending to consistently nominate mostly films that only an extremely limited number of people even have the option of seeing. But I think that's why the Academy was so over the moon about Everything Everywhere All At Once last year. It was, by the Academy’s standards, a populist blockbuster while having all the pretentious prestige their membership demands.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Is Wanda Maximoff a mutant? If so, why was she not introduced as one in the X-Men movies or mentioned in them?
Answer: Wanda Maximoff was introduced as a member of the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants. She was apprehended by Sentinels specifically because she was a mutant. She was examined by every expert in biology, and they all believed her to be a mutant. And then a man named Isaac Perlmutter decided that the Fox corporation, by abiding by the contracts Marvel had signed with it, was bilking Marvel out of money. And so he reigned holy hell down on the X-Men and the Fantastic Four, because Fox owned the film rights to those properties. There’s a lot to say about this period of time, but one of the biggest elements of it was several longstanding mutant characters were revealed to not be mutants. In particular Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch. The High Evolutionary just sort of announces that he was lying the entire time. And there is no attempt to explain how this could possibly be true. They have given the Maximoff twins an entirely new origin story that makes zero sense and there’s been no attempt reconcile it with any their history. Their new history, that they are Serbian and descended from a powerful witch… runs into a little problem with the fact that the all powerful demon Chthon has now spent Wanda’s entire life confusing her with the daughter of Magda Lensherr who gave birth to a set of twins, also named Wanda and Pietro, on Mount Wundagore. And we now have just no idea what happened to those twins. Let’s just say I have a lot of questions for Bova. WHAT DO YOU KNOW, BOVA! What house of lies have you built for yourself? This whole story beat basically erases what had become Quicksilver’s entire point as a character, which is that he is the heir to Magneto. It also means that whole “House of M” incident was Wanda doing a hate crime in addition to a genocide. It’s bad. And no one likes it, but it won’t change because the MCU versions of those characters are no mutants. Which leads, from an objective point of view, some ludicrous story beats as they attempt to reverse this story while not reversing it at all. Wanda, you met Magneto as a full grown adult and you hated him. And I could probably count on one hand the number of times you even met Polaris. Officially Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch are not mutants and not the children of Magneto, but also are mutant enough to go through mutant resurrection and are the *spiritual* children of Magneto. Honestly, we just need a retcon that Wanda was futzing around with reality this whole time, and yes they are the mutant children of Magneto. They aren’t mutants in the MCU because, at the time they were introduced, Marvel’s licensing deal with Fox meant that Marvel could not use the word “mutant” or mention “Magneto” in any context. So an alternative explanation had to be created, which was that a rock did it. Fox could have introduced the Scarlet Witch. Due to their peculiar status as both Avengers and X-Men characters, Quicksilver and the Scarlet Witch could be used by both studios. Fox essentially had free reign with the characters, while Marvel had to abide by extremely strict guidelines. But the Scarlet Witch is very unimportant in the X-Men line, historically. After she leaves the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants in X-Men #11 she will never again be on a mutant team. She will show up every so often, but pretty much is strictly an Avengers character. This is in contrast to Quicksilver who has several long periods as a member of a mutant team, most notably X-Factor in the ‘90s. If you were adapting the X-Men for a two hour movie, of even a movie series, Scarlet Witch is likely a character you would skip. Prior to House of M she just isn’t that important. She appeared in all three X-Men cartoons, and in all three they were mostly about her being the daughter of Magneto. If you aren’t giving Magneto children there is no reason to include the Scarlet Witch in anything X-Men related. Peter Maximoff has a sister in X-Men: Days of Future Past and that’s about as much Wanda as was necessary for the whole franchise.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What are some of the best books you read in 2023, and why?
Answer: Well I did read a few books in 2023. I read sixteen books this year, which is actually quite lite for me, but there was a combination of one book I really disliked and struggled to get through and a bunch of extremely long books. Here were the best books among them: This is the best book I have read this past year, by far. And probably the best book to understand what is happening in Israel right now. In 2012 a bus carrying kindergarteners from the West Bank city of Anata on a fieldtrip to a playpark called Kids Land had an accident, overturned, and caught on fire. The book mostly focuses on Abed Salama, the father of a five-year-old boy on the bus, and his attempts to find where his son is. As emergency services simply didn’t show up to the accident, the children were loaded into cars passing by, which were then taken to hospitals all over the area. The Salama family only had green IDs and were restricted to only the hospital in Ramallah, and could not check the hospital in Jerusalem. Jewish American journalist Nathan Thrall expands outward from this accident to interview everyone at the scene, revealing the many fascinating and horrifying details of their lives. It is a book about peace, but a brutal and violent peace where an apolitical accident an untenable political system. It is unbelievably good. Maureen Ryan is one of the most influential TV critics being published today, and Burn it Down is her scathing indictment of the Hollywood system that brutally exploits and abuses people. The book opens with the story of how producer Scott Rudin drove his assistant to suicide… and after that it is just a parade of horrors about how all of your favorite shows were horrible, miserable, exploitative and abusive places to work at. Ryan is significantly less interested in going over the physical and sexual abuse, though she does include a lot of that, as she is in psychological and financial abuse. She considers the Hollywood standby of “well, no one got beat up or sexually assaulted…” to be woefully inadequate. And so the real meat of the book are stories about a showrunner getting angry that a writer’s episode was more popular with the fans than his, and so skipping her when assigning upcoming episode. Or a studio deciding it simply does not like a particular actress that is a co-lead on one of their shows, and so deliberately feeding the press stories to make her look bad. And racism. So, so, so, so very much racism. Ryan does not lack for ways to correct these problems, but as you can tell from the title, she is not overly confident in the efficacy of the system to reform itself. In the early 2000s Ali Davis was the sole woman working at a video rental store which had an extensive collection of adult videos. This book, adapted from her blog (remember when blogs were a thing?) is a collection of all her utterly bizarre experiences. Although perhaps the most bizarre thing is how normalized working with a vast collection of adult videos becomes. There are all sorts of weirdly fascinating details in the book, and it is also wickedly funny. Yes, I read all seven books in The Dark Tower series. When I was in high school I developed a deep love for Stephen King, but even when I was reading The Stand I didn’t read The Dark Tower. And this year I said to myself, “I’m gonna do it. I am going to read The Dark Tower.” Needless to say it took up the bulk of my reading this past year. The Dark Tower is Stephen King’s magnum opus about the Gunslinger Roland’s journey to the Dark Tower that is at the center of his world. And along the way he has to save the entire multiverse. It is Stephen King writing a spaghetti western and also The Lord of the Rings. It’s rich, it’s dense, it’s fantastic. It’s extremely strange. And it is kind of fascinating to watch Susannah go from the least important main character to the most important. Many of the set pieces are unbelievably fantastic. Reading it made me fall in love with Stephen King all over again. So those were the best books I read this year.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Who are some of the strongest villains in the X-Men comics? Is Onslaught considered one of the strongest?
Answer: Onslaught is one of the strongest. Not the strongest, but one of the strongest. If we are counting all people they have ever fought, then the strongest would probably be the Dark Phoenix, but despite Marvel’s insistence otherwise, the Dark Phoenix only ever happened once and is not a regular villain of the X-Men. She is a one time aberration. The strongest person who could be rightly considered one of their rogues gallery is probably the Adversary. The Adversary is an extra-dimensional demonic being of incalculable power. Forge’s shamanic tradition exists entirely to oppose him. And Forge’s mentor Nazé spent most of his life prepping him to fight the Adversary, up until Forge abandoned his tribe to go fight in the Vietnam War. The Adversary took possession of an alien that had taken the form of Nazé and that is his principle form on Earth, which is an extremely complicated story to explain. The Adversary is an incomprehensibly ancient and powerful thing, and only the smallest hint of itself ever manifests on Earth. But that small portion is still apocalyptically bad. The second strongest X-Men villain is probably Jamie Braddock. Jamie is the older brother of longstanding member of the X-Men Betsy Braddock, and Captain Britain. Jamie is a reality warping mutant, but whose power is to manipulate on the quantum level. He sees reality as a series of strings that he pulls and manipulates and reconfigures. He’s also completely insane. Before his powers manifested, Jamie was heavily in debt due to his chronic gambling and got involved in a bunch of illegal activity in Africa. In order to punish him for his many, many, many crimes, he was imprisoned in a house and tortured… for years. Which is where he was found by Sat-Yr-9 who awakened his powers. Jamie is able to manipulate reality on the most basic and fundamental levels, but with a brain that is so broken he doesn’t even know what reality is any more. The third strongest I would probably say is Proteus. Proteus is the son of Moira MacTaggart and is an Omega Level reality warper. But he is also a parasitic being. He is pure psionic energy, and so moves from host body to host body by means of possession. In the process he burns whomever he is possessing out, killing them. He has a vulnerability to metal, and so the metal form of Colossus fatally disrupted him, leaving him dead. At least until the Scarlet Witch remade reality in the House of M which revived him. After Proteus is probably where I would stick Onslaught. And after him would probably the Magus.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is the best book about the origins of war and human nature?
Answer: This is almost certainly not what you are asking for, but it is actually what you should look at. But it is To Start a War by Robert Draper. It’s a book that attempts to explain one of the biggest mysteries of the twenty-first century: why the fuck did America decide to invade Iraq? Draper interviewed hundreds of people in the Bush administration, and paints an extremely compelling case that the organizational structure of that administration allowed two highly motivated individuals (Paul Wolfowitz and Douglas Feith) to drive the entire government into a war. And I can tell you from personal experience that almost every page of the book will make you want to throw it at the wall in blind fury. George W. Bush hated long meetings, he hated arguments. One of Condoleezza Rice’s roles in the administration was to preempt conflict. Rice understood well her boss’s inclinations. President Bush preferred short, orderly meetings, with minimal discursiveness, focused on a single recommendation that had been issued by the team arrayed before him. “He wanted people to do their jobs and come up with a policy,” explained one of Rice’s senior staffers. As Rice herself remarked during one Principals Committee meeting, “If I bring a gross disagreement between cabinet officers to the president, I’ve failed at my job.” In the aftermath of Desert Storm there was a Shiite uprising in Iraq which was brutally suppressed by Saddam Hussain. Paul Wolfowitz, who was at the time Undersecretary of Defense for Policy, argued that the US should intervein in support of the uprising. Which was a side that lost when Norman Schwarzkopf argued that the US would advance no strategic goals by getting involved in the internal affairs of Iraq. Since then Wolfowitz had spent basically the entire time arguing for the US to remove Saddam from power in Iraq. And he had become close, personal friends with a notable crank, Laurie Mylroie. She believed that Saddam was behind the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, and had published a book on it (a book that was fairly easily disproven). By the time 9/11 happened, Wolfowitz had been hammering at the nail of trying to convince the United States to remove Saddam for ten years, and along the way had become a crank about it. In the aftermath, he fervently believed that Saddam was behind the attack, and no one could dissuade him. So, when Wolfowitz began diverting the Bush administration’s meetings to the subject of Iraq, no one was going to argue against him, because Bush would have hated that. Remember that bit about how Bush ran his meetings? Yeah, it’s really important. Within the conflict adverse Bush administration, one particularly willful individual could pull the entire organization off course. He was helped by the fact that Saddam had been behind a failed assassination plot of George Bush Sr., though that is vastly overstating how effective that plot had been. Bush Jr. was still harboring a lot of resentment towards the dictator. So he wasn’t prone to taking the side that would seemingly been of benefit to Saddam. Adding to this was that Donald Rumsfeld, the Secretary of Defense, was just an abrasive, micromanaging human being. He was the kind of person who was a very petty tyrant in his fiefdom. Conflicting opinions were not going to be heard in the Defense Department. And he would welcome anything that made the Defense Department look good at the expense of other agencies. Which often meant attacking and undermining Secretary of State Colin Powell. Colin Powell was the only person who ever advocated that invading Iraq wasn’t a wise course of action. And even that was tentative, and when he did he was shot down by those around him. That was when Powell had argued that going after Iraq would destroy any effort to build a vast post-9/11 coalition. “Then maybe it’s not a coalition worth having” had been Rumsfeld’s rejoinder. His standing in the Bush administration was often weak, with Karl Rove against him because he thought Powell was looking to be president one day. Possibly Primarying Bush. With the administration dragged into believing that invading Iraq was the best course of action, they now needed to build a case for it. That’s where the current under secretary of Defense for Policy, Doug Feith, steps in. Feith, whose father had been a committed Zionist and whose grandparents had been murdered in concentration camps, was an ardent supporter of Israel and believed Saddam to be that country’s greatest foe. At the time the CIA was being iced out of the administration, as Bush expected people to give him what he wanted. And the CIA consistently giving reports that Iraq had nothing to do with Al-Qaeda or 9/11 was not what he wanted. During the same period, Feith held a meeting with several of his senior aides. Quietly, with the door closed, he told them, “We’ve got to find proof that Saddam was involved in this.”60 In the coming weeks, Feith would establish the Policy Counter Terrorism Evaluation Group, a small in-house shop to analyze terrorism-related intelligence—or more to the point, according to one of PCTEG’s members, to be “looking for the connections between Iraq and Al Qaeda.” Of course, this was the CIA’s job. Feith created a fake CIA inside the Defense Department whose sole job was just to figure out how Saddam connected to 9/11. They actually put up a giant sheet of butcher paper on the wall with one end labeled “Osama Bin Laden” and the other “Saddam Hussain” and worked at filling in towards the middle. This was supported by Wolfowitz who had grown very frustrated by endlessly tasking analysts to look for the Al Qaeda-Saddam connection only for them to say there wasn’t one. CIA director George Tenet considered George W. Bush his “first customer” and worked really hard to please him. And he frequently displeased Bush as all the exciting leads of a connection between Iraq and Al Qaeda proved to be illusory. In response Tenet created a task force known as the Red Cell whose job was literally just to speculate, or in the parlance of the administration “outside the box thinking.” Very crucially the Red Cell included no one whose area of expertise was the Middle East or counterterrorism. During its first week, the Red Cell produced a document for the Principals Committee speculating about Saddam’s involvement in 9/11. Departing from the standard CIA treatment, the Red Cell paper acknowledged “unanswered questions” and “tried to develop the strongest case for Iraqi involvement,” recalled a Cell member. The Red Cell plan worked, as the administration, in particular Dick Chaney, was extremely pleased with their, again, speculation. Which was bolstered by the CIA giving the administration more raw intelligence. Basically just rumors that no one had checked yet. Bush, in seemingly inverse proportion to his pre-9/11 detachment, was now immersed in reports of suspected terrorist activity. In addition to the Presidential Daily Briefing furnished by the CIA, the FBI now supplied the president with a daily threat matrix. The intelligence in it was raw, closer to rumor than to fact. This started a very depressing cycle where some tantalizing evidence would emerge, someone would be dispatched to check it out, and everything would be debunked. But the administration would not accept the debunking. It happened over and over and over. For example, German intelligence had interviewed an Iraqi source they called “Curveball” who claimed he built mobile biological laboratories. When they heard about this, it obviously excited the administration. However, what Curveball described was, in fact, a mobile pharmaceutical vehicle that was manufactured in Spain whose plans were posted on the internet. Also posted on the internet were speculative UN-SCOM documents that laid out all the details Curveball’s story. And finally the Germans talked to the individual who was supposedly Curveball’s boss on the project and he flatly denied the whole thing. Curveball, the amazing source who solved all the mysteries of how Iraq could have a biological weapons program that left no trace, was just a guy with an internet connection. The administration refused to accept the conclusion that Curveball was obviously faking. And they went in front the UN to talk about mobile biological weapons. This happened many times. The administration was, in essence, manufacturing evidence that they, themselves, were the most fervent believers of. They spent all day stewing in speculation about Iraq, because that’s what people kept giving them, because that’s what they kept demanding. I realize this question is probably meant to be about how humans evolved into beings who commit wars… but if you want a book on how wars start… read To Start a War. Wars require a massively complex bureaucracy with many different personalities to move in one specific direction. How do wars originate? This is how they originate. It’s distressing, to use an understatement, to learn that the Iraq War was mostly a product of bad bureaucratic management. But if you want to learn about the human nature that drives war… that’s the human nature. Robert Draper takes a massive cast of individuals and really shows how their personal foibles drove the US into what remains a completely pointless war. Read the book. It’s fantastic.

Question: I have forgotten about Finn in Star Wars. What was the point of his story again?
Answer: The point of Finn’s story in Star Wars was that Storm Troopers were human beings and not faceless mooks. You were supposed to feel horror at the fact that every time they kill a Strom Trooper in the original series they were killing a unique sentient human being who had never been given the chance to be anything other than the front line of a fascist state. It should have been what a lot of the clone storylines were in the TV show The Clone Wars. By deeply humanizing many different clones, it ultimately made the events of Revenge of the Sith far more tragic. But, honestly, they couldn’t even maintain that for the film that introduced the concept. Because even Finn himself treated every other Storm Trooper as cannon fodder in the very movie that introduced him. Ultimately the heroes needed to shoot people without pausing the action to acknowledge that it was all really tragic. Luckily the big secret that Finn was trying to tell Rey in Rise of Skywalker was never revealed. Because if J.J. Abrams concept that he was Force sensitive was true, then it would completely undo the only good thing about his storyline, which was that he was just a normal Storm Trooper. That he was special. Better than. Superior. And that he couldn’t have been just any regular Storm Trooper and all of them could have been him.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What do you think about the fact that the new Wednesday Addams TV series is partially blatantly copied from Harry Potter?
Answer: It’s blatantly copied from the X-Men. It has Harry Potter overtones, but the core of the show is the X-Men. It’s just the X-Men. Wednesday is about a special school where unique individuals, most of whom have special powers, go to study in an effort to protect them from a world which hates and fears them. That’s… the X-Men. These special people are called “outcasts” who frequently suffer the bigotry of the normal people around them. Everyone, within the universe of the show, knows werewolves exist. Wednesday is a show about the conflict normal people (for lack of a better term) and outcasts. That’s the core of the show, it’s something that comes up in every episode. I suppose it is a minor spoiler, but that’s what the entire plot of the show is about. The show’s villain's plan is just a minor variation on every genocidal human villain in the X-Men. Instead of a giant robot it’s just… well you can watch the show and find out. The Harry Potter influences are most aesthetic and are very shallow. There’s a school (there’s also a school in the X-Men). There are four main species (this is something very emphatically stated in the first episode and then is basically never important again). There’s some intra-school games. They wear uniforms. There’s a botany class. The teachers can be shady. Most of it is either really generic, or very shallow. And the core conflict of Wednesday is very explicitly not the conflict of Harry Potter. But the core themes of the show are lifted directly from the X-Men. The set up of the show is directly the X-Men. It isn’t surprising, given that the X-Men is ripped off all the time. Including previously by Tim Burton (I see you Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children).

Name: Johan Torres
Question: How is She-Hulk different from other Hulks? Is she known for her intelligence?
Answer: She-Hulk is extremely intelligent. Her field of expertise, the law, is just not a particularly flashy field, so she really doesn’t get credit for how smart she is. Plus her cousin is in the top ten geniuses in the Marvel Universe, so she gets a little over shined. But it really isn’t her intelligence that makes her different. She isn’t even the smartest gamma mutate. The gamma mutation process takes subconscious desires, insecurities, fears, and emotions and manifests them into reality. A Hulk will be whatever is going on inside the person’s psychology. That’s why gamma mutates shift a lot. And why the most volatile gamma mutate, Bruce Banner, has so many alternate forms. Jennifer Walters was a mousy law student who had no friends and no social life. No one even knew she existed. She was the kind of person who is extremely unremarkable and unmemorable. When Bruce gave her that blood transfusion she transformed into the center of attention. She became the most glamorous, gregarious, vivacious, and fun person that anyone could ever meet. What makes She-Hulk different from the other Hulks is that she is the fun Hulk. Jennifer loses none of her intelligence when she is She-Hulk, instead certain aspects of her personality get heightened. It’s been compared to being drunk. She is more impulsive, more willing to take risks. But still has all of her shrewd intelligence. She’s perfectly functional, perfectly rational, and doesn’t experience any of the disassociation that Bruce does. It’s why Jennifer has wanted to stay as She-Hulk at all times. She-Hulk is one of Marvel’s most interesting characters. And whenever they futz around with her core personality and traits it always results in a bad She-Hulk story.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What do you think of the movie I.S.S.?
Answer: It was fun, short, and very silly. It is not amazing science-fiction, but for being a fairly simple movie set in space it was a really good time. I.S.S. is set on the International Space Station where American astronauts, Foster, Campbell, and Bennett, and Russian cosmonauts, Vetrov and brothers Nicholai and Alexey Pulov, are working together on various scientific pursuits. Foster is the most recent astronaut, and she is studying growing synthetic organs with lab mice. Except that her mice went mad from being in too confined a space and attacked each other. Which is absolutely not foreshadowing. Foster is in the window that faces the Earth, when she sees a series of explosions across the continental US. The I.S.S. is out of communication with the Earth for awhile, but Bennett receives a communique that a nuclear war has broken out between the United States and Russia, and the I.S.S. is considered of paramount strategic importance. They are given the orders to take the station by any means necessary. They quickly work out that the Russians likely have the same orders. That’s when the space madness takes hold. I love a good space madness story, and, honestly, there was a nuclear war on Earth and the characters have no idea what’s going on, is one of the better premises. Better than Sunshine’s which was flying too close to the sun (wait, am I just now figuring out that that film is about the myth of Icarus?). People murdering each other in space is always a fun time. At ninety-six minutes, the film is very short. And it really feels like it could have used two more characters to up the body count. Once the murder starts up, things move extremely fast. I.S.S. is fun. It’s not particularly deep. And someone gets a screwdriver to the neck, how can you hate that?

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why is Captain Christopher Pike only a secondary, background character in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds? What happened to the Capitan? Why is he mostly portrayed as "meek, barefoot and in the kitchen"?
Answer: Has Captain Pike ever been barefoot? As far as in the kitchen goes, Pike liking to cook gives an excuse for various characters to gather informally. Similar to the poker games on The Next Generation. And any combination of characters can gather as, they would be there by invitation. It also gives Pike an excuse to be in scenes he, by all rights, shouldn’t. There’s no reason for Pike to be at Spock’s V'Shal dinner, except he made the food. It also allows for a degree of familiarity. In “Those Old Scientists” when Boimler and Mariner are brought to speak to Pike, he is cooking. Which shows they aren’t really in trouble, as he isn’t in professional captain mode. Despite, technically disciplining them, he is also letting his guard down in that conversation… which also allows them to let their guard down. Pike’s love of cooking is a great character trait, and one which has allowed for a lot of opportunities in the show. As far as meek goes. Pike was willing to drop dead from oxygen deprivation in the middle of a lawyer’s office, if she didn’t help him. That doesn’t seem very meek. Pike is diplomatic, he’s also funny, and he’s extremely sensitive. He’s possibly the most empathetic captain they have ever had. The Federation kept the Enterprise out of the war with the Klingons in order to ensure that if they lost, there would still be something to ensure their ideals lived on. So Pike isn’t battle-hardened, but he isn’t meek. And, behind the scenes, Anson Mount was a brand new father when Star Trek: Strange New Worlds was filming its second season. He asked the production to pull back on his workload in order to be with his child. And you can tell, at least in the first half of the season, they are trying to work around his availability. He actually hired a lawyer in the trial episode, instead of deciding he was qualified to be a lawyer like Benjamin Sisko did. [It] came from the necessity of Anson just had a baby, and he needed to spend time with his kid. So we knew that, of course, and we had nine months to prepare for that, so our showrunners wrote an episode that kicked the door down in terms of fun and action, and really leans heavily on what makes these other characters so awesome. Strange New Worlds has a strong enough ensomble that they can let the person who is, ostensibly, the lead spend time with his family and allow all the other characters to take the center for a spat of episodes.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What are Emma Frost's powers? Does she use them to try and take over the X-Men? Why or why not?
Answer: Emma Frost’s main power is telepathy. She is considered one of the five most powerful telepaths on Earth, and its probably the best at combat telepathy. She was considered a suitable host for the Phoenix Force, back when it only picked telepaths. And her genes were used to create a telepathic superweapon. She is powerful enough that Wolverine, who was in a different state, just thought a question very hard at her and she called him with an answer in minutes. Her secondary mutation is to transform into an organic diamond that is roughly the equivalent of Colossus’s organic steel form. In this form she has super strength and rediculous durability. She can essentially tank any hit. She can not access her telepathy in this form, but she is completely immune to all telepathy. Due to a flaw in the form she also can not feel any emotions while in diamond form. She does take over the X-Men, but that’s mostly because no one else was there to lead them at the time. Jean was dead, Xavier was in Genosha, Storm was in Tokyo, Cyclops was crying over his wife dying (again). And honestly, the structure of the X-Men is such that more or less anyone can start up an X-Men team whenever they want. The X-Men break on ideological lines all the time. You just say, “To me, my X-Men” and bam, you’ve taken over an X-Men team. But really her main superpower is just being really, really ridiculously rich. As in so rich it has become a running joke how rich she is. Just Scrooge McDuck levels of rich.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Theories: What could have happened to the MCU's X-Men? And do you think they are the same Fox cast or the ones that will be presented in the future?
Answer: Honestly, I probably wouldn’t have bothered with an explanation of why the X-Men weren’t involved in any of the MCU stuff up until now. But if I had to explain it… I would simply say any of the precognitive mutants (Destiny, Blindfold, Legion, Betsy Braddock) or any of the time travelers (Cable, Bishop, Rachel Summers, Hope Summers) had simply told everyone of importance that all the nonsense that has gone on in the MCU up until now was going to be resolved without their assistance. And that it was far, far, far more important to prepare for the emergence of genocidal robots than bother with any of that. “I see… Iron Man snapping his fingers and everything is resolved adequately.” Depending upon which characters you use, the X-Men have the advantage of having partial knowledge of the future. This is actually thematically important to the X-Men, within the franchise it is important to show where choosing fear and hate leads. One of the brilliant things the Krakoa era of X-Men comics sets up is that the Sentinels always win. The end of every timeline is always machine dominance of Earth. Give that information to the right characters and nothing that has happened in the MCU so far merits consideration (outside of maybe assassinating Tony Stark before he ever creates the Iron Man armor). And they are absolutely not going to use the Fox cast. If they wanted to use the Fox cast they would have already started making a movie with them.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why are only mutants able to use their abilities in the movie "X Men" when they come of age?
Answer: There are mutants who are born with active powers. They are special branch called “changlings.” But the problem with powers at birth is that is when a human is most vulnerable. This is probably best illustrated by Mystique chucking Nightcrawler down that waterfall. Mystique can protect herself from those villagers. Nightcrawler can't. And that's what happened to most of the changlings. Overwhelmingly they got weeded out of the gene pool. If mutation is delayed until a point at which the mutant is capable of surviving independently, meaning puberty, then it is way more likely to live and to have children. There are a relative handful of changlings in the comics: Multiple Man, Nightcrawler, Apocalypse, Selene, Meggan, and Cable all off the top of my head. But in a lot of these cases you see, specifically, why delaying activation of mutants abilities until puberty would be advantageous. Nightcrawler and Apocalypse both had people trying to kill them at birth. And Meggan was locked up for most of her life with her family thinking she was a monster. Only Selene, whose tribe considered her a goddess manifested, wasn't in danger from birth.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: If you were hired by FOX or MARVEL to create an X Men movie franchise, what would your approach be?
Answer: No one would let me do this… but… here is what I would do with the X-Men: This would be a TV show, It’s the most interesting group of characters in the entire franchise. It would be part Game of Thrones, part Succession, part House of Cards. It’s a group of people attempting to ensure a nation’s survival from the menace of genocidal robots, but also all of them have ulterior motives. With all the backstabbing and power plays that entails. This will be self-contained and not in continuity with any other series. This would also be a TV show, and also not in continuity with anything else. It would be a procedural crime drama. But the characters would all be ex-superheroes who basically washed out of the job. A group that largely doesn’t really have much in the way of life skills and doesn’t have anything better to do. This would be a movie. It would be sort of the opposite of Black Panther. It would be about Africa from the perspective of a homeless teenager. Looking at problems, while also really showcasing resiliency and beauty. Storm is, obviously, extremely tied to nature, and so there would have to be a lot of real, practical, not CGI created shots of Africa. It would be Storm vs. the Shadow King, as she attempts to flee Cairo and travel to her mother’s homeland of Kenya. This would be a period film set in 1859 where Mystique has to prevent the premature rise of Apocalypse. I would want it to go full Penny Dreadful, and just be as rediculous and over-the-top as possible. Bring in everyone. The Hellfire Club, Destiny, Selene. Have the origin of Mr. Sinister. You know there is an entire miniseries about Apocalypse and Dracula having a blood feud in London in the 1800s. Pull ideas from that. It’s the Oscar-bait movie! It’s a very serious drama about Magneto hunting down Nazi war criminals in the aftermath of World War II. It’s based on the story “I, Magneto” from Classic X-Men #19. And then he eventually discovers the existence of Operation Paperclip, which causes him to lose his faith in humanity (specifically, not mutants). It’s meditative, it’s dark, it’s somber. Wolverine is the most popular X-Man. There’s no way Wolverine isn’t getting his own movie series. But in my version, he’s paired with Jubilee. The most flippant and irreverent choice. Possibly also Kwannon, too. Really make it the team from the Lady Mandarin arc from X-Men #257, and just be the most bananas and unstable team possible. I don’t know what they are doing, probably fighting Omega Red. But Jubilee eats a lot of chilli dogs and blows a lot of bubbles with her gum. And the big finale is set in a mall. Possibly set to the song “Let’s Go to the Mall” from Canadian icon Robin Sparkles which is, now, also owned by Disney. In fact, the whole movie should just be a real ’80s vibe. So, in an ideal world, we would be doing a two part Captain Britain movie filmed back to back adapting the Alan Moore comics. But that would absolutely not be what Alan Moore wants. Instead what we will be adapting is the “Ghost of Braddock Manor” where Jamie Braddock attacks Excalibur in the middle of a party. And since Kwannon will be in Wolverine, Betsy will be here, replacing Rachel. Because as much as I love Rachel… she would be a nightmare to explain even in a TV show, let alone a movie. The vibe for this movie is horror comedy. Bad things are happening, but also silly things. And here’s the big, main event. The big X-Men movie. The in-continuity movie that is the tentpole of the entire franchise. The team in the movie would be the Extinction Team from Uncanny X-Men vol. 2. With a few swapouts. I’d switch Danger for Angel, specifically, because the plan if for a trilogy. Because Angel loses his wings in this movie, attempts suicide in the next one (with everyone believing he is successful), and we will be doing the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse in movie three. But the antagonist in this film will be Genosha. Magneto will come to the conclusion that the entire concept of the X-Men and the ideology they stand for is hopelessly flawed, and leave at the film’s end. It would be an extremely different team, with an extremely different vibe from the Fox films, but one very grounded in the themes of the X-Men. I would love nothing more than expanding any of these pitches into a full treatment. But Marvel studios would never do any of these ideas. Even if they absolutely should.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What if the reason behind Generation X is that they read Stephen King books way too young?
Answer: Generation X is super messed up, and with as large (if not larger) perception gap between who they are and who they think they are as the Boomers. But none of that is due to Stephen King. He certainly isn't the reason Generation X has been memed into one long scream for the manager. As Zack Budryk noted, Stephen King is the first pretty ubiquitous adult author that Generation X (and Millennial!) kids would encounter who actually wrote something they'd be interested in. Even if your parents didn't have a Stephen King book, someone was. And King wrote about sex and violence and monsters and scary stuff. If you are thirteen are you really going to want to read a John Grisham novel or the novel about a monster clown that kills kids? I can say from personal experience that it was really easy to go from Goosebumps and Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark to Carrie. Carrie was the first Stephen King novel I read, and anyone who knows me knows I am still deeply obsessed with that story. But anyone who has read King knows that kids are, if anything, getting a lot of great lessons from him. Fundamentally all of his novels are about perseverance in the face of insurmountable adversity. You can kill the demonically evil clown, you can kill the master vampire. And sure, you might die along the way, but you can defeat the Anti-Christ even in his Las Vegas stronghold. No, it wasn't King who messed up Generation X. Ronald Reagan is a far more likely culprit. In America if you ever ask, “why is this thing fucked up?” the answer will almost always be either slavery or Ronald Reagan…. and frequently both. And Generation X got the full force of Reaganism blasted in their face for their entire childhood/adolescence. Generation X is a generation that could probably have used more Stephen King books and fewer attempts to destroy unions.

Question: Are actors like Brad Pitt or DiCaprio are overwhelmingly attractive on their own, or they somehow attractive because they are already famous? Would they still be considered hot if they were just ordinary businessman, Truck Drivers, Janitors?
Answer: They would, most likely, still be considered attractive. But they wouldn’t have access to the best dieticians and personal trainers in the world. They wouldn’t have hair and makeup people. They wouldn’t have stylists. They wouldn’t have amazing dermatologists and estheticians. And, let’s be real here, they wouldn’t have the best (and most discrete) plastic surgery. If they weren’t famous, they’d probably be attractive for their age. Not attractive for any age. Depending upon all sorts of life choices. Hollywood is so good at this that Brad Pitt was a smoker until 2022 (and still might be). Smoking, of course, leads to premature aging. It and tanning are the worst things a person can do if they want to keep looking youthful. There’s nothing natural about celebrities, even when they are just walking around. There is an obscene amount of work put into keeping them looking like that.

Question: Why do Democrats want to raise taxes? Don't they know that people don't like paying taxes and will vote them out of office?
Answer: The funny thing is that a political party raised your taxes… but it wasn’t the Democrats. The law they passed initially lowered taxes for most Americans, but it built in automatic, stepped tax increases every two years that begin in 2021 and that by 2027 would affect nearly everyone but people at the top of the economic hierarchy. All taxpayer income groups with incomes of $75,000 and under — that’s about 65 percent of taxpayers — will face a higher tax rate in 2027 than in 2019. In order to pay for the permanent corporate tax cuts, the Republicans raised your taxes. But they did it in a sneaky way. They specifically raised them after the 2020 election. So they wouldn’t get blamed for people’s taxes going up, and if they lost the White House they could blame the Democrats for their own tax law. If you noticed a massive hike in your taxes around that time, and I certainly did, it was Trump who raised your taxes.

Question: What does Westworld have to say about race and ethnicity?
Answer: The most interesting thing that Westworld says about race and ethnicity is in how the park itself treats race. Westworld is about a theme park populated by robots that allows guests to playact being in the Old West. And, as is to be expected, the park is unbelievably racist. Extremely racist in really obvious ways. Eh, they want a strong-but-silent type. Something brutal. Dehumanized. They probably want the guests to feel better when they're kicking his ass. -Westworld Designers making a Native American character The design team for Westworld creates an entire “tribe” of Native Americans (the Ghost Nation) whose sole characteristic is to be savages. The whole point of the park is that it is a theme park version of the Old West, and what would the Old West be without its savage Indians? They take an actual culture, something that really exists, and create an artificial version of it (as in they are literally robots). A caricature of real history, real spiritual beliefs, real culture, expressly for the purpose of creating a profitable theme park. This is something that crops up over and over and over throughout the show. The Hispanic characters are all banditos. And there is a very brief scene set in The Raj. And wow… the Raj…. The Raj is one of Westworld’s sister parks. And it is set in the British colonial period of India, where the guest get to live out the fantasy of being a British citizen colonizing India. Complete with lots of extremely deferential Indian servants. It’s the most on the nose thing in the entire show. Another one of the parks is Shogunworld, where guests can live out their Japanese fantasies. But a core problem with Shogunworld is that all the characters and plotlines of Shogunworld were just lifted directly from Westworld. They’ve just been slapped with a Japanese aesthetic. It’s very intentionally the shallowest possible engagement with Japanese culture and history. To the people making the parks, race and ethnicity are just a way to spice up the park with something exotic. There is no attempt to engage with the cultures they are ripping off, just to exploit them for cash. And it is a very specific style of racism, it’s the racism of Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom. It is racism as a corporate product. Racism that makes for a fun adventure and bums people out if you mention it. Explicitly textually they say they are making the park racist (though not using that word), because that would be more fun for the guests. The parks we keep seeing are historical parks, but not like actual history. They are history as tourist trap. They are, quite literally, what an elderly white man would think is fun. And the main person aiding in creating these parks is a white guy edge lord. The main guest we meet is a white guy. But what gets really interesting is that voice of the corporation, the person who is on the board, is a black woman. These are the people in charge of Westworld Charlotte Hale is profoundly interesting, because while Robert Ford is an artist, and Lee Sizemore is hack artist, Charlotte is a capitalist. The park is a product to her, and the park is not even the main product, it is the means to get to the main product. Much of her storyline in the first season is playing the creative people off each other in order to advance her own financial interests. She could not give less of a shit about any of the problematic elements within the park. She even very explicitly indulges in them. Cornel West has a saying, “We’ve tried black faces in high places.” A black capitalist is not going to fix the myriad of problems in the park, simply because she is black. She has already signed onto the entire project, she is already a part of the problem. Charlotte is a symptom, not a savior. She has no solidarity, and over two seasons consistently exacerbates every problem rather than attempts to fix them. It is revealed that the first host to gain sentience was, in fact, one of those savage Indians, whose sole purpose was to be evil and then get killed by the guests. He was so overlooked that he lived out nine years in the park, without anyone realizing he was off his game loop. He had been spreading sentience to other hosts, but since they were mostly the Native Americans, no one even noticed, because no one gave a shit about the Native Americans in the park. The people making the park created a marginalized group for spice and decoration, and then proceeded them to marginalize them so completely they didn’t even realize they became self-aware. Westworld very rarely directly comments on race. The comments about wanting dehumanized Native Americans are among the very few direct mentions of race. But race is ever present on the show. It’s a show that is conscious about the commodification of race, and presents it in all of its horror. It is intentionally presenting the parks as tawdry and then asking you to extrapolate out from there. Like, one of the parks is literally colonial India, where you play a colonist.

Question: The woke BBC strikes again. Not only does Dr Who turn black but so does his assistant as Millie Gibson is replaced by Varada Sethu. Any white person still watch this trash?
Answer: They are currently filming Ncuti Gatwa’s second series, not his first. Millie Gibson will be in every episode of his first series, which is already completed. She will also be in three episodes of the second series. This report specifically comes from the Daily Mirror, but according to Deadline, this particular reporter has sources inside the Doctor Who production team. No one has officially commented on why she was dropped, other than that apparently Russell T. Davies made the ultimate decision. But Ncuti Gatwa made what appears to be a very pointed Instagram story when the news broke. We do not know what is behind the change. I certainly can’t do anything other than speculate. But I can tell you that this news story reads pretty closely to many, many, many other news stories where something happened behind the scenes that we won’t learn about until a decade or two from now. Just like on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, or Lost, or Sleepy Hollow. And, in fact, Doctor Who. Read basically any interview with Christopher Eccleston where he is asked about coming back to Doctor Who. Read Eccleston’s thoughts about Russell T. Davies, specifically. I am consistently amazed at how anti-woke people are completely, single-mindedly obsessed with the entertainment industry, and yet abjectly refuse to learn how it actually works. You would be able to talk about these things with so much more sophistication if you read Burn it Down by Maureen Ryan, than just regurgitating forum messages about NewsMax articles.
